Covers De Theologia I-XLIII, De Fide I-XXII, De Authoritate Scripturae Pars I through XLVII, Pars II through XXXV, Pars III through XLI, and Pars IV through VIII (adversaries' first argument: Scripture cannot prove Scripture; retorsion; first-principle reply; Spirit efficacy; divinity marks). source_text:
I. THEOLOGIA, juxta vocis etymon, significat sermonem de Deo. Et sumitur in genere pro omni doctrina quae agit de Deo rebusque divinis. Itaque, cum de Deo duobus modis agi possit: primò ex principiis naturali lumine notis: deinde ex principiis, quae modo supernaturali a Deo patefacta sunt: hinc quoque duplex solet distingui Theologia: Una, scilicet, Naturalis: Altera Supernaturalis.

II. Theologia naturalis vocatur pars illa Philosophiae, quae de ente immateriali et Deo praecipue tractat. Sic Aristoteles ipse Metaphysicam appellat libro primo Metaphysicorum. Theologia vero supernaturalis est doctrina illa de Deo, quae a revelatione divina ortum habet. Et haec Theologia absolute dicitur et antonomasticè. Et de hac sola nobis deinceps est agendum.

III. Porro, duplex est habitus qui revelatione nititur, unus quo simpliciter credimus et amplectimur quae verbo Dei continentur. Et hic habitus non est aliud quam fides ipsa: Alter quo quis aptus ea quae fides credit, distincte explicare, variisque rationibus asserere et vindicare, et inde legitimas deducere consequentias. Et hic habitus proprie Theologia dicitur.

IV. Theologia autem sic sumpta se habet ad fidem, sicut scientia ad intelligentiam. Etenim fides est habitus principiorum: Theologia vero habitus conclusionum. Fidei primarium et praecipuum objectum sunt veritates quaedam a Deo immediate et expresse revelatae. Theologiae vero proprie objiciuntur, quae mediate et virtualiter tantum revelata sunt, id est, quae a primis illis immediate revelatis per discursum colliguntur. Itaque Theologia, licet a fide distinguatur, fidem tamen praesupponit, et quodammodo includit. At vero fides non necessario secum trahit Theologiam.
english: Theology, by the etymology of the word, means speech about God. Taken generally, it names every teaching that treats of God and of divine things. And because God can be treated of in two ways — first from principles known by the natural light, then from principles which God has made known in a supernatural manner — a twofold theology is commonly distinguished: one natural, the other supernatural.

Natural theology is that part of philosophy which treats chiefly of immaterial being and of God. Aristotle himself calls metaphysics by this name in the first book of the Metaphysics. Supernatural theology, however, is that teaching about God which has its origin from divine revelation. This theology is called theology absolutely and by antonomasia. It is of this alone that we must treat from here on.

Further, the habit that rests on revelation is twofold. One is that by which we simply believe and embrace what is contained in the word of God; and this habit is nothing other than faith itself. The other is that by which a person is fitted to explain distinctly the things that faith believes, to assert and defend them with various reasons, and from them to draw legitimate consequences. This habit is properly called theology.

Theology, taken in this way, stands to faith as science stands to understanding. For faith is the habit of the principles; theology is the habit of the conclusions. The primary and principal object of faith is certain truths immediately and expressly revealed by God. The proper objects of theology are those revealed only mediately and virtually — that is, those gathered by reasoning from those first immediately revealed truths. So theology, though distinguished from faith, still presupposes faith and in a way includes it. But faith does not necessarily bring theology along with it.

source_text:
V. De Theologia autem in Scholis multa disceptari solent. Sed quae nunc de hoc argumento docere nobis propositum est ad haec capita referentur. 1. Quae sit, et quanta Theologiae necessitas. 2. Quae sit illius natura, ubi in genus ejus et differentiam inquirendum. 3. Denique quae sit Theologiae dignitas, et praestantia supra reliquas scientias.

VI. Quod ad primum attinet, certum est Theologiam per se non esse singulis ad salutem necessariam, id est, non esse necesse, ut omnes qui ad vitam aeternam perveniunt, Theologica sint scientia praediti: in Ecclesia enim omnes non sunt doctores ut docet Apostolus 1. Cor. 12. nec ob id tamen salute privantur. Siquidem ad singulorum salutem sufficit fides, non vero necessario exigitur de rebus fidei plenior et amplior cognitio.

VII. Verumtamen Theologia, hoc est, talis de rebus divinis scientia, quae ipsam fidem tueri, explicare et suadere possit, in Ecclesia necessaria est, ad hoc ut Ecclesia stet et conservari queat, adeoque ut singuli salutem consequantur. Hoc docet Apostolus Ephes. 4. Ubi praeter caetera affirmat Christum in Ecclesia sua doctores instituisse εἰς καταρτισμὸν τῶν ἁγίων ad concinnationem sanctorum et corporis Christi aedificationem: et ne simus pueri qui fluctuemus et circumferamur omni vento doctrinae. Unde patet periculum esse, ne, si doctores in Ecclesia non sint, ejus compages dissolvatur, et aedificium ruat, privatique a fide excedant, multis et variis erroribus abrepti. Praetereaque idem Apostolus Tit. 1. exigit, tanquam conditionem in Episcopo necessariam, ut potens sit exhortari in doctrina sana, et eos qui contradicunt redarguere: quod praestare non potest is, qui in sacris eruditus non est supra fidelium vulgus.
english: Many things are commonly disputed about theology in the schools. But what we now propose to teach on this subject will be referred to these heads: first, what and how great is the necessity of theology; second, what is its nature, where we must inquire into its genus and difference; third, what is the dignity of theology and its excellence above the remaining sciences.

As to the first: it is certain that theology is not in itself necessary for each person unto salvation — that is, it is not necessary that all who come to eternal life be endowed with theological science. For in the church all are not teachers, as the Apostle teaches ([[1 Corinthians 12:29 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 12:29]]); nor are they for that reason deprived of salvation. For the salvation of individuals, faith suffices; a fuller and wider knowledge of the things of faith is not necessarily required.

Nevertheless theology — that is, such a science of divine things as can defend, explain, and commend the faith itself — is necessary in the church, so that the church may stand and be preserved, and so that individuals may obtain salvation. This the Apostle teaches ([[Ephesians 4:11-14 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:11-14]]), where besides other things he affirms that Christ appointed teachers in his church for the perfecting of the saints and the building up of the body of Christ, and so that we may not be children tossed and carried about by every wind of teaching. From this it is plain that there is danger, if there are no teachers in the church, that its frame be dissolved, the building fall, and private persons fall away from the faith, carried off by many and various errors. And the same Apostle requires as a necessary condition in a bishop that he be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict ([[Titus 1:9 >> Bible:Titus 1:9]]) — which cannot be done by one who is not more learned in sacred things than the common run of the faithful.

source_text:
VIII. Et certe nunquam fuit Ecclesia sine talibus viris, qui supra piam et fidelem plebem in rebus divinis doctrina eminerent. Namque olim doctores istiusmodi erant Patriarchae et Prophetae, qui suas habebant scholas et discipulos: qui filii Prophetarum in Scriptura dicuntur. Cujus generis schola fuisse putatur collis Dei qui memoratur 1. Samuel. 10. Et inde accepisse nomen, quod in eo doctrina divina traderetur. Similiter 2. Chron. 34. mentio fit Mishneh, in quo dicitur habitasse Hulda Prophetissa. Quae vox a multis vertitur schola, seu collegium, quod Gallica nostra versio secuta est. Quoniam ex usu linguae Chaldaicae et Rabbinicae radix discere et docere significat. Unde textus Talmudicus Hebraeis dicitur Mishnah quasi doctrinam, seu disciplinam dicas, per quandam antonomasiam.

IX. Post Prophetarum quoque tempora Ecclesia Judaica suos habuit Theologos, qui dicebantur Sapientes, Magistri, et Scribae. Quo titulo Esdras ipse insignitur in libro qui nomen ejus praefert. Et de hoc quoque genere fuerunt, qui dicuntur in Evangelio doctores et periti legis. A quibus Christus clavem scientiae auferens, ipsam tradidit Apostolis, Pastoribusque et Doctoribus, qui pro parte sua sunt eorum successores.

X. Verum praeter Episcopos et Pastores ordinarios, in quibus aliqua saltem exigitur Theologiae cognitio, Ecclesia Christiana jam ab initio suas habuit scholas, et Doctores doctrinam sacram in iis profitentes, et exponentes divinas literas. Inprimis celebris fuit schola Alexandrina, in qua, si creditur Hieronymo, libro de scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis, continua serie fuerant, ab Evangelistae Marci temporibus, ad ipsius usque tempora, Ecclesiastici Doctores. Quorum praecipue memoratur Pantaenus, et, qui eum excepit, Clemens Alexandrinus.

XI. Et certe ex ipsa fidei necessitate Theologicae scientiae necessitas infertur. Fides enim propagari et durare non potest, nisi sint qui fidem doceant, suadeant et tueantur. At non est cujusvis fidelis hoc praestare: sed eorum tantum qui sunt in Scriptura rebusque divinis periti. Itaque ad fidei et Ecclesiae conservationem, et per consequens ad hominum salutem, Theologia necessaria est, hoc est, in Ecclesia necessarij sunt viri rerum divinarum periti, qui fidem in aliis generent, foveant et nutriant: licet non necesse sit ut singuli ita docti et periti sint.
english: And certainly the church never existed without such men, who by doctrine in divine things stood above the pious and faithful people. For of old doctors of that kind were the patriarchs and the prophets, who had their own schools and disciples — those called in Scripture the sons of the prophets. A school of that kind is thought to have been the hill of God mentioned in ([[1 Samuel 10 >> Bible:1 Samuel 10]]). And it is thought to have taken that name because divine teaching was handed down there. Likewise in ([[2 Chronicles 34 >> Bible:2 Chronicles 34]]) mention is made of the Mishneh, in which Huldah the prophetess is said to have lived. That word is translated by many as school, or college, which our French version has followed. For from the usage of the Chaldee and Rabbinic tongue the root signifies to learn and to teach. Whence the Talmudic text is called by the Hebrews the Mishnah, as if you were to say doctrine, or discipline, by a certain antonomasia.

After the times of the prophets also the Jewish church had its own theologians, who were called Wise Men, Masters, and Scribes. With that title Ezra himself is marked in the book that bears his name. And of this same kind were those who in the Gospel are called doctors and experts of the law. From them Christ, taking away the key of knowledge, handed it to the apostles, and to pastors and teachers, who for their part are their successors.

But besides ordinary bishops and pastors, in whom at least some knowledge of theology is required, the Christian church from the beginning has had its own schools, and doctors professing sacred teaching in them and expounding the divine writings. Especially famous was the Alexandrian school, in which, if Jerome is believed in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, there had been in an unbroken series, from the times of the evangelist Mark down to Jerome's own times, ecclesiastical doctors. Of whom Pantaenus is especially remembered, and Clement of Alexandria, who succeeded him.

And certainly from the very necessity of faith the necessity of theological science is inferred. For faith cannot be propagated and endure unless there are those who teach, commend, and defend the faith. But it is not for every believer to do this — only for those who are skilled in Scripture and in divine things. So for the preservation of the faith and of the church, and consequently for the salvation of men, theology is necessary: that is, in the church there must be men skilled in divine things, who generate, foster, and nourish faith in others — though it is not necessary that each person be so taught and skilled.

source_text:
XII. Sic ergo de Theologiae necessitate patet. Jam vero ut quid ea sit, clare et distincte teneamus, primo in genus ejus inquirendum est. Quaeritur ergo primo an Theologia nostra sit scientia. Super qua re dicimus Theologiam scientiam non esse accurate loquendo, et juxta definitionem scientiae ab Aristotele positam. Etenim scientia secundum Aristotelem est assensus evidens: Atqui conclusiones Theologicae non sunt evidentes. Et hoc quia colliguntur ex principiis inevidentibus. Fides enim est habitus principiorum Theologicorum. Atqui fides est habitus inevidens. Nam Apostolus fidem opponit aspectui: 2 Corinth. 5. Per fidem, inquit, ambulamus non per aspectum. Et Hebr. 11. docet fidem eorum esse quae non videntur. Fides, inquit, est rerum quae sperantur substantia, et eorum quae non videntur argumentum.

XIII. Illa autem dicuntur esse evidentia, quae per se intellectum movent ad sui cognitionem, id est, quae seipsa menti suadent et commendant, et luce sua mentem ita feriunt et convincunt, ut non possit non iis assentiri. Quod fidei nostrae mysteriis non convenire palam est. Non sunt enim res per se notae, quarumque veritas ex se menti nostrae se prodat. Sed quod illis assentimur, id facimus propter authoritatem et testimonium Dei, qui ea Verbo suo revelavit et confirmavit.

XIV. Verum hic est distinguendum inter evidentiam consequentis et consequentiae. Conclusiones enim Theologicae non sunt quidem evidentes: sed consequentia tamen, qua ex principiis suis deducuntur, evidens est. Ex praemissis quidem inevidentibus: sed evidenter colliguntur. Exempli causa, Christum esse verum Deum et verum hominem, fidei principium est, quod ex se non est evidens, sed propter solum Dei testimonium creditur. At inde tamen evidenter sequitur in Christo duas esse voluntates, divinam unam et alteram humanam. Ideoque hac in parte Theologiae nihil deest ad veram scientiae rationem.

XV. Licet autem Theologia scientia non sit proprie et stricte loquendo, et juxta scientiae conditiones omnes ab Aristotele positas, nullus tamen est habitus mentis ad quem magis accedat, et ad quem potius debeat revocari. Est enim cognitio certa evidenter deducta ex principiis certis, quae, licet inevidentia sint, non minus tamen certa sunt, quam si essent evidentia. Ideoque recte et convenienter scientia dicitur, nec alio aptiori nomine designari potest.
english: So much, then, is clear about the necessity of theology. But now, that we may hold clearly and distinctly what it is, we must first inquire into its genus. The first question, therefore, is whether our theology is a science. On which we say that theology is not a science accurately speaking, and according to the definition of science laid down by Aristotle. For science according to Aristotle is an evident assent: but theological conclusions are not evident. And that is because they are gathered from inevident principles. For faith is the habit of the theological principles. But faith is an inevident habit. For the Apostle opposes faith to sight: ([[2 Corinthians 5:7 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 5:7]]) — By faith, he says, we walk, not by sight. And ([[Hebrews 11:1 >> Bible:Hebrews 11:1]]) teaches that faith is of things that are not seen. Faith, he says, is the substance of things hoped for, and the argument of things that are not seen.

Now those things are said to be evident which of themselves move the intellect to the knowledge of them — that is, which of themselves persuade and commend themselves to the mind, and by their own light so strike and convince the mind that it cannot but assent to them. That this does not suit the mysteries of our faith is plain. For they are not things known of themselves, whose truth of itself lays itself open to our mind. But that we assent to them, we do because of the authority and testimony of God, who revealed and confirmed them by his Word.

But here a distinction must be made between the evidence of the consequent and the evidence of the consequence. For theological conclusions are indeed not evident: yet the consequence by which they are drawn from their principles is evident. From inevident premises, to be sure — but they are gathered evidently. For example: that Christ is true God and true man is a principle of faith, which of itself is not evident, but is believed because of God's testimony alone. Yet from it it evidently follows that in Christ there are two wills, one divine and the other human. And so in this respect theology lacks nothing toward the true character of a science.

Although, however, theology is not a science properly and strictly speaking, and according to all the conditions of science laid down by Aristotle, still there is no habit of the mind to which it more nearly approaches, and to which it ought rather to be referred. For it is a certain knowledge evidently deduced from certain principles, which, though they are inevident, are no less certain than if they were evident. And so it is rightly and fittingly called a science, nor can it be designated by any more apt name.

source_text:
XVI. Porro Theologia scientia est una specie, non multiplex. Licet enim de rebus valde diversis agat, exempli gratia, de Deo, de Angelis, de homine, de virtutibus et vitiis, quae videntur ad prorsus diversas scientias pertinere, omnia tamen illa in una ratione communi conveniunt, sub qua Theologiae obversantur et objiciuntur. Quae ratio communis est revelatio divina. Ista enim quae dixi non quovis modo cadunt sub Theologi considerationem: sed quatenus per divinam revelationem cognosci possunt. Nam verbi causa, de natura, viribus et officio hominis non docet Theologus quaecunque doceri possunt, sed ea tantum quae ex verbo Dei didicit et collegit.

XVII. Est autem hic notandum, non quaecunque Deus quovis modo revelat ad Theologiae objectum pertinere. Potest enim Deus multis quaedam privatim revelasse, quae non cadunt sub hanc scientiam. Sed hic per revelationem intelligimus illam, quae Ecclesiae toti communis est, et in communem ejus utilitatem est facta, quamque Deus scriptis voluit consignari. Siquidem non ex privatis revelationibus huic aut illi factis, sed ex Scriptura sacra, assertiones suas probare debet Theologus.

XVIII. Porro Theologia non videtur esse scientia mere speculativa, neque mere practica, sed practica simul et speculativa. Et hoc quia Theologia de multis rebus agit, quae spectant ad scientiam tam practicam, quam speculativam. Deum enim contemplatur et mysteria divina, quae sub actionem non cadunt: tum quoque vitae praecepta dat, docetque qui sint mores homine Christiano digni.

XIX. Verumtamen Theologiam censemus potius esse practicam quam speculativam. Siquidem universa Theologia versatur in explicatione, et defensione eorum quae continentur in Scripturis. Atqui doctrina in Scripturis contenta, ex ipsius Dei docentis et revelantis scopo, ad actionem refertur, videlicet ad Dei et proximi dilectionem. Neque doctrinae hujus scopum assecutus est, qui non quaecunque ex verbo Dei didicit, ad finem illum refert. Affirmat enim Christus Matth. 22. legem atque Prophetas pendere ex his duobus mandatis, nempe, Dominum Deum tuum diliges toto corde, et tota anima, et proximum sicut teipsum. Deinde dicit Paulus Rom. 15. Quaecunque scripta sunt ad nostram doctrinam scripta esse, ut per patientiam, et consolationem Scripturarum spem habeamus. Sed praesertim maxime ponderanda sunt ejus verba, 2. Tim. 3. Tota Scriptura divinitus inspirata, utilis est ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad disciplinam quae est in justitia; ut perfectus sit homo Dei, et ad omne bonum opus perfecte instructus.

XX. Huc facit, quod Evangelium ab eodem Paulo dicitur doctrina quae est secundum pietatem, 1 Tim. 6. Hoc enim aliunde non est, nisi quod praecipuus Evangelii scopus, est nos ad pietatem formare. Imo articuli illi qui maxime videntur pertinere ad contemplationem, nimirum de filii Dei divinitate et incarnatione, mysterium pietatis ab Apostolo dicuntur in specie, cap. 3. ejusdem Epistolae. Adde quod Theologicorum principiorum habitus est fides. At vera fides habitus est practicus. Ejusdem vero generis est habitus principiorum, et habitus conclusionum.
english: Further, theology is one science by species, not many. For although it treats of things that are very diverse — for example, of God, of angels, of man, of virtues and vices, which seem to belong to altogether different sciences — still all those things agree in one common formal reason, under which they confront and are objected to theology. That common reason is divine revelation. For the things I have named do not fall under the theologian's consideration in any way whatever, but only insofar as they can be known through divine revelation. For example, concerning the nature, powers, and duty of man the theologian does not teach whatever can be taught, but only those things which he has learned and gathered from the word of God.

Here it must also be noted that not whatever God reveals in any manner whatever pertains to the object of theology. For God may have revealed certain things privately to many persons, which do not fall under this science. But here by revelation we understand that which is common to the whole church, and which was made for its common usefulness, and which God willed to be consigned in writing. For the theologian ought to prove his assertions not from private revelations made to this person or that, but from sacred Scripture.

Further, theology does not seem to be a science merely speculative, nor merely practical, but practical and speculative at once. And that is because theology treats of many things that belong to practical science as well as to speculative. For it contemplates God and the divine mysteries, which do not fall under action; and it also gives precepts of life, and teaches what manners are worthy of a Christian man.

Nevertheless we judge theology to be practical rather than speculative. For the whole of theology is occupied in the explanation and defense of the things contained in the Scriptures. But the teaching contained in the Scriptures, from the scope of God himself who teaches and reveals, is referred to action — namely to the love of God and of neighbor. Nor has anyone attained the scope of this teaching who does not refer whatever he has learned from the word of God to that end. For Christ affirms in ([[Matthew 22:37-40 >> Bible:Matthew 22:37-40]]) that the law and the prophets hang on these two commandments: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself. Then Paul says in ([[Romans 15:4 >> Bible:Romans 15:4]]) that whatever things were written were written for our learning, that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope. But above all his words in ([[2 Timothy 3:16-17 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16-17]]) are to be weighed: All Scripture is inspired by God, and is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for discipline which is in righteousness; that the man of God may be perfect, and thoroughly furnished unto every good work.

To this belongs the fact that the Gospel is called by the same Paul a teaching according to godliness ([[1 Timothy 6:3 >> Bible:1 Timothy 6:3]]). For that is for no other reason than that the chief scope of the Gospel is to form us unto godliness. Indeed those articles which seem most to pertain to contemplation — namely concerning the divinity and incarnation of the Son of God — are called by the Apostle in specie the mystery of godliness, in chapter 3 of the same epistle ([[1 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:1 Timothy 3:16]]). Add that the habit of the theological principles is faith. But true faith is a practical habit. And the habit of the principles and the habit of the conclusions are of the same genus.

source_text:
XXI. Quod ad objectum Theologiae spectat, notandum est, aliquando objectum scientiae dici quicquid scientia quovis modo considerat. Ita Theologiae objectum non est unum. Multa enim et valde diversa considerat, Deum, Ecclesiam, Angelos, Sacramenta. Quae omnia tamen in una communi appellatione conveniunt, quatenus sub Theologi considerationem cadunt. Nam quaecunque tractat Theologus possunt vocari res divinae. Sunt enim, vel Deus ipse, vel alia quae ad Deum aliquo modo ordinantur. Nec quicquam a Theologo proprie consideratur; nisi cum aliquo respectu ad Deum. Itaque, si quis de objecto Theologiae quaerat, non inepte responderi potest, objectum illud esse res divinas.

XXII. Sed ut plurimum objectum scientiae cujuspiam dicitur, id cujus scientia praecipue intendit cognitionem nobis dare, et propter quod cetera omnia considerat: quia, scilicet, ad ejus ampliorem et perfectiorem notitiam conducunt. Hujusmodi objectum Theologiae Deus est, quod plerique omnes fatentur, et docet ipsa Theologiae vox, quae, ut supra notatum est, significat sermonem de Deo: sed non convenit, an illud objectum sit Deus simpliciter, ut Deus est: an vero sub certo aliquo respectu. Prius illud tuentur Scholastici celebriores Thomam Aquinatem secuti, statuuntque objectum Theologiae esse Deum, prout Deus est, atque ut loquuntur sub ratione Deitatis. Verum hoc nobis videtur nimis laxum et generale. Neque scopus Theologiae est nos simpliciter in Dei, ut Deus est, cognitionem ducere; sed de Deo agit cum aliquo ad homines respectu.

XXIII. Itaque convenientius Theologiae objectum dici potest Deus, ut Deus est, et servator hominum. Tota quippe Scriptura Deum nobis sub hoc respectu proponit. Ac praecipue intendit nos docere quae sint erga homines Dei beneficia, quemque vicissim ab illis cultum exigat et obedientiam. Si quae vero alia tangit, id facit ad ista magis declaranda et confirmanda. Exempli gratia, cum tradit esse tres in Deo Personas, Patrem, Filium, et Spiritum sanctum, scopus ejus non est simpliciter nos hanc veritatem docere: sed per id vult nos clarius et uberius informare, de modo redemptionis atque salutis nostrae, quae per Christum nobis parta est, et per Spiritum nobis applicatur et obsignatur. Et similiter Dei attributa, ut justitia et misericordia enarrantur in Scripturis relate ad homines, ut scilicet sciant, quatenus Dei justitia ipsis timenda sit, et quodnam debeant in ejus misericordia quaerere perfugium.
english: As for the object of theology, it is to be noted that sometimes the object of a science is said to be whatever the science considers in any way. So the object of theology is not one. For it considers many and very diverse things: God, the church, angels, the sacraments. Yet all these agree in one common appellation, insofar as they fall under the theologian's consideration. For whatever the theologian treats can be called divine things. For they are either God himself, or other things ordered in some way to God. Nor is anything properly considered by the theologian except with some respect to God. So if anyone asks about the object of theology, it can not ineptly be answered that that object is divine things.

But for the most part the object of any science is said to be that of which the science principally intends to give us knowledge, and on account of which it considers all the rest — because, namely, they lead to a fuller and more perfect acquaintance with it. Of this kind the object of theology is God, which almost all confess, and which the very word theology teaches, which, as was noted above, means speech about God. But it is not agreed whether that object is God simply, as God is, or rather under some certain respect. The former is defended by the more celebrated scholastics following Thomas Aquinas, and they state that the object of theology is God as God is, and, as they speak, under the reason of deity. But this seems to us too loose and general. Nor is the scope of theology to lead us simply into the knowledge of God as God is; rather it treats of God with some respect to men.

Therefore the object of theology can more conveniently be said to be God, as God is, and the savior of men. For the whole of Scripture proposes God to us under this respect. And it principally intends to teach us what benefits of God are toward men, and what worship and obedience he in turn requires of them. But if it touches any other things, it does so in order to declare and confirm these more. For example, when it teaches that there are three Persons in God — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — its scope is not simply to teach us this truth; but by it it wills to inform us more clearly and richly concerning the manner of our redemption and salvation, which was procured for us through Christ, and is applied and sealed to us through the Spirit. And likewise the attributes of God, such as justice and mercy, are narrated in the Scriptures in relation to men, so that they may know how far the justice of God is to be feared by them, and what refuge they ought to seek in his mercy.

source_text:
XXIV. Porro semel cognita Theologiae natura, in promptu est colligere, quae sit ejus dignitas, et praestantia supra reliquas scientias. Et primo quidem, eam satis ostendunt, quae de Theologiae objecto jam dicta sunt. Ex objecti enim dignitate, solet scientiarum aestimari dignitas. At Theologiae objectum, ut dictum est, est Deus Opt. Max. qui cetera omnia in infinitum dignitate superat, cum sit ipse essentiae et perfectionis infinitae.

XXV. Prima Philosophia agit quidem de Deo, sed de tanto objecto pauca tradit et exigua, prae iis quae in hac disciplina traduntur. Etenim Theologia Dei naturam et attributa longe uberius et luculentius enarrat, quam Metaphysica. Deinde multa de Deo mysteria aperit, Philosophis prorsus incognita: veluti in Deo tres esse personas, licet una sit essentia, Deique Filium pro nobis incarnatum et mortuum esse, et multa similia.

XXVI. Tum quoque, licet Deus sit Theologiae objectum principale, quia, ut modo docuimus, nil considerat, nisi in ordine et respectu ad Deum; de multis tamen praeter Deum agit Theologia, neque est ulla scientia, quae ad plura se extendat, cujusque tam late pateat objectum. Plurima enim praeclara edisserit de creaturis spiritualibus, Angelis scilicet, tam bonis quam malis, de quibus vix quicquam potest assequi ratio humana. Ibi habemus perfectam Ethicam, et regulam bene vivendi longe sanctiorem et sublimiorem quibuscunque sapientum hujus saeculi praeceptis. Neque Theologiae desunt praecepta politica atque oeconomica, quae multa ex Scriptura sacra depromi possunt.

XXVII. Adde quod per hanc disciplinam homo in veram sui cognitionem ducitur, eaque de seipso discit, quae aliunde doceri non potest. Siquidem haec sola generis humani originem aperit, variosque hominis status. Cumque facile sit animadvertere in natura humana magnam miseriam et perturbationem, sola Theologia illius causam et remedium docet; tantique aperit mali magnitudinem. Super qua re jam olim frustra aestuavit et anhelavit Philosophia.

XXVIII. Imo doctrina sacra non pauca Geographica et Historica complectitur, quae magnam lucem affundunt Historiae atque Geographiae. Et sine ejus face praelucente ignota essent mundi primordia, et gentium pene omnium origines, nec ullum Chronologia certum initium haberet, primaque et maxime veneranda in totum latens antiquitas. Denique Scriptura sacra, Theologiae nostrae fons, et regula prima, passim quaedam Physica aspergit, quae non leviter juvant scientiam naturalem. Ut, verbi causa, illud Salomonis Ecclesiastae primo, de fontium et fluviorum a mari origine, et in idem mare per circulum perpetuum reditu.
english: Further, once the nature of theology is known, it is ready to hand to gather what its dignity is, and its excellence above the remaining sciences. And first, indeed, those things already said about the object of theology show it sufficiently. For from the dignity of the object the dignity of the sciences is usually estimated. But the object of theology, as has been said, is God Most High, who surpasses all other things infinitely in dignity, since he himself is of infinite essence and perfection.

First philosophy does indeed treat of God, but concerning so great an object it hands down few and slight things compared with those handed down in this discipline. For theology narrates the nature and attributes of God far more richly and clearly than metaphysics. Then it opens many mysteries about God altogether unknown to the philosophers — as that there are three persons in God though the essence is one, and that the Son of God was incarnate and died for us, and many like things.

Then also, although God is the principal object of theology — because, as we have just taught, it considers nothing except in order and respect to God — still theology treats of many things besides God, and there is no science that extends itself to more things, or whose object lies open so widely. For it discourses on many excellent matters concerning spiritual creatures, namely angels both good and evil, of which human reason can scarcely attain anything. There we have a perfect ethics, and a rule of living well far holier and more sublime than any precepts of the wise of this age. Nor does theology lack political and economic precepts, many of which can be drawn from sacred Scripture.

Add that through this discipline a person is led into a true knowledge of himself, and learns those things about himself which cannot be taught from elsewhere. For this alone opens the origin of the human race, and the various states of man. And since it is easy to notice in human nature a great misery and disturbance, theology alone teaches its cause and remedy, and opens so great a magnitude of the evil. Over which matter philosophy long ago seethed and panted in vain.

Indeed sacred teaching embraces not a few geographical and historical matters, which pour great light on history and geography. And without its torch shining ahead, the beginnings of the world would be unknown, and the origins of almost all nations, nor would chronology have any certain beginning, and the first and most venerable antiquity would lie wholly hidden. Finally sacred Scripture, the fountain of our theology and its first rule, scatters here and there certain physical matters which not lightly assist natural science — as, for example, that saying of Solomon in the first chapter of Ecclesiastes ([[Ecclesiastes 1:7 >> Bible:Ecclesiastes 1:7]]), concerning the origin of springs and rivers from the sea, and their perpetual return by a circle into the same sea.

source_text:
XXIX. Sed quantum haec scientia commendatur ab objecto, eam tantundem commendat ejus autor. Reliquae enim scientiae illustri aliquo viro tanquam praecipuo authore gloriantur. Aristoteles habetur Philosophorum princeps, et Medicorum Hippocrates: Mathematicae vero disciplinae parentem agnoscunt Euclidem. At Theologia Deum sibi vindicat authorem, a quo sacra haec doctrina emanavit. Non enim libitu hominis allata est olim prophetia, ut Petrus Apostolus ait, sed acti a Spiritu sancto loquuti sunt sancti homines Dei, qui primum eam scriptis consignarunt.

XXX. Non sine numine quidem inventae sunt bonae artes, et disciplinae: et ipsum rationis lumen descendit a Patre luminum, qui est naturae motor et gubernator. Sed principia, quibus Theologia nititur, sunt expressa Dei dicta et oracula, quibus manifestantur ea, quae non potuerunt innotescere, nisi per lumen ratione altius.
english: But as much as this science is commended from its object, so much also does its author commend it. For the remaining sciences glory in some illustrious man as their chief author. Aristotle is held the prince of the philosophers, and Hippocrates of the physicians; and the mathematical disciplines acknowledge Euclid as their parent. But theology claims God for itself as author, from whom this sacred teaching has flowed forth. For prophecy was not brought in of old by the will of man, as the Apostle Peter says ([[2 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:21]]); but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit, who first consigned it in writing.

Not without the deity, indeed, were the good arts and disciplines invented; and the light of reason itself descends from the Father of lights ([[James 1:17 >> Bible:James 1:17]]), who is the mover and governor of nature. But the principles on which theology rests are the express sayings and oracles of God, by which those things are made manifest which could not have become known except by a light higher than reason.

source_text:
XXXI. Unde fit ut Theologia certitudine superet reliquas omnes scientias. Siquidem illae nituntur ratione humana, quae falli potest, et est errori obnoxia. Sed Theologia recumbit in veritatem Dei, qui nec falli, nec fallere potest. Multi quidem circa veritates Theologicas addubitant, iisque Theologiae principia, et conclusiones minus certa videntur, quam ea quae traduntur in scientiis humanis. Sed id non obstat quo minus in se sint certissima: sicut Sol non desinit esse splendidissimus, licet caeci et lippientes lucem ejus, aut omnino non, aut obscure tantum percipiant.

XXXII. Verum hic animadvertendum, quum ponimus Theologiam certiorem esse aliis scientiis, nos id ita non intelligere, quasi certitudo illa solum esset ex parte objecti. Etenim illa quae Deus revelavit, non tantum sunt in se certissima, sed etiam per habitum fidei, et Theologiae certius cognosci possunt, quam ullae veritates per solum lumen rationis notae. Ita ut qui in fide et rerum divinarum scientia roboratus est, certior sit, et magis persuasus de veritatibus divinis, quam sit de ulla alia veritate. Atque sic fidei et Theologiae habitus, in se et ex propria specie, certitudine antecellit habitus scientiarum mere naturalium, licet omnes non aequaliter participent illum habitum, et sit in uno firmior, in alio vero minus firmus.
english: Hence it comes about that theology surpasses all the remaining sciences in certainty. For those rest on human reason, which can be deceived and is liable to error. But theology reclines upon the truth of God, who can neither be deceived nor deceive. Many indeed waver about theological truths, and to them the principles and conclusions of theology seem less certain than the things handed down in the human sciences. But that does not hinder them from being in themselves most certain — just as the sun does not cease to be most splendid, though the blind and the bleary-eyed either do not perceive its light at all, or perceive it only obscurely.

But here it must be noticed that when we set theology as more certain than the other sciences, we do not so understand it as if that certainty were only on the side of the object. For the things which God has revealed are not only most certain in themselves, but can also be known more certainly through the habit of faith and of theology than any truths known through the light of reason alone. So that one who is strengthened in faith and in the science of divine things is more certain, and more persuaded, concerning the divine truths than he is concerning any other truth. And thus the habit of faith and of theology, in itself and from its own species, excels in certainty the habit of the merely natural sciences — although not all participate that habit equally, and it is firmer in one person and less firm in another.

source_text:
XXXIII. Sed in nulla re magis Theologiae dignitas et excellentia elucet quam in praestantia finis et usus ejus. Etenim, inter disciplinas practicas, quo alicujus disciplinae finis ulterior est et magis universalis, eo disciplina illa dignior et praestantior est. Ita Politica praestat scientiae militari, quia militaris scientiae finis est victoria, quae medium est ad adipiscendam publicam pacem et tranquillitatem, quae politicae scientiae finis est, et bonum aliquod majus. At hujus scientiae finis summus est et ultimus omnium, perfecta scilicet hominis beatitudo, cui subordinantur caeterarum omnium artium atque disciplinarum fines.

XXXIV. Disciplinae et artes reliquae particulare aliquod hominis bonum curant. Medicina v. g. corporis sanitatem: Jurisprudentia, facultates: Politica, publicam pacem et tranquillitatem. Sed harum nulla sufficit ad hominem beandum. Theologia vero integram hominis felicitatem curat, et suggerit quaecunque desiderantur ad bene beateque vivendum.

XXXV. Ad id quidem etiam contendit Philosophia. Sed scopum suum minus assequitur, et quaecunque bona homini procurare conatur, intra hujus vitae ambitum continentur. At Theologia vitam et felicitatem aeternam offert, et praestat iis qui sequuntur ejus ductum. Et sic docet praesentem vitam instituere, ut non tantum pro hujus vitae statu beati simus, sed ita ut ad sempiternam beatitudinem perducat.
english: But in no matter does the dignity and excellence of theology shine forth more than in the excellence of its end and use. For among practical disciplines, the further and more universal the end of any discipline is, the more worthy and excellent that discipline is. So politics excels military science, because the end of military science is victory, which is a means to obtaining public peace and tranquillity — which is the end of political science, and some greater good. But the end of this science is the highest and last of all: namely the perfect beatitude of man, to which the ends of all the other arts and disciplines are subordinated.

The remaining disciplines and arts care for some particular good of man. Medicine, for example, the health of the body; jurisprudence, estates; politics, public peace and tranquillity. But none of these suffices to make a person blessed. Theology, however, cares for the whole happiness of man, and supplies whatever things are desired for living well and blessedly.

Philosophy also strives toward that, indeed. But it attains its scope less fully, and whatever goods it tries to procure for a person are contained within the compass of this life. But theology offers eternal life and happiness, and renders them to those who follow its leading. And so it teaches how to order the present life, that we may be blessed not only for the state of this life, but in such a way that it leads through to everlasting beatitude.

source_text:
XXXVI. Itaque summo jure sacra haec disciplina sapientia dici debet. Etenim juxta ipsum Aristotelem, Sapientia est scientia rerum praestantissimarum. Sed ut patet ex dictis, Theologia de rebus praestantissimis agit: videlicet de Deo et mirandis ejus operibus, tam in creatione quam in redemptione nostra. Deinde quoque de rebus respectu nostri maximi momenti, et quae nosse nostra maxime interest, nempe de summa nostra felicitate, et de vita secundum Deum recte instituenda, quae via est ad illam felicitatem adeundam. Nec tantum de rebus praestantissimis agit, verum etiam praestantissimo modo: scilicet non ex humanae rationis inventis, sed ex divina revelatione.

XXXVII. Praeterea inter notas sapientiae recenseri solet, quod versetur circa maxime difficilia et a sensu remota. Deinde quod ab alia scientia non pendeat. Ac demum quod dirigat et judicet scientias alias, tanquam earum arbitra et domina. Quae omnia apprime in Theologiam quadrant.

XXXVIII. Etenim primo nobis mysteria aperit longe difficillima, quae in se non tantum sunt a sensibus remota, sed mentis humanae captum longe superant. Sunt enim, ut ait Apostolus, quae nec oculus vidit, neque auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt: sed Deus ea nobis revelavit per Spiritum suum, qui Spiritus omnia scrutatur, etiam profunditates Dei, 1 Cor. 2.

XXXIX. Secundo Theologia non pendet ab ulla alia scientia. Etenim una scientia ab alia pendere dicitur duobus modis. 1. Quum scientia quaedam ab altera sumit sua principia, quae superioris istius scientiae sunt conclusiones. Et ita ars urbes muniendi a Geometria pendet. Conclusiones enim Geometricae sunt istius artis principia. Deinde quum finis unius scientiae refertur ad finem scientiae alterius. Et ita militaris a politica pendet: quandoquidem finis militaris refertur ad politicae finem, et est medium ad illum consequendum. Utroque vero isto modo Theologia est plane independens. Nam, cum finis Theologiae sit finis hominis ultimus, aeterna scilicet ejus beatitudo, ad nullum finem referri potest, sed ad illum omnia necessario referuntur. Tum quoque nulla est humana scientia, a qua Theologia sua principia sumat: sed illa immediate habet ex revelatione Dei, cujus sunt effata et pronunciata.
english: Therefore by highest right this sacred discipline ought to be called wisdom. For according to Aristotle himself, wisdom is the science of the most excellent things. But as is clear from what has been said, theology treats of the most excellent things: namely of God and of his wonderful works, both in creation and in our redemption. Then also of things of the greatest moment with respect to us, and which it is of the highest interest for us to know — namely of our highest happiness, and of life rightly ordered according to God, which is the way to attaining that happiness. Nor does it treat only of the most excellent things, but also in the most excellent manner: namely not from the inventions of human reason, but from divine revelation.

Besides, among the marks of wisdom it is commonly reckoned that it is occupied about things most difficult and remote from sense; next, that it does not depend on another science; and finally that it directs and judges the other sciences, as their arbiter and mistress. All of which fit theology exactly.

For first it opens to us mysteries far most difficult, which in themselves are not only remote from the senses, but far surpass the capacity of the human mind. For they are, as the Apostle says, things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have ascended into the heart of man; but God has revealed them to us by his Spirit, who searches all things, even the depths of God ([[1 Corinthians 2:9-10 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:9-10]]).

Second, theology does not depend on any other science. For one science is said to depend on another in two ways. First, when a certain science takes its principles from another, which principles are conclusions of that superior science. So the art of fortifying cities depends on geometry; for geometrical conclusions are the principles of that art. Then, when the end of one science is referred to the end of another science. So military science depends on politics; since the military end is referred to the political end, and is a means to attaining it. But in both of those ways theology is plainly independent. For since the end of theology is the last end of man — namely his eternal beatitude — it cannot be referred to any end, but all things are necessarily referred to it. Then also there is no human science from which theology takes its principles; but it has them immediately from the revelation of God, whose are the utterances and pronouncements.

source_text:
XL. At inquies, Theologi in suis argumentis saepe utuntur propositionibus, quae non sunt revelatae, sed notae solo lumine rationis, et plurimae in Theologia reperiuntur argumentationes, in quibus una tantum praemissarum est revelata, altera vero una est ex conclusionibus cujusdam scientiae naturalis. Respondeo Theologiam, quum quaedam sumit ex aliis scientiis, id non facere ex necessitate, sed ad rem magis illustrandam, et ut se hominibus infirmis accommodet. Etenim per se sola sibi sufficit, omnesque necessarias conclusiones potest ex revelatis principiis probare. Itaque, quum aliquid a naturalibus scientiis mutuatur, id non facit tanquam inferior, quae ad superiorem recurrere cogitur: sed tanquam domina, quae libere utitur facultatibus ancillarum.

XLI. Et revera Theologia caeterarum scientiarum est arbitra et domina, quae ipsas dirigit, et de ipsis judicat, ipsa a nulla alia scientia judicanda. Nam reliquae omnes disciplinae, exigendae sunt ad ejus amussim, ut quicquid habent cum Theologia non consonum rejiciatur, neque admittatur quicquam quod cum Theologiae principiis non congruat.

XLII. Atque sic in Philosophia varii errores detecti, ut v.g. de origine mundi, quem Philosophorum alii aeternum, alii ex materia factum existimarunt: nulli vero, ex nihilo, prout est revera, creatum, nisi Theologia monstrante et manu ducente: Et in multis aliis, ubi Philosophi haerebant, nec rem habebant satis exploratam, eam Theologia posuit in aperto; et sustulit omnem dubitationem. Ut patet in negotio de divina providentia, et animae immortalitate.

XLIII. Jure merito ergo doctrina sacra titulo Sapientiae ornanda est, qui etiam ipsi saepe in Scriptura tribuitur: ut quum Apostolus Evangelium vocat, sapientiam quae in mysterio est: ipsumque dicit esse gentibus quidem stultitiam, et Judaeis scandalum: at vero iis qui credunt, Dei potentiam atque sapientiam, 1. Cor. 1. et 2.
english: But you will say: theologians in their arguments often use propositions which are not revealed, but known by the light of reason alone; and many argumentations are found in theology in which only one of the premises is revealed, while the other is one of the conclusions of some natural science. I answer that when theology takes certain things from other sciences, it does not do so from necessity, but to illustrate the matter more, and to accommodate itself to weak persons. For by itself alone it is sufficient to itself, and can prove all necessary conclusions from revealed principles. So when it borrows anything from the natural sciences, it does not do so as an inferior compelled to run back to a superior, but as a mistress who freely uses the faculties of her handmaids.

And in truth theology is the arbiter and mistress of the other sciences, which directs them and judges concerning them, herself to be judged by no other science. For all the remaining disciplines are to be measured by her rule, so that whatever they have not consonant with theology is rejected, and nothing is admitted which does not agree with the principles of theology.

And so various errors in philosophy have been detected — as, for example, concerning the origin of the world, which some of the philosophers thought eternal, others made from matter; but none thought it created from nothing, as it truly is, except with theology showing and leading by the hand. And in many other matters where the philosophers stuck fast and did not have the thing sufficiently explored, theology set it in the open and took away all doubt — as is plain in the business of divine providence and of the immortality of the soul.

Therefore by right and merit sacred teaching is to be adorned with the title Wisdom, which is also often attributed to it in Scripture: as when the Apostle calls the Gospel the wisdom which is in a mystery; and says that it is to the nations foolishness, and to the Jews a stumbling-block; but to those who believe, the power of God and the wisdom of God ([[1 Corinthians 1:18-24 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 1:18-24]]; [[1 Corinthians 2:6-8 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:6-8]]).

source_text:
I. FIDES Theologice sumpta in genere, est assensus quem Deo loquenti praebemus, quum aliquid verum esse certo nobis persuademus, ad id Divina Authoritate moti. Ac per hoc fides distinguitur ab opinione, quae assensus est timidus et incertus. Item a scientia, quae quidem assensus est certus, sed qui demonstratione, aut evidenti aliquo argumento, non vero cujusquam testimonio nititur. Denique a fide humana, quae in authoritate hominum acquiescit.

II. Itaque quivis assensus, adhibitus etiam eis, quae verbo Dei continentur, fides non est censendus. Si quis enim aliquod religionis dogma, veluti universorum creationem ex nihilo, certo et firmiter teneat: non tamen ad id impulsus revelatione divina, sed ratione quadam, quae ipsi necessaria videtur, eatenus fidem non habet. Ut nec qui Israelitici populi historiam credit ex relatione Josephi Historici, non vero historicis sacris fidem adhibens. Quod et de iis dici potest, qui verae et orthodoxae religioni adhaerescunt, sed tantum ex consuetudine, et ad id sola majorum authoritate moti.

III. Fidei vero varias, sive species, sive gradus, ex Scripturis assignare licet. In quibusdam enim fides intellectu theoretico haeret: et ita nudum et simplicem assensum praebent iis, quae verbo Dei proponuntur, ut ad recte agendum inde non moveantur, nec reddantur meliores. Ita credidit Simon Magus praedicationi Philippi, cujus tamen cor non erat rectum, quique in amarissimo felle, et nexu injustitiae positus erat, ut habetur Actorum 8. Ita quoque crediderant in nomen Christi, illi quibus tamen Christus non credebat seipsum, quod probe nosset omnes, prout legimus, Johan. 2. Et hanc suo modo participant ipsi daemones, qui dicuntur apud Jacobum credere et contremiscere.
english: Faith, taken theologically in general, is the assent we give to God speaking, when we are certainly persuaded that something is true, moved to it by divine authority. By this, faith is distinguished from opinion, which is a timid and uncertain assent. Likewise from science, which is indeed a certain assent, but one that rests on demonstration or some evident argument, not on anyone's testimony. Finally from human faith, which rests in the authority of men.

Therefore not every assent, even when given to things contained in the word of God, is to be counted as faith. For if someone holds some doctrine of religion with certainty and firmness — for example the creation of all things out of nothing — yet is not driven to it by divine revelation, but by some reason that seems necessary to him, to that extent he does not have faith. Nor does the one who believes the history of the Israelite people from the report of Josephus the historian, and does not give faith to the sacred historians. The same can be said of those who cling to the true and orthodox religion, but only from custom, and moved to it by the authority of their ancestors alone.

But various species or grades of faith may be assigned from the Scriptures. In some people faith sticks in the theoretical intellect alone: and so they give a bare and simple assent to what is proposed in the word of God, yet are not moved thereby to act rightly, nor are they made better. So Simon Magus believed Philip's preaching, yet his heart was not right, and he was in the bitterest gall and the bond of injustice, as is recorded in Acts 8. So also those had believed in the name of Christ to whom nevertheless Christ did not entrust himself, because he knew all people thoroughly, as we read in John 2. And even the demons themselves share in this in their own way, who are said in James to believe and tremble (James 2:19).

source_text:
IV. Haec est fides, quae a nostris historica dicitur. Quam denominationem ab objecto non accipit: quasi sit eorum tantum, quae historice narrantur in Scripturis. Siquidem qui hac fide praediti sunt, vera credunt quaecunque in sacris literis habentur; non minus promissiones, dogmata et praecepta, quam historias et narrationes. Multi enim impii de promissionum Evangelicarum veritate non ambigunt, nec daemones eas revocant in dubium. Sed ista fides vocatur historica, a modo quo versatur circa suum objectum. Scilicet quemadmodum cum legimus historias ad nos nihil pertinentes, eas nude contemplamur, nec inde afficimur et commovemur intus: ita qui fidem illam habent, quae verbum Dei docet, otiose speculantur, nec ea ad praxin referunt.

V. An autem haec fides vera dicenda sit, quaeritur. Affirmant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae. Et hoc iis aliquo sensu concedi potest. Quippe ista fides credit ea tantum quae vera sunt, et ea severe credit, non ficte et simulate. Sed tamen ea sola fides absolute vera nobis videtur appellanda, quae justificans et salutaris est, qualem illam esse negamus.

VI. Ab hac fide non longe differt fidei gradus alter, quem in Scriptura licet observare. Sunt enim in quibus fides non solum illuminat mentem theoreticam, sed et practicam quadantenus afficit; ita ut non simpliciter Evangelicae veritati credant: sed inde laetitia nonnulla titillentur, atque a vitiis suis et mundanis cupiditatibus aliquo modo abstineant. Verumtamen ista fide mens eorum tantum leviter est imbuta, nec satis alte penetravit, et radices egit in corde. Neque etiam prorsus vere et sincere vitiis et cupiditatibus propriis renunciant, semperque amor mundi et rerum terrenarum in praecordiis haeret. Unde fit, ut si crux paulo gravior toleranda sit, et ingruat persecutio, scandalum patiantur, et fidem abjiciant. Quod et saepe faciunt cupiditatibus suis obsequentes, et sollicitudinibus hujus vitae gravati.

VII. Hi sunt quos notat Christus in parabola, nempe qui Verbum Dei cum gaudio statim accipiunt, radicem tamen non habent in se; sed temporarii sunt: orta vero afflictione, vel persecutione propter sermonem, statim offenduntur. Tales etiam illi de quibus Petrus 2. epist. 2. Qui cum prius effugerint pollutiones mundi per agnitionem Domini et Servatoris Jesu Christi, his rursum implicati superantur; unde fit ultima eorum conditio deterior priore. Et de hoc quoque genere sunt illi, quibus Apostolus tam severe minatur cap. 6. et 10. ad Hebr. Hanc fidem scholae nostrae temporariam vocant: appellatione sumpta ex Christi verbis, quae modo citavimus.
english: This is the faith that our writers call historical. It does not take that name from its object, as though it belonged only to things narrated historically in the Scriptures. For those who have this faith believe as true whatever is contained in the sacred writings — promises, doctrines, and precepts no less than histories and narratives. Many of the ungodly do not doubt the truth of the Gospel promises, and even the demons do not call them into question. But this faith is called historical from the way it turns about its object. Just as when we read histories that do not concern us, we contemplate them bare and are not inwardly affected or moved by them: so those who have that faith which the word of God teaches speculate idly and do not refer those things to practice.

Whether this faith ought to be called true is asked. The Doctors of the Roman Church affirm it. And this can be granted them in some sense. For that faith believes only what is true, and believes it in earnest, not fictively and with pretense. Yet only that faith seems to us absolutely deserving to be called true which is justifying and saving — which we deny that historical faith to be.

From this faith another grade of faith does not differ far, which may be observed in Scripture. For there are those in whom faith not only illumines the theoretical mind, but also affects the practical mind to some extent; so that they do not merely believe the Gospel truth simply, but are tickled with some joy from it, and in some measure abstain from their vices and worldly desires. Yet by that faith their mind is only lightly imbued; it has not penetrated deeply enough, nor taken root in the heart. Nor do they renounce their own vices and desires wholly truly and sincerely, and love of the world and of earthly things always clings in the breast. Hence it comes about that if a somewhat heavier cross must be borne, and persecution rushes in, they take offense and cast away the faith. Which they also often do when they yield to their desires and are weighed down by the cares of this life.

These are the ones Christ marks in the parable: those who at once receive the Word of God with joy, yet have no root in themselves, but are temporary; and when affliction or persecution arises because of the word, they are immediately offended (Matthew 13:20-21). Such also are those of whom Peter writes in his second letter: who, after they had first escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, are again entangled in them and overcome; so that their last condition is worse than the first (2 Peter 2:20). And of this kind also are those whom the Apostle so severely threatens in Hebrews 6 and 10. Our schools call this faith temporary, taking the name from Christ's words which we have just cited.

source_text:
VIII. Sed et est quaedam fides, quae inter peculiaria Spiritus dona recensetur 1 Cor. 12. 9. quaeque non omnibus, qui sunt in Ecclesia, obtingit: sed paucis quibusdam; prout visum est Spiritui Sancto. Haec est fides, per quam miracula eduntur, unde quoque nomen est sortita. Atque in ea reperitur, qui a Deo vocatus ad edenda miracula, et super hac re promissionem habens, quemadmodum Apostoli habuerunt ex ore Christi, et multi alii ex interna Spiritus revelatione, non haesitat, nec diffidit: sed certo persuasus est Deum posse et velle stupenda illa opera per ipsum efficere. De hac fide loquitur Christus Marc. 11. 22. dum discipulis ait, Habete fidem Dei. Amen dico vobis, quicunque dixerit huic monti, Tollitor, et projicitor in mare, nec dubitaverit in corde suo, sed crediderit futura quae dicit, fiet ei quicquid dixerit. Hujus quoque fidei defectum, discipulis exprobrat Matt. 17. 20. dum refert in eorum incredulitatem causam, cur non potuissent daemonem ejicere. Et ad hanc respicit Apostolus, 1 Cor. 13. Si habeam, inquit, omnem fidem, ita ut montes transferam, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil sum.

IX. Denique est alia fides, cui Scriptura justitiam et salutem nostram tribuit, ad quam nos vehementer et frequenter hortatur, quamque summis laudibus et elogiis ornat. Et haec est, quam justificantem, salutarem, vivam, veramque nuncupamus.

X. Hic autem nobis est lis cum Doctoribus Ecclesiae Romanae: confundunt enim illi fidem justificantem cum illa quam modo historicam diximus, nullamque inter eas distinctionem ponunt: sed volunt plane unam et eandem esse. Tum etiam docent fidem miraculorum, nihil esse aliud quam excellentem quendam gradum fidei justificantis.
english: But there is also a certain faith which is counted among the peculiar gifts of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:9), and which does not fall to all who are in the Church, but to a few, as it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit. This is the faith through which miracles are wrought, from which it has also received its name. And it is found in the one who, called by God to work miracles and having a promise concerning this matter — as the Apostles had from the mouth of Christ, and many others from an inward revelation of the Spirit — does not hesitate or distrust, but is certainly persuaded that God is able and willing to accomplish those stupendous works through him. Of this faith Christ speaks in Mark 11:22 when he says to the disciples, Have faith in God. Amen I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, Be taken up and cast into the sea, and does not doubt in his heart but believes that what he says will happen, it will be done for him, whatever he says (Mark 11:22-23). He also reproaches the disciples for the defect of this faith in Matthew 17:20, when he refers the cause why they could not cast out the demon to their unbelief. And to this the Apostle looks in 1 Corinthians 13:2: If I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.

Finally there is another faith, to which Scripture attributes our righteousness and salvation, to which it urgently and often exhorts us, and which it adorns with the highest praises and elogies. And this is the faith which we name justifying, saving, living, and true.

But here we have a dispute with the Doctors of the Roman Church: for they confuse justifying faith with that which we have just called historical, and put no distinction between them, but want them to be plainly one and the same. Then they also teach that the faith of miracles is nothing other than a certain excellent grade of justifying faith.

source_text:
XI. At fidem justificantem ab historica debere distingui, probare non est difficile. Si enim fides historica eadem esset cum justificante, tum quicunque fidem historicam haberet, hoc ipso haberet fidem justificantem: At hypocritae, et impii multi praediti sunt fide historica, qui tamen fide justificante carent. De hac enim Scriptura dicit, Quicunque credit non perire, sed vitam aeternam habere, et Christum esse finem legis in justitiam omni credenti: atque Evangelio justitiam Dei patefactam in omnes, et super omnes qui credunt. Unde patet neminem esse tali fide praeditum, qui non sit justitiae et salutis particeps. Ac proinde iis qui sunt in statu perditionis, et manent in peccato, si credere dicantur, aliam fidem esse assignandam.

XII. Et certe quod ad haec loca dicunt Pontificii sententiam nostram juvat. Aiunt enim, quod Scriptura dicit, Quicunque credit vitam aeternam habet, intelligi debere de iis qui credunt sicut oportet, et toto corde: atque quod multi sint qui credunt in Filium, nec tamen vitam habent; inde esse, quod male credant, et non ex toto corde, et sicut oportet: ut videre est apud Bellarminum libro primo de justificatione, capite decimo, paragrapho Adde quod. At quis potest cum aliqua ratione affirmare eandem fidem esse, qua quis bene credit, et qua quis male credit: qua aliquis credit ut oportet, et qua aliquis credit ut non oportet? aut fidem illam qua quis male credit, nec toto corde, et sicut oportet, fidem esse justificantem, quam Apostolus dicit in justitiam imputari? Romanorum capite quarto.

XIII. Deinde fidem miraculorum non esse gradum eminentem fidei justificantis, manifestum est etiam, ex eo quod quidam ista fide sunt donati, qui tamen non habent fidem justificantem. Multis enim qui Christo dicent, Nonne per nomen tuum prophetavimus, et in nomine tuo daemonia ejecimus, et virtutes multas fecimus? respondebit Christus, Non novi vos, ut testatur Christus ipse Matt. 7. 22. Adde quod Apostolus 1. Corint. 12. 9. fidem signorum numerat inter varia spiritus charismata, quae Pontificii vocant Gratias gratis datas. Atqui gradus eminens fidei justificantis ad gratiam gratum facientem pertinet. Datur enim ad salutem ejus, qui eam habet: non vero, ut illa dona Spiritus gratuita, ad salutem aliorum. Tum si fides miraculorum esset gradus excellens fidei justificantis, Christus, exprobrans discipulis fidei illius defectum, non diceret ipsis, Si fidem haberetis sicut granum sinapi, diceretis huic monti, Transi hinc, et transiret, et nihil esset impossibile vobis. Granum enim sinapi denotat aliquid minimum in Scripturis, et tantundem est ac si Christus diceret, Si vel tantillum fidei haberetis.
english: But that justifying faith ought to be distinguished from historical faith is not hard to prove. For if historical faith were the same as justifying faith, then whoever had historical faith would by that very fact have justifying faith. Yet many hypocrites and ungodly people are endowed with historical faith who nevertheless lack justifying faith. For of this faith Scripture says that whoever believes does not perish but has eternal life (John 3:16), and that Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4); and that in the Gospel the righteousness of God is revealed to all and upon all who believe (Romans 1:16-17). From which it is plain that no one is endowed with such faith who is not a partaker of righteousness and salvation. And therefore to those who are in a state of perdition and remain in sin, if they are said to believe, another faith must be assigned.

And certainly what the Pontificians say about these places helps our sentence. For they say that when Scripture says whoever believes has eternal life, it ought to be understood of those who believe as they ought and with the whole heart; and that the reason many believe in the Son and yet do not have life is that they believe badly, and not with the whole heart, and not as they ought — as may be seen in Bellarmine, book one On Justification, chapter ten, paragraph Adde quod. But who can with any reason affirm that it is the same faith by which someone believes well and by which someone believes badly; by which someone believes as he ought and by which someone believes as he ought not? Or that the faith by which someone believes badly, and not with the whole heart, and not as he ought, is the justifying faith which the Apostle says is imputed for righteousness (Romans 4)?

Next, that the faith of miracles is not an eminent grade of justifying faith is also manifest from this: that some are gifted with that faith who nevertheless do not have justifying faith. For to many who will say to Christ, Did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works? Christ will answer, I never knew you, as Christ himself witnesses (Matthew 7:22). Add that the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 12:9 numbers the faith of signs among the various charisms of the Spirit, which the Pontificians call graces given freely (gratiae gratis datae). Yet an eminent grade of justifying faith belongs to grace that makes acceptable (gratia gratum faciens). For it is given for the salvation of the one who has it — not, like those free gifts of the Spirit, for the salvation of others. Then if the faith of miracles were an excellent grade of justifying faith, Christ, when reproaching the disciples for the defect of that faith, would not say to them, If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mountain, Move from here, and it would move, and nothing would be impossible for you (Matthew 17:20). For a grain of mustard seed denotes something very small in the Scriptures, and it amounts to the same as if Christ said, If you had even a tiny bit of faith.

source_text:
XIV. Est autem fides justificans, qua non tantum intellectus theoreticus illustratur, ut certo credat iis, quae verbo Dei docentur; sed et ita mens hominis practica afficitur, ut illa ad praxin referat, et sibi applicet. Si quidem vere fidelis ita credit, exempli causa, promissionibus Evangelii, de remissione peccatorum, de felicitate et gloria aeterna, ut in illis summum suum bonum et beatitudinem, ad quam ipsi sit totis viribus aspirandum, sitam esse firmiter et efficaciter judicet: ita fidem adhibet redemptionis nostrae mysteriis, ut in iis consolationem, et pacem conscientiae sibi quaerendam plane existimet: denique sic divina mandata considerat, ut secundum ista sibi vitam esse exigendam certo apud se constituat.

XV. Unde liquere potest, fidem justificantem ita diversam esse a fide historica, et temporaria, ut omnem ejus virtutem includat; atque sic ab ea distingui, ut perfectum ab imperfecto: sive ea distinctione, qua gradus superior ab inferiori differt. Etenim fides justificans ad reliquas fidei species se habet, quemadmodum anima rationalis ad sensitivam et vegetativam; quarum vim et facultates, vitam, sensum et motum eminenter complectitur, et gradum rationis addit. Nam sic quoque fides justificans facit, ut omnia credamus quae verbo Dei docentur, quod praestat fides historica. Et si Deus aliquid speciale promittat, et ad patrandum miraculum vocet, tum etiam vim supplet fidei miraculosae; nec qui jam credit Dei verbo, ut par est, si ad eum dirigatur specialis promissio, opus habet novo habitu, ut assensum illi praebeat. Unde est quod Apostolus vim et efficaciam salutaris fidei commendans, ipsi tribuit varia opera miraculosa, quae sancti viri olim patraverunt, aut quae in eorum gratiam facta sunt: dicens, Fide Patres mare rubrum transgressos, et fide moenia Jericho concidisse, et fide quosdam ora leonum obturasse, et extinxisse vim ignis. Hebr. 11. Sed supra reliquas fidei species fides justificans habet, quod mentem theoreticam luculentius irradiat, et practicam plenius imbuit, ac altius penetrat, acrioremque veritatis sensum, et firmiorem assensum animis nostris ingignit, quam fides historica, sive temporaria. Tum etiam quaecunque ex verbo Dei hausit ad actionem refert, vitamque instituendam: atque quo diximus modo, sibi applicat.

XVI. Quae quidem applicatio recte est intelligenda, et quo sensu jam expositum est. Non vero ita quasi proprius fidei justificantis actus, quo ab aliis fidei speciebus discernitur, in eo consistat, ut quis in animum inducat sibi esse remissa peccata seque esse Dei filium ad vitam praedestinatum, et salutis fore certo participem. Etenim haec persuasio, si legitima sit, fidem necessario praesupponit, et ex ea oritur: adeoque actus ejus primarius esse non potest. Cum enim remissio peccatorum, et vita aeterna in Evangelio nemini promittatur absolute, sed sub conditione fidei et resipiscentiae: ut de gratia Dei et salute nostra certi simus, necesse est ut prius nobis constet de fide, et resipiscentia nostra. Unde manifestum est certitudinem illam fidei esse consequens, non vero ipsam fidem: aut si quis ad fidem pertinere velit, saltem ejus actum non esse primarium.
english: Now justifying faith is that by which not only the theoretical intellect is illumined, so that it certainly believes the things taught by the word of God, but also the practical mind of man is so affected that it refers those things to practice and applies them to itself. For the truly faithful person so believes, for example, the promises of the Gospel concerning remission of sins and eternal happiness and glory, that he firmly and effectually judges his highest good and blessedness — to which he must aspire with all his strength — to be placed in them; so he gives faith to the mysteries of our redemption that he plainly thinks consolation and peace of conscience are to be sought for himself in them; finally he so considers the divine commandments that he certainly resolves within himself that life is to be lived according to them.

From which it can be clear that justifying faith is so diverse from historical and temporary faith that it includes all their virtue; and is so distinguished from them as the perfect from the imperfect — or by that distinction by which a higher grade differs from a lower. For justifying faith stands to the remaining species of faith as the rational soul stands to the sensitive and vegetative; whose force and faculties — life, sense, and motion — it eminently embraces, and adds the grade of reason. For so also justifying faith makes us believe all things taught by the word of God, which historical faith performs. And if God should promise something special and call someone to work a miracle, then it also supplies the force of miraculous faith; nor does the one who already believes the word of God as he ought, if a special promise is directed to him, need a new habit in order to give assent to it. Hence it is that the Apostle, commending the force and efficacy of saving faith, attributes to it various miraculous works which holy men once wrought, or which were done for their sake: saying that by faith the fathers crossed the Red Sea, and by faith the walls of Jericho fell, and by faith some stopped the mouths of lions and quenched the power of fire (Hebrews 11). But above the remaining species of faith, justifying faith has this: that it more brightly irradiates the theoretical mind, more fully imbues the practical, penetrates more deeply, and begets a sharper sense of truth and a firmer assent in our souls than historical or temporary faith. Then also whatever it has drawn from the word of God it refers to action and to the ordering of life; and in the way we have said, it applies it to itself.

Which application is indeed to be understood rightly, and in the sense already set out. Not, however, as though the proper act of justifying faith, by which it is discerned from the other species of faith, consisted in this: that someone should bring himself to think that his sins are remitted, and that he is a child of God predestined to life, and will certainly be a partaker of salvation. For this persuasion, if it is legitimate, necessarily presupposes faith and arises from it; and therefore cannot be its primary act. For since remission of sins and eternal life are promised in the Gospel to no one absolutely, but under the condition of faith and repentance: in order that we may be certain of the grace of God and of our salvation, it is necessary that it first be clear to us concerning our faith and repentance. From which it is manifest that that certainty of faith is a consequent, not faith itself; or if someone wishes it to belong to faith, at least that it is not its primary act.

source_text:
XVII. Sed ut fidei natura plenius intelligatur, necesse est de ejus objecto et subjecto, causa et effectibus paulo latius disserere. Et quidem ex dictis patet, fidei objectum esse quae a Deo revelata sunt, et quatenus sunt a Deo revelata. Ut objectum materiale fidei sint ea quae verbo Dei continentur: formale vero sit ipsa authoritas et veritas divina.

XVIII. Itaque Bellarminus non recte disputat adversus nostros, quasi fidei salutaris objectum ad solam promissionem remissionis peccatorum omnino restringerent. Quippe fidei illius objectum statuimus, non tantum ea quae promittuntur in Evangelio, sed et alia quaecunque in verbo Dei docentur, narrantur, et praecipiuntur. Quod docet Apostolus Hebr. 11. ubi de fide justificante loquens, dicit, Fide nos intelligere aptata esse saecula verbo Dei, ut quae videntur non sint ex apparentibus facta. Itemque Noe per fidem credidisse admonitioni divinae de venturo diluvio, qua territus arcam construxit ad servandam domum suam.

XIX. Verum hic est notandum, omnia, quae fidei nostrae objiciuntur, non perinde ad ejus objectum pertinere. Sicut enim in objectis scientiarum humanarum, quaedam sunt quorum cognitio praecipue intenditur, et ista objectum praecipuum vocantur: ut verbi causa, in Logica syllogismus et demonstratio: alia vero quae tantum proponuntur ad priorum istorum elucidationem, atque ut facilius et uberius cognoscantur: et haec sunt scientiae objectum secundarium, et minus praecipuum, ita quoque res se habet in fidei doctrina. Quaedam enim fidei objiciuntur primario et praecipue, quaedam vero secundario et minus praecipue. Objectum autem illud praecipuum, sunt ea sine quibus ad salutem perveniri non potest, nec vita recte institui: quales sunt qui vocantur articuli fidei, mysteria salutis summatim complectentes, itemque praecepta divina. Sed multa alia verbum Dei continet, quae ad istorum tantum confirmationem et cognitionem ampliorem pertinent, ut sint, verbi causa, historiae variae et miracula quae narrantur in Scripturis: et ista sunt objectum fidei secundarium.

XX. Porro quae ad fidei praecipuum objectum pertinent, ea distincte credi necesse est; caetera vero sufficit, si confuse credantur. Distincte creduntur ea, quae fides apprehendit seorsim et sigillatim. Et haec est fides quae dicitur explicata. Confuse, quae non apprehenduntur in particulari, sed tantum in aliquo communi principio, in quo continentur: et haec est fides quam vocant implicitam. Exempli gratia, Qui credit librum Judicum esse divinitus inspiratum, nec tamen eum legit, nec de eo quicquam recitari audivit: is quidem credit veras esse historias quae illic habentur, sed implicite et confuse. Qui vero legit illas historias, novitque sigillatim quae in eo libro narrantur de Samsone et Gedeone, caeterisque populi Israelitici Ducibus, is earum habet fidem explicatam et distinctam.

XXI. Sed cum Deus non simul et semel totam redemptionis et salutis doctrinam hominibus manifestaverit, sed multis modis, multisque partibus: ac primo obscurius, deinde clarius; inde sequitur, secundum varia temporum discrimina, fidem magis aut minus explicitam esse debuisse. Revelatio enim est fidei mensura: atque quo plura distincte revelantur, ad plura fidem extendi necesse est.
