Ac proinde a nobis, quibus Evangelium clare patefactum est, multorum articulorum fides explicita, ceu necessaria exigitur, quorum sub Veteri Testamento, fides implicita olim sufficiebat.

XXII. Sed et hic animadvertendum, quod dicimus fidem implicitam multorum, quae Dei verbo continentur, sufficientem esse, non ita accipi debere, quasi in qualicunque praecipuorum fidei capitum notitia laudabile sit acquiescere, nec amplior sit cognitio quaerenda. Quamvis enim paucorum articulorum fides distincta, tanquam ad salutem plane necessaria exigatur, tamen et hoc certum est, unumquemque teneri omnem operam adhibere, ut pro vocationis modo, in doctrina salutis magis magisque proficiat, pleniusque et copiosius in verbo Dei instruatur. Ad quod sedulo fideles hortatur Apostolus Col. 2. 2. et 3. 16. Ac proinde graviter errant et peccant illi, qui sub praetextu fidei implicitae stupidam et crassam plebis ignorantiam fovent.
english: But that the nature of faith may be more fully understood, it is necessary to discuss its object and subject, cause and effects a little more widely. And indeed from what has been said it is plain that the object of faith is the things that have been revealed by God, and insofar as they have been revealed by God. So that the material object of faith is the things contained in the word of God; but the formal object is the divine authority and truth itself.

Therefore Bellarmine does not dispute rightly against our writers, as though they altogether restricted the object of saving faith to the bare promise of remission of sins. For we set the object of that faith as not only the things promised in the Gospel, but also whatever else is taught, narrated, and commanded in the word of God. Which the Apostle teaches in Hebrews 11, where speaking of justifying faith he says that by faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that the things which are seen were not made of things which appear (Hebrews 11:3). And likewise that Noah by faith believed the divine warning about the coming flood, by which, being moved with fear, he built an ark for the saving of his house (Hebrews 11:7).

But here it must be noted that not all things which are set before our faith belong equally to its object. For just as in the objects of the human sciences some things are those whose knowledge is chiefly intended, and those are called the principal object — as, for example, in Logic the syllogism and demonstration — while others are proposed only for the elucidation of those former things, and so that they may be known more easily and more richly, and these are the secondary and less principal object of the science: so also the matter stands in the doctrine of faith. For some things are set before faith primarily and chiefly, and some secondarily and less chiefly. Now that principal object is the things without which one cannot arrive at salvation, nor can life be rightly ordered: such as those called the articles of faith, summing up the mysteries of salvation, and also the divine precepts. But the word of God contains many other things which pertain only to the confirmation of those and to a fuller knowledge of them — as, for example, the various histories and miracles narrated in the Scriptures — and those are the secondary object of faith.

Further, the things that belong to the principal object of faith must be believed distinctly; for the rest it is enough if they are believed confusedly. Those things are believed distinctly which faith apprehends separately and one by one. And this is the faith which is called explicit. Confusedly, those which are not apprehended in particular, but only in some common principle in which they are contained: and this is the faith which they call implicit. For example, one who believes that the book of Judges is divinely inspired, and yet has not read it, nor heard anything from it recited: he indeed believes that the histories contained there are true, but implicitly and confusedly. But one who reads those histories, and knows one by one what is narrated in that book about Samson and Gideon and the other leaders of the Israelite people, has an explicit and distinct faith of them.

But since God has not at once and once for all manifested the whole doctrine of redemption and salvation to men, but in many ways and in many parts — and first more obscurely, then more clearly — it follows that according to the various differences of times faith ought to have been more or less explicit. For revelation is the measure of faith: and the more things are distinctly revealed, the more things faith must be extended to. And therefore from us, to whom the Gospel has been clearly made known, an explicit faith of many articles is required as necessary, for which under the Old Testament an implicit faith formerly sufficed.

But here too it must be observed that when we say an implicit faith of many things contained in the word of God is sufficient, this ought not to be taken as though it were praiseworthy to rest in any sort of knowledge of the principal heads of faith, and as though no fuller knowledge were to be sought. For although a distinct faith of a few articles is required as plainly necessary to salvation, yet this also is certain: that each person is bound to use every effort, according to the manner of his calling, to advance more and more in the doctrine of salvation, and to be more fully and richly instructed in the word of God. To which the Apostle diligently exhorts the faithful (Colossians 2:2 and 3:16). And therefore those gravely err and sin who, under the pretext of implicit faith, foster the stupid and crass ignorance of the people.

source_text:
I. De authoritate Scripturae acriter disputatur inter Orthodoxos et Pontificios. Nempe quaeritur, Unde Scriptura sacra suam authoritatem habeat. Utrique autem per Scripturae authoritatem intelligunt dignitatem, secundum quam meretur fidem in omnibus quae quocunque modo dicit, et summam ex fide obedientiam in iis quae mandat et prohibet.

II. Sed distinguunt hic Pontificii, et fatentur quidem Scripturam in se suam authoritatem non aliunde quam a Deo habere: Verum authoritatem illam, quoad nos, ab Ecclesiae testimonio pendere contendunt. Haec scilicet eorum mens est. Quod Scriptura omni fide et reverentia digna sit, id esse quia promanavit a Deo fonte omnis veritatis, et supremo omnium Domino: Verum non aliunde certo et indubitate sciri posse Scripturam a Deo prodiisse, quam quia id Ecclesia testatur. Ita ut, quod Scriptura sit veritatis irrefragabilis, summumque in conscientias habeat imperium, inde sit quod Deum habeat authorem; quod vero certo agnoscitur Deum authorem habere, id jam ab Ecclesiae testimonio pendeat.

III. Nostri vero Scripturae sacrae authoritatem neque in se, neque quoad nos, ab Ecclesiae testimonio et authoritate suspendunt. Siquidem asserunt posse aliunde agnosci sacros libros a Deo prodiisse, quam ex testantis Ecclesiae voce: neque quod fideles hos libros tanquam divinos suscipiunt, id eos facere propter Ecclesiae authoritatem: sed Scripturam ipsam sufficere ad praebendam sui notitiam.
english: The authority of Scripture is sharply disputed between the Orthodox and the Pontificians. The question is: whence sacred Scripture has its authority. Both sides, however, understand by the authority of Scripture that dignity according to which it merits faith in everything it says in any way, and the highest obedience from faith in the things it commands and forbids.

But here the Pontificians make a distinction. They grant that Scripture in itself has its authority from nowhere else than from God; yet they contend that that authority, as it concerns us, hangs on the Church's testimony. This is their mind: that Scripture is worthy of all faith and reverence because it proceeded from God, the fountain of all truth and the supreme Lord of all; yet that one cannot know certainly and without doubt that Scripture came forth from God from any other ground than that the Church witnesses it. Thus, that Scripture is of irrefragable truth and has the highest empire over consciences comes from its having God as author; but that it is certainly acknowledged to have God as author already hangs on the Church's testimony.

But our writers do not hang the authority of sacred Scripture, either in itself or as it concerns us, on the Church's testimony and authority. For they assert that the sacred books can be acknowledged to have come forth from God from another ground than the voice of the witnessing Church; and that when the faithful receive these books as divine, they do not do so because of the Church's authority; but that Scripture itself is enough to furnish knowledge of itself.

source_text:
IV. Convenit ergo inter partes unde Scripturae sua authoritas competat: non convenit vero unde ipsi talem authoritatem competere cognoscatur. Atque ita facilis et expeditus videtur controversiae status: Verumtamen quum ventum est ad concertationem, et utraque pars mentem suam explicat clarius et in particulari, tum magna in hac quaestione oritur obscuritas et confusio; vixque licet assignare qua in re partes proprie dissideant.

V. Itaque, ut, quantum in nobis est, celeberrimae huic quaestioni lucem aliquam afferamus, rem totam accuratius tradere conabimur. Et primo quidem investigabimus, et exponemus modum quo Scriptura nobis pro divina innotescit. Deinde inquiremus in sententiam Pontificiorum, quam agnoscere atque percipere non est ita expeditum et promptum ut videri posset. Ac postremo inde eruto controversiae statu explicabimus qui sit Pontificiorum hac in parte error, illumque confutabimus.

VI. Porro circa modum, quo in Scripturae sacrae cognitionem devenimus, quatuor praecipue discutienda erunt. 1. An Scriptura sacra lucem aliquam habeat qua se praebeat agnoscendam, et quae qualisque sit illa lux. 2. Quae sint in hoc negotio Spiritus Sancti partes, et quousque illius opera necessaria sit, ut aliquis Dei Verbum et Scripturam agnoscat. 3. Quid Ecclesiae hac in re tribuendum sit, et quantum valeat ejus testimonium. 4. Denique quo praesertim fundamento nitatur fides illa, quam Scripturae adhibemus ut verae et divinae.
english: The parties therefore agree whence Scripture's own authority belongs to it; they do not agree whence it is known that such authority belongs to it. And so the state of the controversy seems easy and ready. Yet when one comes to the fight, and each side explains its mind more clearly and in particular, then great obscurity and confusion arise in this question; and one can scarcely assign in what the parties properly disagree.

Therefore, so that, as far as in us lies, we may bring some light to this most celebrated question, we will try to set out the whole matter more carefully. And first we will investigate and set out the way in which Scripture becomes known to us as divine. Then we will inquire into the Pontificians' sentence, which is not so ready and prompt to acknowledge and perceive as it might seem. And finally, once the state of the controversy has been drawn out from that, we will explain what the Pontificians' error is in this part, and will refute it.

Further, concerning the way by which we come to knowledge of sacred Scripture, four things chiefly will have to be discussed. First: whether sacred Scripture has some light by which it presents itself to be acknowledged, and what that light is and of what kind. Second: what parts the Holy Spirit has in this business, and how far His work is necessary for someone to acknowledge the Word of God and Scripture. Third: what is to be attributed to the Church in this matter, and how much its testimony avails. Fourth: finally, on what foundation especially that faith rests which we give to Scripture as true and divine.

source_text:
VII. Quod ad primum attinet, in hac quaestione nostri tanquam fundamentum substernunt, Scripturam sacram in se lucem quandam habere, qua, seclusa omni Ecclesiae authoritate, per se innotescere possit. Et certe Scriptura pluribus in locis seipsam luci comparat. Sed hoc ita tantum in genere notatum parum lucis affert huic controversiae. Itaque necesse est distinctius tradere quae sit illa Scripturae lux et evidentia. Quippe per lucem illam non intelligimus nisi evidentiam quandam veritatis, quam in Scriptura percipiunt fideles, et qua Scriptura sui divinitatem mentibus eorum probat.

VIII. Porro distingui potest duplex evidentia: una quam vocare licet mathematicam seu Metaphysicam; altera vero quae moralis dici potest. Evidentiam metaphysicam voco illam, quae competit primis principiis per se notis, et conclusionibus per hujusmodi principia demonstratis. Moralis autem est illa quae cernitur in rebus quae quidem demonstrari non possunt, sed ejusmodi tamen indiciis et argumentis suadentur, ut de iis vir prudens et peritus dubitare nequeat et dissensum a se impetrare. Sic Aeneidem esse scriptam a Virgilio, et orationes in Verrem, Catilinam et Antonium, a Cicerone.
english: As for the first point: in this question our writers lay down as a foundation that sacred Scripture has in itself a certain light by which, with all authority of the Church set aside, it can become known through itself. And certainly Scripture in many places compares itself to light. But this noted only in general brings little light to this controversy. Therefore it is necessary to set out more distinctly what that light and evidence of Scripture is. For by that light we understand nothing but a certain evidence of truth which the faithful perceive in Scripture, and by which Scripture proves its own divinity to their minds.

Further, a twofold evidence can be distinguished: one which may be called mathematical or metaphysical; another which can be called moral. I call metaphysical evidence that which belongs to first principles known of themselves, and to conclusions demonstrated through principles of that kind. Moral evidence, however, is that which is seen in things that cannot indeed be demonstrated, yet are urged by such marks and arguments that a prudent and skilled man cannot doubt them or wrest dissent from himself. So it is that the Aeneid was written by Virgil, and the orations against Verres, Catiline, and Antony by Cicero.

source_text:
IX. Evidentia, quae Scripturae competit, non est prioris generis. Etenim Scripturam esse divinitus inspiratam res non est per se nota, sicut haec principia, Totum est majus sua parte. Idem non potest simul esse et non esse. Nec etiam istud demonstrari potest logice, seu mathematice, ut patet experientia. Nec enim ullus unquam potuit hujus veritatis aliquam afferre demonstrationem. Adde quod, si res ita se haberet, assensus ille, quem sacrae Scripturae adhiberemus, scientia esset, non fides, siquidem ipsius scientiae definitio est, quod sit habitus demonstrativus.

X. Igitur Scriptura sacra non habet aliam lucem, sive evidentiam, praeter illam quam moralem diximus. Etenim quamvis non sit per se notum, nec etiam possit proprie demonstrari Scripturam sacram a Deo prodiisse: attamen hoc tam multis, et tam probabilibus argumentis suadetur, habetque Scriptura in se tot et tam insignia divinitatis suae notas et indicia, ut inde vir pius et prudens efficaciter inducatur ut credat illam esse veram et divinam.
english: The evidence that belongs to Scripture is not of the former kind. For that Scripture is divinely inspired is not a thing known of itself, as these principles are — The whole is greater than its part; The same thing cannot at once be and not be. Nor can that be demonstrated logically or mathematically, as experience shows. For no one has ever been able to bring any demonstration of this truth. Add that if the matter stood so, the assent we would give to sacred Scripture would be science, not faith, since the definition of science itself is that it is a demonstrative habit.

Therefore sacred Scripture has no other light or evidence besides that moral evidence we have named. For although it is not known of itself, nor can it properly be demonstrated, that sacred Scripture came forth from God, yet this is urged by so many and so probable arguments, and Scripture has in itself so many and so marked notes and indications of its divinity, that from them a pious and prudent man is effectively led to believe that it is true and divine.

source_text: XI. Atque ut argumentorum istorum specimina quaedam hic proferamus, Scripturam illam, quam pro sacra habemus, revera talem esse, et divinitus inspiratam, probatur ex conditione eorum qui primi illam tradiderunt, et pro divina commendarunt. Etenim, si Scriptura sacra vera et divina non est, oportet ut scriptores sacri, qui profitentur se Deo inspirante scripsisse, et ea quae scribunt aut esse a se visa, aut sibi divinitus revelata testantur, impostores fuerint quibus propositum fuerit homines decipere, et mundo illudere. At haec suspicio cadere non potest in Prophetas et Apostolos, quorum opera Scriptura nobis consignata est. Quibus enim est animus decipere, illi eo intendunt, vel lucri cupiditate, vel voluptatis alicujus causa, vel spe gloriae cujusdam, et voluptatis potiundae. Ita qui superstitionis alicujus authores fuerunt ii certe suis commentis opes et dignitates sibi conciliarunt: ut exempli causa, Mahumetes qui fabulis suis mundum decipiendo summum sibi suisque arrogavit imperium. Sed Prophetis et Apostolis tale quid affingi non potest, nisi valde impudenter, et contra omnem veritatis speciem. Si enim res ex sensu hominum aestimetur, omnes illi fere fuerunt miserrimi, et conditione abjecta et contempta: neque sua praedicatione ullas sibi in mundo pepererunt divitias, aut ullum imperium et apud homines gloriam. Contra vero doctrina illa, quam verbo et scriptis suis asseruerunt, concitavit in eos concivium suorum et externorum hominum odium, et reddidit eos obnoxios infinitis opprobriis, atque contumeliis: imo in certum vitae periculum conjecit, adeo ut eorum plerique scripta suo proprio sanguine obsignarint.
english: And so that we may bring forward here certain specimens of those arguments: that the Scripture which we hold as sacred is truly such, and divinely inspired, is proved from the condition of those who first handed it down and recommended it as divine. For if sacred Scripture is not true and divine, then the sacred writers, who profess that they wrote as God inspired them, and who testify that the things they write were either seen by them or divinely revealed to them, must have been impostors whose design was to deceive men and mock the world.

But this suspicion cannot fall on the Prophets and Apostles, by whose work Scripture has been consigned to us. For those who mean to deceive aim at that either from desire of gain, or for the sake of some pleasure, or in hope of some glory and of obtaining pleasure. Thus those who were authors of some superstition certainly won wealth and dignities for themselves by their inventions — as, for example, Muhammad, who by deceiving the world with his fables arrogated the highest empire to himself and his own. But such a thing cannot be affixed to the Prophets and Apostles except very shamelessly and against every appearance of truth.

For if the matter is estimated by the sense of men, nearly all of them were most miserable, and of a cast-down and despised condition; nor by their preaching did they produce for themselves any riches in the world, or any empire and glory among men. On the contrary, that doctrine which they asserted by word and writings stirred up against them the hatred of their fellow-citizens and of outsiders, and made them liable to infinite reproaches and insults; nay, it cast them into certain danger of life, so that most of them sealed their writings with their own blood.

source_text: XII. Nec dici potest eos per incogitantiam incidisse in tales aerumnas. Nam illi munus suum aggredientes praescii fuerunt harum calamitatum, et ultro sese exercendos et cruciandos tot malis tradiderunt. Moses quidem populi Israelitici dux fuit et sacerdos: sed tamen quam parum sibi suisque studuerit inde manifestum est, quod principatum et sacerdotium non transmisit ad posteros suos, sed servum suum Josuam ducem populi post se designavit, et fratrem suum Aaronem in sacerdotem, Deo mandante, inauguravit. Quam autem a vana gloria sacri scriptores alieni fuerint, inde patet, quod, si quid magnum aut praeclarum ab ipsis gestum vel dictum fuit, id totum Deo acceptum referunt: imo in illis ipsis scriptis, quae tanquam divinitus inspirata commendant, candide notant suos naevos atque defectus: Et si quid in ipsis tenue et humile ac inglorium fuit, istud non dissimulant. Ita Moses annotavit suam diffidentiam et diffidentiae poenam, quam Deus ipsi imposuit: itemque fratris sui Aaronis idololatriam et Mariae sororis murmura.
english: Nor can it be said that they fell into such hardships by thoughtlessness. For when they took up their office they foresaw these calamities, and voluntarily handed themselves over to be exercised and tormented by so many evils. Moses indeed was leader and priest of the Israelite people; yet how little he cared for himself and his own is plain from this: that he did not transmit the principate and the priesthood to his posterity, but designated his servant Joshua as leader of the people after him, and, at God's command, inaugurated his brother Aaron as priest.

And how far the sacred writers were from vain glory is plain from this: that if anything great or illustrious was done or said by them, they refer it wholly to God as received from Him; nay, in those very writings which they commend as divinely inspired they candidly note their own blemishes and defects; and if anything in them was slight and humble and without glory, they do not disguise it. Thus Moses recorded his own diffidence and the penalty of that diffidence which God imposed on him; and likewise his brother Aaron's idolatry and his sister Mary's murmurings.

source_text: XIII. Deinde doctrinam et Scripturam illam, quam pro divina habemus, vere divinam esse, valde credibile reddit fides, quae illi in mundo habita est. Paucis enim annis Evangelium Christi totum fere orbem pervasit; et statim atque coepit gentibus praedicari, innumeros invenit ubique sectatores, omnis aetatis, sexus et conditionis: adeo ut unus Paulus ab Hierosolymis in Illyricum usque, brevi admodum temporis spatio, omnia repleverit Evangelio Christi, sicut ipse scribit ad Romanos c.15. Istud autem provenire non potuit nisi a vi quadam divina, quae doctrinam illam sacram comitata est: et ut notat idem Paulus loco citato, a virtute divini Spiritus, illam cordibus hominum insculpentis, variisque prodigiis et signis confirmantis.
english: Next, that the doctrine and that Scripture which we hold as divine are truly divine is made very credible by the faith which the world has given them. For in a few years the Gospel of Christ pervaded almost the whole world; and as soon as it began to be preached to the nations, it found countless followers everywhere, of every age, sex, and condition — so much so that one Paul, from Jerusalem even to Illyricum, in a very short space of time filled all things with the Gospel of Christ, as he himself writes to the Romans (Romans 15:19). But that could not have come about except from a certain divine force that accompanied that sacred doctrine; and as the same Paul notes in the place cited, from the power of the divine Spirit engraving it on men's hearts and confirming it with various prodigies and signs.

source_text: XIV. Etenim, si res in se consideretur, omnia obstare debuisse, quominus doctrinam illam, et Scripturam, quae est illius fundamentum, homines reciperent. Primo doctrinae ipsius genius. Nam credenda proponit mysteria plurima quae sensus humanus stultitiam judicat: eaque jubet et exigit quae maxime repugnant humanis affectibus: ut scilicet Christi crucem bajulemus, nos ipsos abnegemus, et pro Christo crucifixo parati simus opes et voluptates relinquere, et vitam profundere. Deinde qui doctrinam illam hominibus annunciarunt, non usi sunt arte et eloquentia, quibus hominum animi flecti solent. Neque apud homines valuerunt authoritate, seu sapientiae et doctrinae fama. Nec fuere viri potentes qui minis et armis terrere potuerint, et ad doctrinam suam amplectendam cogere: sed fuerunt plerique viri rudes et idiotae, vitam tolerantes mechanicis artibus: ex Judaeorum gente caeteris omnibus contempta et exosa: ab iis, qui tum sapientes et docti existimabantur, pro barbaris et inscitis habiti. Adde quod praedicabant hominibus alii religioni innutritis, quique multis et magnis praejudiciis occupati erant. Etenim superstitionem, a qua avertabantur, a majoribus acceperant, eamque firmatam videbant populorum consensu, sapientum calculo, et magna tum authoritate. Denique vix dici potest quot et quam acres et potentes hostes doctrina, scripturis nostris contenta, habuerit. Judaeorum enim magistri, et Philosophi gentium magno conatu eam impugnabant. Ac priores quidem suam authoritatem opponebant: posteriores vero in eam omne ingenii acumen exercebant, et facundiam explicabant. Et praeterea magistratus et principes saeculi atrocissime persequebantur eos, qui eam amplexi fuerant, et in eos omni genere suppliciorum saeviebant. Cum ergo nihil eam humanitus adjuverit, contra vero omnia habuerit adversa, necesse est ut illius incrementum, et propagatio unius Dei virtuti ascribatur. Cum si quae alia secta et religio late serpsit, et multos sectatores invenit, id factum sit humanis mediis. Nam Mahumetismus ex Arabia brevi per provincias multas propagatus est: sed id factum est armis, et vi aperta. Deinde quod doctrina illa in multis carni adblanditur.
english: For if the matter is considered in itself, everything ought to have stood in the way of men receiving that doctrine, and Scripture which is its foundation. First, the genius of the doctrine itself. For it sets before us to be believed very many mysteries which human sense judges folly; and it commands and exacts things that most of all repugn human affections — namely that we bear Christ's cross, deny ourselves, and for Christ crucified be ready to leave wealth and pleasures and pour out our life (Matthew 16:24).

Next, those who announced that doctrine to men did not use art and eloquence, by which men's minds are usually bent. Nor did they prevail among men by authority, or by fame of wisdom and learning. Nor were they powerful men who could terrify by threats and arms and compel people to embrace their doctrine; but most of them were rude and unlettered men, earning their living by mechanical arts, from the nation of the Jews, despised and hated by all others, and held for barbarians and ignorant by those who were then thought wise and learned. Add that they were preaching to men nursed in another religion, and occupied by many and great prejudices. For the superstition from which they were being turned away they had received from their ancestors, and they saw it established by the consent of peoples, the vote of the wise, and great authority then.

Finally, it can scarcely be said how many and how sharp and powerful enemies the doctrine contained in our scriptures had. For the teachers of the Jews and the philosophers of the nations assailed it with great effort. The former opposed their own authority; the latter exercised against it all the sharpness of their ingenium and unfolded their eloquence. And besides, the magistrates and princes of the age most atrociously persecuted those who had embraced it, and raged against them with every kind of punishment. Since therefore nothing aided it humanly, and on the contrary it had all things adverse, it is necessary that its increase and propagation be ascribed to the power of the one God. For if any other sect and religion has crept widely and found many followers, that was done by human means. Muhammadanism spread briefly from Arabia through many provinces; but that was done by arms and open force. Next, that doctrine in many things flatters the flesh.

source_text: XV. Praeterea divinum aliquid in Scriptura arguit constantia, numerus, et conditio martyrum, qui eam suo sanguine obsignarunt. Cum enim per naturam homini nihil sit vita charius, unde factum, ut tot homines pro defensione Scripturae, et doctrinae quam tradit, mortem libenter oppetiverint, nisi a vi quadam divina quae penitus eorum animis insiderat? Aliquando quidem saevitum est in quosdam haereticos et superstitiosos, et pauca forte reperiri possunt exempla eorum, qui ex animi quadam ferocia et obstinatione mori potius elegerunt, quam ut a semel arrepto errore dimoveri se paterentur. Sed nullus est error, nulla superstitio et doctrina humana, quae multos habuerit sectatores tam obstinatos, ut, cum abnegata sua impietate evadere possent salvi et incolumes, supplicia tamen et tormenta perferre non recusaverint. Verum quum Apostolica et prophetica doctrina, et Scriptura, primum per orbem propagari coepit, necdum censeri posset traditione majorum et consuetudine firmata, quibus maxime radicibus humana instituta hominum animis solent adhaerescere, non pauci quidam reperti sunt, sed infinitae hominum myriades, omnis aetatis, omnis sexus, omnis conditionis, viri, foeminae, pueri, senes, literati, idiotae, qui durissima quaeque mortis genera perpessi sunt, potius quam Scripturae doctrinam abnegarent: licet sola ejus abnegatione possent non solum vitam redimere, sed etiam bonis et honoribus suis cum concivibus aequali jure frui. Neque censeri possunt ferocia vel stupiditate aut animi quodam morbo in mortem certam ruisse: cum saepe ab ipsis hostibus extorserint testimonium animi recte compositi, et inculpatae vitae, et in ipsa morte testati fuerint summam modestiam, summam humanitatem et animi praesentiam. In quo certe, nisi quis ultro claudat oculos, facile digitus Dei notari poterit.
english: Besides, something divine in Scripture is argued by the constancy, number, and condition of the martyrs who sealed it with their own blood. For since by nature nothing is dearer to a man than life, how did it come about that so many men willingly sought death for the defence of Scripture and of the doctrine it hands down, unless from a certain divine force that had settled thoroughly in their minds? Rage has sometimes been spent on certain heretics and the superstitious, and a few examples can perhaps be found of those who from a certain fierceness and obstinacy of mind chose rather to die than to suffer themselves to be moved from an error once seized. But there is no error, no superstition and human doctrine, that has had followers so obstinate that, when by denying their impiety they could escape safe and unharmed, they nevertheless refused not to endure punishments and torments. But when the Apostolic and prophetic doctrine, and Scripture, first began to be propagated through the world — and could not yet be reckoned established by the tradition of the ancestors and by custom, the deepest roots by which human institutes usually cling to men's minds — not a few only were found, but infinite myriads of men, of every age, sex, and condition, men, women, boys, old men, the lettered and the unlettered, who endured every harshest kind of death rather than deny Scripture's doctrine: although by that denial alone they could not only redeem life, but also enjoy their goods and honors with fellow-citizens by equal right. Nor can they be reckoned to have rushed into certain death by fierceness or stupidity or some disease of mind: since they often extorted from the enemies themselves testimony of a rightly composed mind and of a blameless life, and in death itself attested the highest modesty, the highest humanity, and presence of mind. In which, certainly, unless someone willingly shuts his eyes, the finger of God can easily be noted.

source_text: XVI. Praeterea doctrinam in Scripturis traditam, adeoque Scripturam, quae fundamentum illius est, divinam esse et a Deo manasse, probatur ex miraculis quae in doctrinae istius confirmationem facta sunt. Cum enim Scripturae et doctrinae caelestis duae sint praecipuae partes, Lex, et Evangelium: lex quidem confirmata est mirabilibus illis quae in deserto contigerunt: ut quod viva vox Dei loquentis e medio ignis audita est, quod quadraginta annis in deserto manna pluit, quod aqua saepius e petra educta est, quodque Israelitarum vestes toto illo tempore attritae non fuerunt, et plura ejusmodi. Evangelio vero testimonium perhibuerunt infinita pene Christi miracula: tum visibilia illa et plane stupenda Spiritus sancti dona, quae effusa sunt in primos credentes: ita ut subito variis et peregrinis linguis loquerentur, morbos quosvis sanarent, daemones expellerent, et miranda alia quam plurima patrarent. Cum enim talia sint supra naturae vires, necesse est Deum in illis exeruisse suam potentiam. At nefas est cogitare Deum voluisse uti sua omnipotentia ad fidem faciendam Scripturae et doctrinae, quae falso et injuria ipsi ascribebatur, quasi voluisset ex pacto cum hominibus mentiri.
english: Besides, that the doctrine handed down in the Scriptures — and so Scripture, which is its foundation — is divine and flowed from God is proved from the miracles done in confirmation of that doctrine. For since Scripture and heavenly doctrine have two chief parts, Law and Gospel: the law was confirmed by those wonders that happened in the desert — that the living voice of God speaking was heard from the midst of fire, that for forty years manna rained in the desert, that water was often led out from the rock, and that the Israelites' clothes were not worn out in that whole time, and more of that kind. To the Gospel almost infinite miracles of Christ bore witness; then those visible and plainly stupendous gifts of the Holy Spirit poured out on the first believers, so that suddenly they spoke in various and foreign tongues, healed any diseases, expelled demons, and performed very many other wonders. Since such things are above nature's powers, it is necessary that God exercised his power in them. But it is unholy to think God willed to use his omnipotence to make faith for a Scripture and doctrine falsely and injuriously ascribed to him, as if he had willed by compact with men to lie.

source_text:
XVII. At inquies, miracula illa facta quidem dicuntur, sed qui scire possumus illa revera facta esse: Nec enim minus incertum videtur, an vera sint illa miracula, quam hoc, an divina sit Scriptura illa in cujus confirmationem facta esse dicuntur. Respondeo. Quod ista revera contigerint, ex ipsis scripturis nostris efficaciter probari posse. Etenim scriptores nostri ista eo modo scripserunt, ut fieri non possit eos hac in re mentitos esse. Negantem enim, sive dubitantem vera esse quae narrant de miraculis istis scriptores nostri, Moses et Paulus, verbi causa, rogabo num velit in dubium vocare Mosen quendam fuisse qui Israelitico populo leges dedit, et quaedam volumina scripsit: Et similiter fuisse quendam Paulum, qui Christianam doctrinam praedicavit, et scripsit quasdam epistolas quae ipsi ascribuntur. Hac de re certe nemo hactenus dubitavit, nec ipsi quidem Athei hoc negare voluerunt, vel ausi fuerunt. Et revera id testatur fama tam constans, tam perennis, ita omnium, etiam adversariorum, consensu recepta, ut de hoc dubitare, delirare plane esset. Crebra enim Mosis et scriptorum ejus mentio fit apud Ethnicos. Neque Judaei et Mahumetani religionis Christianae hostes infestissimi, Apostolos nostros fuisse et scripsisse negant, sive dubitant. Quod si quis illud vellet pertinaciter in dubium vocare, eo adigendus esset, ut dubitationis suae causam afferret, et rationem aliquam cur fidem non habeat concordi totius orbis testimonio. Et cur credat potius Plinium, et Titum Livium fuisse et scripsisse, quam Mosen atque Paulum. Et certe frustra in hoc probando laboramus, quandoquidem res est in confesso. Neque enim illi, qui verbum Dei rejiciunt, negant authores illos, quos pro sacris habemus, fuisse vel scripsisse, sed illos vera non scripsisse blasphemant.

XVIII. Age ergo videamus an fieri possit, ut vera non sint ea quae de miraculis istis a Mose et Paulo narrantur. Certe, si vera non sunt, aut decepti sunt illi in scribendo, existimantes contigisse ea, quae revera non contigerant: aut scripserunt animo fallendi, et conati sunt falsa pro veris obtrudere. Prius dici non potest. Non enim illa tanquam aliunde accepta referunt, sed a seipsis gesta sive visa testantur. Oportet ergo ut voluerint fallere Moses Israelitas, et Paulus Corinthios, Galatas et alios. Et sic sentiunt homines profani qui Mosen et Paulum accusant imposturae. Videndum igitur an fuerint impostores, qui conati sint suadere iis ad quos scribebant, et in quorum manus sua scripta tradebant, haec et illa prodigia et miracula facta fuisse, cum tamen illorum nihil factum fuerit.
english: But you will say: those miracles are indeed said to have been done, yet how can we know they really were done? For it seems no less uncertain whether those miracles are true than whether that Scripture is divine in whose confirmation they are said to have been done. I answer that those things really happened can be proved efficaciously from our scriptures themselves. For our writers wrote those things in such a manner that they cannot have lied in this matter. For the one denying or doubting that what our writers Moses and Paul narrate about those miracles is true, I will ask, for example, whether he wills to call into doubt that there was a certain Moses who gave laws to the Israelite people and wrote certain volumes; and likewise that there was a certain Paul who preached Christian doctrine and wrote certain epistles ascribed to him. About this matter certainly no one has hitherto doubted, nor have the atheists themselves willed or dared to deny it. And really that is witnessed by a fame so constant, so perennial, so received by the consent of all — even of adversaries — that to doubt about this would plainly be to rave. For frequent mention of Moses and of his writings is made among the Gentiles. Nor do Jews and Muhammadans, most hostile enemies of the Christian religion, deny or doubt that our Apostles were and wrote. If someone would stubbornly wish to call that into doubt, he would have to be driven to bring a cause of his doubt, and some reason why he does not give faith to the concordant testimony of the whole world — and why he believes rather that Pliny and Titus Livius were and wrote than Moses and Paul. And certainly we labor in vain in proving this, since the matter is in confession. For those who reject God's word do not deny that those authors whom we hold as sacred were or wrote, but blaspheme that they did not write true things.

Come then, let us see whether it can be that those things narrated by Moses and Paul about those miracles are not true. Certainly, if they are not true, either those men were deceived in writing, thinking things had happened which really had not; or they wrote with a mind to deceive and tried to thrust false things for true. The former cannot be said. For they do not report those things as received from elsewhere, but testify them as done or seen by themselves. Therefore Moses must have willed to deceive the Israelites, and Paul the Corinthians, Galatians, and others. And so profane men feel who accuse Moses and Paul of imposture. It remains to see whether they were impostors who tried to persuade those to whom they were writing, and into whose hands they were handing their writings, that these and those prodigies and miracles had been done, when nevertheless nothing of them had been done.

source_text:
XIX. Certe solent impostores, et illi, quibus est animus decipere, sic procudere sua mendacia, ut facile non possint argui mendacii ab iis, quos deceptos volunt. Ita Numa, qui Romanae superstitionis ritus plerosque instituit, fingebat se de nocte colloquia habere cum Nympha Egeria: verum solum cum sola, et quorum nemo testis esse poterat. In Alcorano quoque Mahumetis portentosa quaedam narrantur, verum non tanquam facta ante hominum oculos, sed quorum fides penes ipsum esset. Si quis vero portenta et somnia narraret, et tamen de eorum veritate provocaret ad sensus eorum quos alloqueretur, ut qui jam commemoraret Mose aquas retro fluxisse, et frumento pluisse nobis inspectantibus, et istud ipsum nobis persuadere vellet, hoc jam non esset impostura, sed dementiae quoddam genus plane inusitatum atque incredibile; Neque hoc cadere potest in eum qui non omnino furit, et atrabile percitus est. Jam vero miranda illa quae habentur apud Mosen, ut quod mare fissum est, quod vox Dei loquentis audita de monte Sinai, quod in deserto pluit manna et coturnicibus, quod aquarum torrentes e petra eruperint et plura ejusdem generis, miranda inquam illa non commemorat Moses, tanquam quae contigerint aliis temporibus, aut in locis distantibus: sed contigisse narrat illo ipso tempore, et eo ipso in loco quo scribebat, imo videntibus, atque advertentibus illis, ob quos scribebat, et in quorum manus sua scripta tradebat. Atque de miraculorum istorum veritate provocat ad oculos, et aures Israelitarum. Vidistis, inquit saepe, et audistis, et eo nomine animum ipsorum erga Deum ingratum graviter et saepe objurgat.

XX. Similiter Paulus Apostolus, cum haberet apud Corinthios quosdam aemulos et invidos, qui Apostolatum ejus conabantur in dubium vocare, et suspectum reddere, de veritate sui Apostolatus provocat ad miracula et signa quae in medio eorum facta erant. Signa, inquit, Apostolatus edita sunt apud vos cum omni tolerantia, per signa, et prodigia, et virtutes: 2. Corinth. 12. v. 12. Et in prioris Epistolae capitibus 12. 13. 14. disserit de miraculosis Spiritus sancti donis, de dono sanationum, de operatione virtutum, de dono prophetiae, et de dono loquendi, et interpretandi peregrinas linguas subito Spiritus afflatu tanquam de rebus in medio eorum notis et usitatis: hortatur eos ad pacem, et monet ne sibi mutuo invideant ob hujusmodi dona, atque etiam reprehendit quod aliquando istiusmodi donis ambitiose uterentur: jubetque ut deinceps id faciant ad aedificationem, et donorum istorum legitimum usum praescribit.
english: Certainly impostors, and those whose mind is to deceive, are accustomed so to forge their lies that they cannot easily be charged with lying by those they want deceived. Thus Numa, who instituted most of the rites of Roman superstition, feigned that he had conversations by night with the nymph Egeria — truly alone with her alone, where no one could be a witness. In Muhammad's Qur'an also certain portentous things are narrated, yet not as done before men's eyes, but whose credit would rest with him alone. But if someone narrated portents and dreams, and nevertheless appealed about their truth to the senses of those he addressed — as if he were already recounting that by Moses the waters flowed back and grain rained while we were looking on, and willed to persuade us of that itself — this would no longer be imposture, but a certain kind of dementia plainly unusual and incredible; nor can this fall on one who is not altogether raving and stirred by black bile. Now those wonders held in Moses — that the sea was split, that the voice of God speaking was heard from mount Sinai, that in the desert it rained manna and quails, that torrents of water burst from the rock, and more of the same kind — those wonders, I say, Moses does not commemorate as things that happened at other times or in distant places: but he narrates them as having happened in that very time and in that very place where he was writing, indeed while those for whom he was writing were seeing and attending, and into whose hands he was handing his writings. And about the truth of those miracles he appeals to the eyes and ears of the Israelites. You have seen, he often says, and you have heard; and by that name he heavily and often rebukes their mind as ungrateful toward God.

Likewise the Apostle Paul, when he had among the Corinthians certain rivals and envious men who were trying to call his apostleship into doubt and render it suspect, appeals about the truth of his apostleship to miracles and signs done in their midst. The signs of apostleship, he says, were published among you with all patience, through signs and wonders and powers (2 Corinthians 12:12). And in chapters 12, 13, and 14 of the former epistle he discusses the miraculous gifts of the Holy Spirit — the gift of healings, the working of powers, the gift of prophecy, and the gift of speaking and interpreting foreign tongues by the Spirit's sudden breath — as things known and customary in their midst: he exhorts them to peace, warns them not to envy one another because of such gifts, and also rebukes that they sometimes used such gifts ambitiously; and he orders that thereafter they do it toward edification, and he prescribes the lawful use of those gifts.

source_text:
XXI. Si ergo ista omnia mendacia sunt et figmenta, certe Moses et Paulus non fuerunt, ut profani criminantur, veteratores et homines callidi, quibus propositum fuit homines decipere et mundo imponere. Nemo enim decipi potest in iis de quibus ad aures, ad oculos, et experientiam illius provocatur. Sed necesse est ut fuerint, absit blasphemiae dicto, homines plane furentes et insani. Atqui scripta eorum, judicibus ipsis Atheis, satis arguunt eos fuisse mentis compotes. Loquuntur enim sibi cohaerentia, et in quibus multum cernere est prudentiae et sapientiae.

XXII. Deinde, fingamus eos fuisse homines inanos, qui summa cum amentia, sive imprudentia scripserint, et pro veris obtruserint ea mendacia de quibus poterant palam et ab omnibus argui; Unde factum igitur ut Israelitae Mosen, Corinthii, Romani, Galatae, aliique Paulum tanquam viros divinos et sanctos suspexerint, et disciplinam eorum susceperint tanta cum reverentia: licet in multis carni ingrata sit, et onerosa et affectibus humanis repugnet: Nec ullum inde ad eos, qui sic decipi voluerunt, si res ex hominum sensu aestimetur, redierit emolumentum. Certe nullum miraculum, neque ullum portentum magis est incredibile quam hoc, doctrinam hominum insanorum, eorumque crassa et taeda mendacia, sine ullo adjumento vel divino, vel humano fidem tantam obtinuisse apud eos ipsos, quibus impossibile erat insaniam et mendacia eorum non agnoscere et animadvertere.

XXIII. Atque hic locum habet priscum illud dilemma, miracula quae narrantur in Scripturis vera sunt, vel non vera: si vera, vera quoque est doctrina et scriptura ad cujus confirmationem adhibita fuerunt. Si autem vera non sint, plusquam miraculum est doctrinam ita a sensu hominum abhorrentem, et refertam tot mendaciis, quae promptum erat cuivis arguere, nihilo minus absque ulla ope divina, vel humana, tanto cum ardore susceptam, et retentam tanta constantia, per exilia, per cruces, per tormenta, frementibus et indignantibus qui in mundo potestate et prudentia eminebant.

XXIV. Quandoquidem igitur quae Moses et Paulus memorant de miraculis factis in confirmationem Legis et Evangelii, eo modo scripta sunt, ut illi quibus scribebant statim agnoscere potuerint verumne an falsum dicerent, cum sint res de quibus ad eorum experientiam et sensus provocatur, et tamen scriptis illis tanta fides habita sit ab illis, qui primi ea susceperunt, et deinceps usque in hodiernum diem, plane necesse est eos vera scripsisse, et vera esse miracula quae narrant, ac proinde veram esse Scripturam et doctrinam in cujus confirmationem Deus illa fieri voluit.
english: If therefore all those things are lies and fictions, certainly Moses and Paul were not, as the profane charge, crafty dealers and cunning men whose purpose was to deceive men and impose on the world. For no one can be deceived in things about which appeal is made to his ears, eyes, and experience. But it is necessary that they were — far be the blasphemous saying — men plainly raging and insane. And yet their writings, with the atheists themselves as judges, prove enough that they were of sound mind. For they speak things coherent with themselves, and in which much prudence and wisdom is to be discerned.

Next, let us feign they were insane men who wrote with the highest madness or imprudence and thrust for true those lies about which they could be charged openly and by all. Whence then did it come about that the Israelites looked up to Moses, and the Corinthians, Romans, Galatians, and others to Paul, as divine and holy men, and received their discipline with so great reverence — although in many things it is ungrateful to the flesh, burdensome, and repugnant to human affections — and that no profit returned therefrom to those who thus willed to be deceived, if the matter is valued from men's sense? Certainly no miracle, nor any portent, is more incredible than this: that the doctrine of insane men, and their thick and foul lies, without any aid either divine or human, obtained so great faith among those very people for whom it was impossible not to recognize and notice their insanity and lies.

And here that ancient dilemma has place: the miracles narrated in the Scriptures are true, or not true. If true, the doctrine and scripture to whose confirmation they were applied are true also. But if they are not true, it is more than a miracle that a doctrine so abhorrent from men's sense, and stuffed with so many lies which anyone was ready to charge, was nonetheless received with so great ardor without any help divine or human, and retained with so great constancy through exiles, crosses, and tortures, while those eminent in the world by power and prudence were raging and indignant.

Since therefore what Moses and Paul recount about miracles done in confirmation of the Law and the Gospel is written in such a manner that those to whom they were writing could at once recognize whether they were saying true or false — since they are things about which appeal is made to their experience and senses — and yet so great faith was given to those writings by those who first received them, and thereafter even to this day, it is plainly necessary that they wrote true things, and that the miracles they narrate are true, and therefore that Scripture and the doctrine in whose confirmation God willed those things to happen are true.

source_text: XXV. Sed praeterea vera esse quae facta perhibentur a Mose miracula, et similiter ea quae tribuuntur Christo et Apostolis ejus, ex ipsa adversariorum confessione patet. Nam quod ad Christum attinet, Judaei qui sunt Christiani nominis hostes infestissimi, nec olim ausi sunt, nec etiamnum audent negare Christum patrasse miracula: sed nescio quid commenti sunt, ut eludant vim argumenti quod inde deducimus; nempe vel Christum illa fecisse arte magica, quam in Aegypto didicerat: vel virtute nominis illius tetragrammati, cujus rectam pronunciationem et expositionem tenebat. Fabulantur enim quicunque nomen illud scit recte pronunciare, posse vi illius nominis quavis opera miranda facere. Cujus commenti vanitas per se patet, nec opus est illud refutare. Solummodo hic notamus non parum inde confirmari veritatem miraculorum Christi: quandoquidem Judaei qui maxime ejus gloriae invident, non audent, neque possunt aperte negare illa facta fuisse. Et similiter Ethnicorum plurimi testimonium Mosi perhibuerunt, et veritatem agnoverunt historiae Mosaicae, ut videre est in libris Josephi contra Appionem, et Eusebii de praeparatione Evangelica.
english: But besides, that the miracles reported as done by Moses are true, and likewise those attributed to Christ and his Apostles, is clear from the adversaries' own confession. For as to Christ, the Jews who are most hostile enemies of the Christian name neither formerly dared, nor even now dare, to deny that Christ performed miracles: but they have invented I know not what to elude the force of the argument we draw therefrom — namely either that Christ did those things by magic art which he had learned in Egypt, or by virtue of that tetragrammaton Name whose right pronunciation and exposition he held. For they fable that whoever knows how to pronounce that name rightly can by its force do any wonderful works. The vanity of that invention is clear of itself, and there is no need to refute it. Here we only note that the truth of Christ's miracles is not a little confirmed thereby: since the Jews who most envy his glory neither dare nor are able openly to deny that those things were done. And likewise very many of the Gentiles bore testimony to Moses and acknowledged the truth of the Mosaic history, as is to be seen in the books of Josephus against Apion, and of Eusebius on the Preparation of the Gospel.

source_text: XXVI. Praecipue vero doctrinae Christianae veritatem probant, et divinam Scripturae originem arguunt Prophetarum praedictiones. Etenim solius Dei est certo et distincte praenosse futura contingentia, et demum multis post saeculis eventura. Ac proinde talia praedicere nemo potest nisi divini Spiritus afflatu. Sed Prophetae multa praedixerunt, quorum nullae in rerum natura causae apparebant, et quae diu post mortem eorum impleta sunt. Ita Esaias Cyrum nominavit, imperiumque, et miram felicitatem illius praedixit, centum quinquaginta annis antequam Cyrus nasceretur. Ita Jeremias Propheta septuaginta annos captivitatis Babylonicae praecise numeravit, priusquam Judaei essent Babylonem abducti. Ita denique Daniel de Monarchia Persarum et Graecorum, de successoribus Alexandri magni, et de Antiocho praesertim Epiphane qui templum Dei profanavit, clare admodum vaticinatus est.
english: Especially do the Prophets' predictions prove the truth of Christian doctrine, and argue Scripture's divine origin. For it belongs to God alone to foreknow future contingencies certainly and distinctly, and things that will come to pass only after many ages. And therefore no one can predict such things except by the afflatus of the divine Spirit. But the Prophets predicted many things for which no causes appeared in the nature of things, and which were fulfilled long after their death. Thus Isaiah named Cyrus, and predicted his empire and wondrous felicity, a hundred and fifty years before Cyrus was born. Thus Jeremiah the Prophet precisely numbered the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity before the Jews were led away to Babylon. Thus finally Daniel prophesied very clearly concerning the Monarchy of the Persians and of the Greeks, concerning the successors of Alexander the Great, and concerning Antiochus especially Epiphanes who profaned the temple of God.

source_text: XXVII. Sed quod praecipuum est, quae nos docet Evangelium de nativitate, de vita, de passione, de morte, de sepultura Jesu Christi, de ejusdem resurrectione et ascensione in coelum: item de fructu mortis et passionis ejus, de Gentium vocatione, Judaicae Gentis desolatione, et abrogatione cultus caeremonialis cum singulis fere harum rerum circumstantiis, reperiuntur in Prophetis clare et aperte praedicta. Inter alia insigne est Esaiae caput 53. ubi de Christi redemptoris nostri morte et passione, et pro peccatis mundi oblatione tam diserte et clare loquitur, ut videatur narrare rem gestam, non futuram praedicere: Et Danielis caput 9. ubi expresse designat tempus, quo Christus adventurus erat, statimque excindendus, et sacrificiis finem impositurus, nimirum post septuaginta annorum septimanas, quas sequuturum erat horrendum totius gentis Judaicae excidium: ita ut conferenti Mosis et Prophetarum oracula de Messia cum Evangelica de Christo historia, mirus ac plane stupendus statim appareat consensus. Unde manifeste probatur et Prophetarum libros esse divinos, quandoquidem continent praedictiones rerum, quae tanto post temporis spatio contigerunt: Et Evangelicam quoque historiam veram et divinam esse, quandoquidem Deus per Prophetas tot ante saeculis ipsi testimonium perhibuit.
english: But what is chief: what the Gospel teaches us concerning the nativity, life, passion, death, and burial of Jesus Christ, concerning his resurrection and ascension into heaven; likewise concerning the fruit of his death and passion, the calling of the Gentiles, the desolation of the Jewish nation, and the abrogation of the ceremonial worship, with nearly every circumstance of these things — these are found clearly and openly predicted in the Prophets. Among other things Isaiah chapter 53 is notable, where he speaks of the death and passion of Christ our Redeemer, and of his offering for the sins of the world, so expressly and clearly that he seems to narrate a thing already done, not to predict a future one (Isaiah 53). And Daniel chapter 9 expressly designates the time at which Christ was to come, and at once to be cut off, and to put an end to sacrifices — namely after seventy weeks of years, which the dreadful destruction of the whole Jewish nation was to follow (Daniel 9): so that for one comparing the oracles of Moses and the Prophets concerning the Messiah with the Gospel history of Christ, a wondrous and plainly stupendous consensus at once appears. Whence it is manifestly proved both that the Prophets' books are divine, since they contain predictions of things that happened after so great a space of time, and that the Gospel history is true and divine, since God through the Prophets bore testimony to it so many ages beforehand.

source_text: XXVIII. Porro haec vaticinia a Christianis non esse conficta testantur Judaei Christianorum hostes, et tamen propheticorum librorum assertatores, atque vindices acerrimi. Et praeterea quod maximum illud religionis Christianae odium non potuit eos compellere, ut vaticinia illa, tantopere ipsis adversa, e libris suis eradent, hoc ipsum, inquam, eos liberat a crimine, cujus Ethnici quidam suspectos eos reddere voluerint, quasi illa de Cyro et Alexandro magno vaticinia libris suis inseruissent ut gratiam istorum regum aucuparentur. Etenim si tantum sibi licere putavissent, non intacta fuissent illa vaticinia quibus a Christianis tantopere urgentur, praesertim illud Danielis de tempore adventus Christi et ejus excidio. Neque unquam aliquid tale de Judaeis suspicabitur, qui compertum habebit quanta religione, ne dicam superstitione erga libros sacros se gerant usque adeo ut librorum singulorum syllabas et apices in numerato habeant: et jejunium publicum indicant, si forte Scripturae codex per incuriam in terram deciderit. Adde quod quicunque attente perleget, et considerabit Prophetarum Danielis et Esaiae libros, facile agnoscet in iis omnia cohaerere, et esse eodem filo et genio contexta, nec quicquam reperiri quod quis merito suspicari possit, illic additum et insertum fuisse contra mentem et sensum authoris; quodque inde possit avelli citra totius operis ruinam et hiatum.
english: Further, that these oracles were not forged by Christians the Jews testify — enemies of the Christians, and yet the keenest assertors and defenders of the prophetic books. And besides, that that greatest hatred of the Christian religion could not compel them to erase from their books those oracles so greatly adverse to themselves — this itself, I say, frees them from the crime of which certain Gentiles wished to render them suspect, as if they had inserted into their books those oracles concerning Cyrus and Alexander the Great in order to court those kings' favor. For if they had thought so much allowed to them, those oracles by which Christians so greatly press them would not have remained untouched, especially that of Daniel concerning the time of Christ's advent and his cutting off. Nor will anyone ever suspect such a thing of the Jews who has ascertained with how great religion — not to say superstition — toward the sacred books they conduct themselves, even to such a degree that they keep the syllables and apices of each book numbered, and appoint a public fast if by chance a Scripture codex has fallen to the ground through carelessness. Add that whoever will attentively read through and consider the books of the Prophets Daniel and Isaiah will easily recognize that in them all things cohere and are woven with the same thread and genius, nor is anything found that anyone could deservedly suspect to have been added and inserted there against the author's mind and sense — and that could be torn away from them without the ruin and gap of the whole work.

source_text:
XXIX. Praeter haec ad conciliandam Scripturae authoritatem et venerationem, multa possunt argumenta sumi a Scripturae antiquitate, a cura Dei in ea conservanda, et a mundi in eam odio, justoque Dei judicio adversus osores et contemptores ejus. Etenim libri Mosis, qui sunt veluti totius Scripturae basis et fundamentum, omnium qui exstant sunt longe antiquissimi. Imo nulla sunt scripta quae Salomonis et Davidis antiquitatem aequent. Et tamen totus pene orbis adversus Scripturam bellum diu gessit, et conatus est illam abolere, ut Judaicis temporibus Antiochus ille Epiphanes: Christianorum vero memoria Imperatores Romani, quorum tanta fuit potentia et tam late patens imperium. Verum quantum sategit mundus eam abolere, tantum vigilavit Dei providentia ut salva et integra hucusque permaneret.

XXX. Neque parvi momenti est gentium, imo sectarum variarum hac in re consensus. Cum hodie vigeant tres praecipuae sectae, in multas alias postea subdivisae, Judaica scilicet, Christiana et Mahumetana quae partem orbis maximam occupant. Judaei, Christiani, et Mahumetani omnes Veteris Testamenti authoritatem agnoscunt. Novum vero Testamentum Judaei quidem rejiciunt, sed Mahumetani illud nobiscum in pretio habent, Christumque saltem tanquam maximum Dei Prophetam venerantur. Quid autem compellere potuit tot populos moribus et sectis inter se discrepantes, et acerrimis odiis sese mutuo prosequentes, ut libros hosce tanquam sacros et divinos probarent, nisi vis ipsa veritatis et divina quaedam efficacia?

XXXI. Quae quidem argumenta licet omnia forte perinde valida non sint, si per se sumantur singula, maximam tamen simul sumpta vim habent ad praestantiam Scripturae probandam et authoritatem illi conciliandam. Quin superiora illa quae latius explicuimus, talia esse judicamus, ut iis valide possit Scripturae authoritas asseri et probari etiam adversus Atheos et profanos, qui nihil regerere et opponere possunt quod vim aliquam habeat, cujusque vanitatem facile non sit ostendere.
english: Besides these, many arguments can be taken toward conciliating Scripture's authority and veneration from Scripture's antiquity, from God's care in preserving it, and from the world's hatred toward it, and God's just judgment against its haters and despisers. For the books of Moses, which are as it were the basis and foundation of the whole of Scripture, are by far the most ancient of all that exist. Indeed there are no writings that equal the antiquity of Solomon and David. And yet almost the whole world long waged war against Scripture and tried to abolish it — as in Jewish times that Antiochus Epiphanes, and in Christian memory the Roman Emperors, whose power was so great and whose empire so widely extended. But as much as the world worked to abolish it, so much did God's providence watch that it should remain safe and entire hitherto.

Nor is the consensus of the nations — indeed of the various sects — of small moment in this matter. Since today three chief sects thrive, afterward subdivided into many others — namely the Jewish, the Christian, and the Mahometan — which occupy the greatest part of the world. Jews, Christians, and Mahometans all acknowledge the authority of the Old Testament. The Jews indeed reject the New Testament, but the Mahometans hold it in esteem with us, and at least venerate Christ as God's greatest Prophet. What then could compel so many peoples, disagreeing among themselves in customs and sects, and mutually pursuing one another with the keenest hatreds, to approve these books as sacred and divine, unless the force of truth itself and a certain divine efficacy?

Which arguments, although perhaps not all equally valid if taken singly by themselves, nevertheless when taken together have the greatest force toward proving Scripture's excellence and conciliating authority to it. Nay, those superior ones which we have explained more widely we judge to be such that by them Scripture's authority can validly be asserted and proved even against atheists and the profane, who can retort and oppose nothing that has any force, and whose vanity it is not hard to show.

source_text: XXXII. Sed praeter argumenta ista quibus asseri potest adversus negantem Scripturae divinitas, Scriptura in se habet illustres admodum notas et indicia veritatis et divinitatis, quibus ipsa se probat et commendat menti bene affectae, et cujus oculus non est occoecatus praejudiciis et perversis affectibus: quamvis inde media ad disputandum apta sumi non possint, aut certe non ita valida atque efficacia. Etenim quemadmodum artis alicujus eximio operi, ut ex. gr. poemati Virgiliano, aut Apellis tabulae, insunt quaedam quibus authorem suum prodit, et ipsi se vindicat: Et haec aperte certe et clare agnoscuntur, licet imperitus ad ista non advertat, nec inde facile possint argumenta duci adversus negantem: Ita Scripturae sacrae alte impressa sunt spiritus divini vestigia, et coelestis originis notae, quas cernunt illi quibus mens obtenebrata non est, et qui sunt rerum divinarum periti, atque inde de illius divinitate certi fiunt: etsi homines ignari et profani ista floccifaciant, aut omnino non animadvertant. Et certe, si qui sunt docti in litteris humanioribus, cum librum quempiam humanum evolvunt, facile notant in eo genium et characterem quendam quo in authoris ejus cognitionem ducuntur. Qua ratione Critici germana scripta suis asserunt authoribus, Aristoteli verbi causa, vel Ciceroni, scripta vero spuria et supposititia expungunt, quamvis saepe istud quod notant et agnoscunt Critici sagaces, vix possint explicare et demonstrare alteri qui non sit in hisce versatus: An dubitabimus scripta Prophetica et Apostolica redolere divinum Spiritum, et iis inesse τι quod percipiat vir pius et doctus, et quo a scriptis humanis et Apocryphis illa internoscat; quanquam istud non posset adversus disputantem et repugnantem demonstrari?
english: But besides those arguments by which Scripture's divinity can be asserted against a denier, Scripture has in itself very illustrious notes and indications of truth and divinity, by which it proves and commends itself to a mind well affected, whose eye is not blinded by prejudices and perverse affections — although means suited for disputing cannot be taken from them, or certainly not means so valid and efficacious. For just as there inhere in some excellent work of art — for example a Virgilian poem, or a painting of Apelles — certain things by which it betrays its author and claims itself for him; and these are recognized openly, certainly, and clearly, although the unskilled does not attend to them, nor can arguments easily be drawn from them against a denier: so deeply impressed on sacred Scripture are the footprints of the divine Spirit, and the marks of heavenly origin, which those discern whose mind is not darkened, and who are skilled in divine things, and who thereby become certain of its divinity — although ignorant and profane men make light of those things, or do not notice them at all. And certainly, if any are learned in humane letters, when they unroll some human book they easily note in it a certain genius and character by which they are led into knowledge of its author. By that reason critics assert genuine writings to their authors — to Aristotle, for example, or to Cicero — but expunge spurious and supposititious writings, although often what sagacious critics note and recognize they can scarcely explain and demonstrate to another who is not versed in these things. Shall we doubt that the Prophetic and Apostolic writings savor of the divine Spirit, and that there inheres in them a something which a pious and learned man perceives, and by which he distinguishes them from human and Apocryphal writings — although that could not be demonstrated against a disputant who resists?

source_text:
XXXIII. Porro ejusmodi divinitatis notae quas Scripturae inesse dicimus animadverti possunt tam in rebus, quam in verbis. Et primo quidem in verbis, sive dicendi modo divinus quidam character per totam Scripturam elucet. Etenim, quum narrat res gestas id facit ingenue, simpliciter et nude, absque ullo fuco, absque ullis phaleris. Scriptores humani quum recitant res magnas, solent signa dare animi solliciti, et metuentis ne sibi non credatur. Conantur enim occulte amoliri, quae magis offendere possent, et rem, quantum in ipsis est, reddere credibilem. Cum vero ipsis de se aliquid dicendum est, vel jactant et ostentant propria facinora, vel timidi sunt et meticulosi, ac utuntur quibusdam excusationibus et praefationibus; quod certe oritur ex quadam imbecillitate, et prodit animum sibi diffidentem et non satis securum. Quod attinet autem ad scriptores sacros, etsi agant de rebus maximis, ac plane stupendis, et saepe eorum ministerio gestis, in eorum tamen narrationibus omnia recta sunt atque simplicia, neque est quidquam quod sapiat animum anxium atque sollicitum, ne ipsi fides denegetur. Sed ubique loquuntur quasi securi de hominum judiciis, rei dignitate et veritate freti: quod magnanimitatem et majestatem quandam Deo dignam arguit.

XXXIV. In Scripturae quoque praeceptis, correptionibus, et hortationibus, facile est observare majestatem quandam divinam. Pari enim authoritate alloquitur reges et plebeios, summos atque infimos, magistratus et privatos. Nemini blanditur, nemini connivet, authorque illius plane se ostendit ἀπροσωπόληπτον, favoris et odii, spei et metus expertem: quique sit idem erga omnes cujuscunque status et conditionis sint. Neque tamen oratio ferox, turgida, atque superba est. Sed in ea quidem apparet mira quaedam gravitas, verum quae lenitate summa, et pio erga homines affectu temperata sit.

XXXV. Cum vero docet, utitur συγκαταβάσει quadam, qua se captui rudium accommodat. Neque iis quae docet ornamenta conquirit ex arte et eloquentia, sed ea proprio pondere et utilitate commendat. Solent humanarum artium et scientiarum magistri, arti cuique terminos peculiares cudere, et ea quae tradunt tegere vocabulorum grandium involucris: ut ita arti suae dignitatem concilient, et mysterii aliquid affingant, quod suspiciat et miretur vulgus. At Scriptura res divinas explicat vocibus et phrasibus humanis, et e vulgo petitis. Cum vult aliquid illustrare, similia et exempla sua non longe quaerit: sed utitur exemplis obviis, et velut e trivio. Nec argumenta ejus talia sunt quae non possint nisi a doctis percipi: sed plerunque ejusmodi ut rusticus et idiota quisque vim eorum agnoscat.

XXXVI. Saepe quidem vocibus et phrasibus Scripturae inest aliquid peregrinum, et quod ab usu communi abhorret. Verum id deputandum est Hebraicae linguae genio, cui aures nostrae assuetae non sunt. Etenim scriptores sacri vel scripserunt Hebraica lingua, ut Moses et Prophetae: vel usi sunt phrasibus, et idiotismis linguae Hebraicae, etiamsi Graece scripserint, ut scriptores Novi Testamenti.

XXXVII. Denique Scriptura ubique candide et ingenue agit. Cumque homines soleant culpando sive laudando, minando sive promittendo res parvas et humiles inflare, et attollere magnificis vocibus et sublimibus metaphoris, Scriptura contra res maximas exprimit stylo plerunque tenui et vulgari, et verbis quae infra rei magnitudinem subsidunt. Quumque minatur et promittit, magnificae quidem sunt ejus promissiones et terrificae minae: sed ita tamen ut rei ipsius momentum, et gravitas longe superet sonum et emphasim verborum. Et tamen a summa illa Scripturae simplicitate nunquam abest gravitas et decor: Imo saepe illi juncta est mira dicendi sublimitas: adeo ut ipse Longinus Rhetor Ethnicus, et Christianorum hostis infestissimus differens περὶ ὕψους, id est, de sublimi genere dicendi, citet illius exemplum ex Mose, Quemadmodum, inquit, Legislator Hebraeorum dixit et facta sunt.
english: Further, such notes of divinity as we say inhere in Scripture can be noticed both in things and in words. And first in words, or in the manner of speaking, a certain divine character shines forth through the whole of Scripture. For when it narrates deeds it does so ingenuously, simply, and nakedly, without any paint, without any trappings. Human writers, when they recite great things, are accustomed to give signs of an anxious mind, fearing lest it not be believed. For they try secretly to remove what could more offend, and to render the matter, as much as in them lies, credible. But when something must be said by them concerning themselves, either they boast and display their own deeds, or they are timid and fearful and use certain excuses and prefaces — which certainly arises from a certain weakness, and betrays a mind distrusting itself and not secure enough. But as for the sacred writers, although they treat of things greatest and plainly stupendous, and often done by their ministry, in their narrations nevertheless all things are straight and simple, nor is there anything that savors an anxious and solicitous mind lest faith be denied them. But everywhere they speak as if secure concerning men's judgments, relying on the dignity and truth of the matter: which argues a magnanimity and a certain majesty worthy of God.

In Scripture's precepts, corrections, and exhortations also it is easy to observe a certain divine majesty. With equal authority it addresses kings and commoners, the highest and the lowest, magistrates and private persons. It flatters no one, connives with no one, and its author plainly shows himself impartial (ἀπροσωπόληπτον) — devoid of favor and hatred, of hope and fear, and the same toward all of whatever status and condition they are. Nor yet is the speech fierce, swollen, and proud. But in it there appears a certain wondrous gravity, yet tempered with the highest gentleness and a pious affection toward men.

But when it teaches, it uses a certain condescension (συγκαταβάσει) by which it accommodates itself to the capacity of the rude. Nor does it seek for what it teaches ornaments from art and eloquence, but commends them by their own weight and usefulness. Teachers of human arts and sciences are accustomed to forge peculiar terms for each art, and to cover what they hand down with wrappers of grand words, that they may win dignity for their art and feign some mystery for the crowd to look up to and wonder at. But Scripture explains divine things with human words and phrases drawn from the crowd. When it wants to illustrate something, it does not seek its likenesses and examples far off, but uses obvious examples, as if from the crossroads. Nor are its arguments such as only the learned can perceive: but usually of such a sort that every rustic and unlearned person recognizes their force.

Often indeed there is in Scripture's words and phrases something foreign, and abhorrent from common use. But that is to be assigned to the genius of the Hebrew tongue, to which our ears are not accustomed. For the sacred writers either wrote in the Hebrew tongue, as Moses and the Prophets, or used phrases and idiotisms of the Hebrew tongue even when they wrote in Greek, as the writers of the New Testament.

Finally Scripture everywhere acts candidly and ingenuously. And whereas men are accustomed, whether blaming or praising, threatening or promising, to inflate small and humble things and raise them with magnificent words and sublime metaphors, Scripture on the contrary expresses the greatest things in a style usually thin and common, and with words that sink below the magnitude of the matter. And when it threatens and promises, its promises are indeed magnificent and its threats terrific: yet so that the moment and gravity of the thing itself far surpass the sound and emphasis of the words. And yet from that highest simplicity of Scripture gravity and decorum are never absent. Indeed there is often joined to it a wondrous sublimity of speaking: so much so that Longinus himself, the Gentile rhetor and most hostile enemy of Christians, treating of the sublime (περὶ ὕψους), cites its example from Moses: "As," he says, "the Legislator of the Hebrews said, and they were done" (Genesis 1:3).

source_text: XXXVIII. Jam vero, si ad res ipsas Scripturae attendamus, in iis apparebunt longe adhuc illustriores et clariores divinitatis notae. Quaecunque autem Scriptura continentur vel sunt historiae et narrationes rerum praeteritarum, vel sunt vaticinia et praedictiones rerum futurarum, vel dogmata et praecepta quae nullam temporis differentiam notant. Porro historiam praecipue duo commendant, nempe rerum veritas, tum quoque pondus et momentum: quae duo Historia sacra eminenti quodam modo sibi vendicat. Et primo quidem historia sacra multa et magna habet veritatis indicia. Vel enim illi ratio, et ipsa rerum natura suffragatur, ut historiae creationis mundi, quem e nihilo atque in tempore factum esse validissimis probatur argumentis. Ut historiae, eorum etiam veterum et externorum monumenta testimonium ejus veritati perhibent, ut ex. gr. in historia de diluvio universali, de aedificatione turris Babylonicae, de conflagratione Sodomae et Gomorrhae, de Israelitarum exitu ex Aegypto, quibus mentio fit apud probatos et priscos historicos quorum fragmenta supersunt apud Eusebium, Josephum et alios: et nonnulli etiam in manibus hominum versantur.
english: Now if we attend to the things themselves of Scripture, notes of divinity still far more illustrious and clearer will appear in them. Whatever Scripture contains is either histories and narrations of things past, or oracles and predictions of things future, or dogmas and precepts that mark no difference of time. Further, two things chiefly commend a history: the truth of the matters, and also their weight and moment — both of which sacred history claims for itself in an eminent way. And first, sacred history has many and great indications of truth. For either reason and the very nature of things give it suffrage, as with the history of the world's creation, which is proved by most strong arguments to have been made from nothing and in time. As for history, even the monuments of ancient and external writers also afford testimony to its truth — for example in the history of the universal flood, of the building of the tower of Babel, of the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, of the Israelites' exit from Egypt — of which mention is made among approved and ancient historians whose fragments survive in Eusebius, Josephus, and others, and some of which are still current in men's hands.

source_text: XXXIX. Adde quod Historia sacra in multis ipsa se probat sua ingenuitate, et verisimilitudine, habetque eas veritatis notas, quas habent probi quique historici, ut videre est in libris Samuelis et Regum. Gentium quoque, urbium et regionum nomina, quae fuerunt olim, et hodie remanent, fidem creant iis quae Scriptura narrat de posteris Noe a quibus post diluvium orbis de novo habitari coepit, et incolis repleri, ut planum sit conferenti nomina illa, quae Moses recitat cum populorum et gentium nominibus. Quae vero fidem videntur superare, et miranda sunt ac plane stupenda, eo modo scripta sunt, ut impossibile sit, qui scripsit esse mentitum, quandoquidem provocat ad testes innumeros a quibus revinci potuit, qui tamen ejus scripta tanquam divina susceperunt, et pro talibus posteris commendârunt: ut supra ostensum est de miraculis quae a Mose narrantur, et de quibus apud Paulum Apostolum mentio.
english: Add that sacred history in many places proves itself by its own ingenuousness and likelihood, and has those notes of truth which every honest historian has, as may be seen in the books of Samuel and of Kings.
