The names of nations, cities, and regions that once were and still remain today also create faith for what Scripture narrates concerning Noah's posterity, from whom after the flood the world began to be inhabited anew and filled with dwellers — plain to anyone who compares those names Moses recites with the names of peoples and nations. But the things that seem to surpass belief, and are wondrous and plainly stupendous, are written so that the writer cannot have lied: he appeals to innumerable witnesses who could have refuted him, yet who received his writings as divine and so commended them to posterity — as was shown above concerning the miracles Moses narrates, and of which mention is made in the Apostle Paul.

source_text: XL. Praeterea Historicis sacris fidem astruit sinceritas et candor eorum, qui tantus est, ut vitia sua non dissimulent, et saepe sibi suisque multas inurant ignominiae notas. Imo Scripturae historiam credibilem reddunt ipsae poetarum fabulae. Si quis enim veteres poetarum fabulas diligenter inspiciat, et cum historia sacra conferat, reperiet istas fabulas umbras quasdam esse rerum, quarum corpus Scriptura habet, et originem traxisse e veris historiis quae traditione filiorum Noe per totum orbem disseminatae sunt, et tandem lapsu temporis corruptae et interpolatae: ut multis exemplis posset fieri manifestum, et rem facilem reddiderunt viri docti, qui hac in re operam posuerunt.
english: Moreover sincerity and candor build faith for the sacred historians — candor so great that they do not hide their own vices, and often brand themselves and their own with many marks of ignominy. Nay, the poets' very fables make Scripture's history credible. For if anyone diligently inspects the ancient poets' fables and compares them with sacred history, he will find those fables to be shadows of things whose body Scripture has, and to have drawn their origin from true histories spread through the whole world by the tradition of Noah's sons, and later corrupted and interpolated by the lapse of time: which could be made plain by many examples, and which learned men who have labored in this matter have made easy to see.

source_text: XLI. Jam vero si quis historiae sacrae pondus et momentum perpendere velit, quae res majoris ponderis et momenti esse fingi possunt, quam quae non modo ad gentem et rempublicam aliquam pertinent, sed ad totam Ecclesiam quam Deus sibi e mundo selegit, imo ad mundum universum, ad angelos Coelorum incolas, et ad Deum ipsum, qui est prima rerum omnium causa. Haec vero sunt circa quae versatur Scripturae sacrae historia. Nam Scriptura nobis recitat quae fuerint hujus universi primordia et incunabula, et quomodo Deus olim omnia condidit et extare jussit: unde genus humanum natum et propagatum est, quomodo per totum orbem terrarum se diffudit, et quae fuerint initio divisiones gentium et linguarum. Narrat angelicorum spirituum apparitiones, et frequentia cum hominibus colloquia: Deique ipsius admiranda facta in Ecclesia regenda et tuenda, humanique generis salute procuranda. Cum quibus si quis conferat historias Graecorum sive Romanorum, nil inveniet cujus momentum et gravitas possit ulla ex parte cum hisce comparari.
english: Now if anyone wishes to weigh the weight and moment of sacred history, what matters of greater weight and moment can be imagined than those which pertain not only to some nation and commonwealth, but to the whole Church which God selected for himself out of the world — nay, to the universal world, to the angels who inhabit Heaven, and to God himself, who is the first cause of all things? These are the things about which sacred Scripture's history turns. For Scripture tells us what were this universe's beginnings and cradles, and how God once founded all things and ordered them to exist; whence the human race was born and propagated; how it spread through the whole earth; and what were at the beginning the divisions of nations and of tongues. It narrates the appearances of angelic spirits and their frequent colloquies with men, and God's own admirable deeds in ruling and guarding the Church and procuring the human race's salvation. If anyone compares Greek or Roman histories with these, he will find nothing whose moment and gravity can in any part match them.

source_text: XLII. Praecipue in vaticiniis et afflatibus Prophetarum divinitatis maxima lux affulget, de qua jam antea diximus, quoniam non tantum sufficit ad pium et fidelem animum persuadendum, sed etiam plurimum valet ad verbi Dei hostes redarguendos, et divinitatem illius comprobandam etiam adversus profanos. Nam si vaticiniorum sacrorum materiam spectes, non sunt de rebus nullius aut exigui momenti, sed quae ad Dei gloriam et totius Humani generis salutem spectant. Neque prophetarum praedictiones perplexae sunt et ambiguae, ut Ethnicorum olim oracula, sed clarae adeo, atque perspicuae, ut in iis personae et locus designentur propriis saepe nominibus, et precise complementi tempus praefiniatur. Neque etiam sunt fallaces et incertae, sed tales ut ipso eventu pleraeque jam comprobatae sint.
english: Especially in the Prophets' oracles and inspirations the greatest light of divinity shines — of which we spoke already above — because it not only suffices to persuade a pious and faithful mind, but also avails much to refute the enemies of God's Word and to prove its divinity even against the profane. For if you regard the matter of the sacred oracles, they are not about things of no or slight moment, but about what looks to God's glory and the salvation of the whole human race. Nor are the prophetic oracles entangled and ambiguous, as the pagans' oracles once were, but so clear and plain that persons and place are often named in them, and the time of fulfillment is fixed beforehand with precision. Nor are they fallacious and uncertain: by the event itself most have already been proved.

source_text:
XLIII. Sua quoque luce non carent, imo multo maximam habent, Scripturae sacrae praecepta et dogmata. Quod ut clarius appareat, notandum est illa duorum esse generum. Multa enim docet et jubet Scriptura quorum homines per naturam notitiam aliquam habent, sed confusam valde atque vacillantem. Verum Scriptura ista luculentius patefecit, et docuit plene atque accurate. Ejusmodi sunt quae Scriptura tradit de Dei natura atque attributis, nempe de Dei essentia aeterna, immensa, et immutabili, et de infinita illius potentia, sapientia, bonitate, atque etiam justitia, de creatione mundi et omnium quae in eo sunt, de providentia Dei qua cuncta conservat, regit, et administrat: Item de hominis officio tam erga Deum, quam erga proximum, qualia sunt esse Deum supra omnia amandum, omnia in ipsius gloriam referenda, ipsum esse sedulo colendum atque invocandum, ipsi fidendum, et in curam illius recumbendum esse. Proximum quoque esse diligendum, omnibus benefaciendum, ferendas esse injurias, humiliter de se sentiendum esse, cogitationes et affectus intimos puros esse servandos, et uno verbo, omnia et singula fere praecepta vitae Christianae, quae omni ex parte pura et sincera esse debet, et a qua debet abesse spurcitia et luxuria omnis. Illa certe et similia probat conscientiae sensus, confirmat ratio, et eorum quaedam rudimenta cernuntur in Ethnicorum libris. Etenim nonnulla de Deo, de pietate atque hominis officio non contemnenda tradunt. Sed tamen obscure, parce, frigide, dubitanter, atque cum plurimorum errorum admixtione. Scriptura vero ista in clara luce ponit, pleneque et aperte docet: ita ut postquam nobis lux illius splenduit, miremur res tam certas atque indubitatas nonnisi tenuiter, dubitanter et obscure a praestantissimis ingeniis perspectas traditasque fuisse. Cum autem ingenia illa praestantissima, res illas, quarum jam veritatem cernimus Scripturae beneficio, ita jejune et obscure tradiderint, Scriptura vero ita plene et perspicue; neque tamen Scriptores sacri eruditione, aut naturae dotibus supra caeteros homines praecelluerint, imo contra fuerint plerique scientiarum humanarum rudes et idiotae, necesse est illos alio quam naturae lumine ductos esse, atque a Deo doctos et inspiratos.

XLIV. Sed praeter ista, quorum homines per naturam tenuem quandam, atque fugientem cognitionem habent, Scriptura sacra multa docet quae rationem superant, neque mens humana illa capere potest, nec eorum habet certa argumenta: Verumtamen tam bene cohaerent cum iis quae probat conscientiae sensus, et de quibus recta ratio convincitur, et prioribus illis tam consentanea sunt, et ita congruenter et apposite superstructa, ut satis appareat non esse commenta humana, sed sapientiae divinae mysteria. Talis est ex. gr. doctrina de peccatorum nostrorum expiatione per Christi Dei et hominis mortem et oblationem in cruce factam, quae congruere maxime cernitur cum Dei justitia et misericordia. Hoc enim modo justitiae Dei satisfactum est, dum peccata nostra in Christo punita sunt, et misericordiae, dum nobis condonata. Et cum hac doctrina cohaeret dogma illud tam sublime et excelsum de tribus personis divinis in una essentia. Nam nisi Dei filius Deus esset, et aequalis patri, sacrificium ejus non fuisset valoris infiniti, quale requirebatur, ut eo peccata nostra expiarentur, quandoquidem infinitam poenam promeruerant. Et talis quoque doctrina de mortuorum resurrectione. Videtur enim esse rationi consentaneum, ut homo qui in corpore bene vel male agit, in corpore quoque poenam, vel mercedem accipiat juste vel injuste factorum: quod cum in hac vita non fiat, justitiae Dei congruit, ut corpora nostra, quae mors in pulverem redegit, animabus suis denuo jungantur, ut ita homini integro, vel bene, vel male sit, prout bene, vel male egerit.

XLV. Sed praeterea maximum divinitatis indicium in Scriptura sacra est ejus efficacia, qua intus in homine agit, partim quidem terrendo conscientias, et peccati sensu afficiendo, partim erigendo animum attritum et conscientias afflictas consolando: Sed praecipue ita hominem immutando, ut peccatum odio habeat, et pietatem veramque virtutem ex animo sectetur: qua quidem efficacia nihil potentius est in fidelibus confirmandis, licet ad assensum compellere non possit eos, qui nondum istam efficaciam senserunt, et adversus Dei verbum obduruerunt. Et tamen homo maxime profanus, etiamsi verbi Dei efficaciam non senserit, si tamen illud attente consideret, facile potest agnoscere hoc verbum tale esse, ut summam tranquillitatem et gaudium generet in iis qui illi firmiter credunt, eosque ad omne bonum opus et omnem virtutem compellat.

XLVI. Atque haec pauca sufficiat delibasse de hoc argumento quod nunquam exhauriri potest, quodque fusius et copiosius tractatur a viris doctis, quorum vestigia sequimur, et qui nobis facem praetulerunt. Hoc autem addendum videtur, nempe characteres hosce divinitatis, quos in Scriptura fulgere diximus, non esse quaerendos in singulis Scripturae partibus a toto separatis, sed in scriptis divinis prout considerantur conjunctim, et secundum se tota. Nec enim putandum est quamvis Canonici libri pericopen, certam habere notam, qua possit ab Apocrypha discerni et distingui.
english: Sacred Scripture's precepts and dogmas also do not lack their own light — nay, they have by far the greatest. That this may appear more clearly, note that they are of two kinds. For Scripture teaches and commands many things of which men have by nature some notice, but very confused and wavering. Yet Scripture has laid those things open more lucidly, and taught them fully and accurately. Of this sort are what Scripture hands down concerning God's nature and attributes — namely concerning God's eternal, immense, and immutable essence; concerning his infinite power, wisdom, goodness, and also justice; concerning the creation of the world and of all that is in it; concerning God's providence by which he conserves, rules, and administers all things; likewise concerning man's office both toward God and toward the neighbor: that God is to be loved above all, all things referred to his glory, himself carefully worshiped and invoked, trusted, and that one is to rest upon his care; that the neighbor also is to be loved, good done to all, injuries borne, oneself thought of humbly, innermost thoughts and affections kept pure — and in a word, nearly all and each of the precepts of the Christian life, which ought to be pure and sincere in every part, and from which all filth and luxury ought to be absent. Those things and the like the sense of conscience proves, reason confirms, and certain rudiments of them are discerned in the pagans' books. For they hand down some things concerning God, piety, and man's office that are not contemptible — yet obscurely, sparingly, coldly, doubtfully, and mixed with very many errors. But Scripture places those things in clear light and teaches them fully and openly: so that after its light has shone on us, we wonder that things so certain and undoubted were seen and handed down only thinly, doubtfully, and obscurely by the most excellent minds. But when those most excellent minds handed down so jejunely and obscurely the things whose truth we now discern by Scripture's benefit, while Scripture handed them down so fully and perspicuously — and yet the sacred writers did not excel other men by erudition or by nature's gifts, but on the contrary most were rude and unlearned in the human sciences — it is necessary that they were led by another light than nature's, and taught and inspired by God.

But besides those things of which men have by nature only a thin and fleeing cognition, sacred Scripture teaches many things that surpass reason, which the human mind cannot grasp, and for which it has no certain arguments. Yet they cohere so well with what the sense of conscience proves and right reason is convinced of, and agree so well with those prior things, and are built upon them so fittingly, that it sufficiently appears they are not human inventions but mysteries of divine wisdom. Such, for example, is the doctrine of the expiation of our sins through the death and offering on the cross of Christ, God and man — which is discerned to agree most with God's justice and mercy. For in this manner God's justice was satisfied while our sins were punished in Christ, and mercy while they were forgiven us. And with this doctrine coheres that dogma so sublime and lofty concerning three divine persons in one essence. For unless the Son of God were God and equal to the Father, his sacrifice would not have been of infinite value, such as was required that by it our sins be expiated, inasmuch as they had deserved infinite punishment. And such also is the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead. For it seems agreeable to reason that a man who acts well or ill in the body should also receive in the body punishment or reward for what was done justly or unjustly — which, since it does not happen in this life, agrees with God's justice that our bodies, which death has reduced to dust, be joined again to their souls, so that it may go well or ill with the whole man according as he acted well or ill.

But moreover the greatest indication of divinity in sacred Scripture is its efficacy, by which it acts inwardly in a man — partly by terrifying consciences and affecting them with the sense of sin, partly by raising the bruised mind and consoling afflicted consciences; but chiefly by so changing the man that he hates sin and pursues piety and true virtue from the soul. By this efficacy nothing is more powerful in confirming the faithful, although it cannot compel to assent those who have not yet felt that efficacy and have hardened against God's Word. And yet even a most profane man, if he has not felt the efficacy of God's Word, yet if he considers it attentively, can easily recognize that this Word is such as to generate the highest tranquillity and joy in those who firmly believe it, and to compel them to every good work and every virtue.

And let these few things suffice as a taste of this argument, which can never be exhausted, and which is treated more fully and copiously by learned men whose footsteps we follow and who have borne the torch before us. But this seems worth adding: that these characters of divinity which we said shine in Scripture are not to be sought in single parts of Scripture separated from the whole, but in the divine writings as they are considered jointly and as wholes in themselves. For it is not to be thought that any pericope of a Canonical book has a certain mark by which it can be discerned and distinguished from the Apocrypha.

source_text: XLVII. Ac praeterea fatendum est divinitatis notas et indicia, quae Scripturae inesse diximus, in singulis Scripturae libris non esse pari fulgore conspicuas. Nam quemadmodum stella luce a stella differt, ita quidam Scripturae libri uberiores et splendidiores divini Spiritus radios emittunt, alii vero longe exiliores et obscuriores. Sic ex. gr. in Veteri Testamento longe impar est divinitatis fulgor in libro Esther, aut libro Ruth, quam sit in Mosis Pentateucho, et Prophetia Isaiae. Neque tam aperta sunt spiritus Christi vestigia in epistola Jacobi, aut Judae, quam in plerisque Pauli epistolis, et quatuor Evangeliis.
english: Besides, we must admit that the marks and signs of divinity we said belong in Scripture do not shine with equal brilliance in every book. Just as one star differs from another in light, so some books of Scripture send out richer and more splendid rays of the divine Spirit, while others send out far feebler and more obscure ones. In the Old Testament, for example, Esther and Ruth are far dimmer in divine brightness than Moses's Pentateuch and the Prophecy of Isaiah. And the vestiges of Christ's Spirit are less open in the epistles of James and Jude than in most of Paul's epistles and the four Gospels.

source_text:
I. Superiori disputatione exposuimus quam lucem, id est, quae argumenta et indicia Veritatis, et originis divinae, habeat Scriptura sacra: sequitur ut inquiramus, quomodo lux illa percipitur, Et An, et Quousque opera Spiritus sancti necessaria sit, ut Scripturam pro vera et divina agnoscamus.

II. Hic autem distinguendum est, inter opinionem quandam fluxam et evanidam, et fidem veram et salutarem, quae Deo sit grata et accepta. Quandam enim opinionem de Scripturae divinitate potest aliquis concipere, eo adductus humanis quibusdam incitamentis, absque ulla Spiritus interna operatione: atque haec est quam Scholae fidem humanam et acquisitam vocant. Sic haeretici multi improbissimi et perversissimi authoritatem Scripturae non negant, illamque divinitus inspiratam agnoscunt. Imo Judaei ipsi infideles Veteris saltem Testamenti authoritatem acriter defendunt: Mahumetani vero utriusque Testamenti libros pro divinis habere, et revereri, perhibentur. Neque tamen necesse est, ut in omnibus illis haereticis et infidelibus Spiritum sanctum agere putemus, et intus eorum mentes illuminare.
english: In the previous disputation we set out what light sacred Scripture has — that is, what arguments and marks of truth and of divine origin. Next we ask how that light is perceived, and whether, and how far, the Holy Spirit's work is needed if we are to acknowledge Scripture as true and divine.

Here, though, we must distinguish a fleeting, vanishing opinion from true saving faith that is pleasing and acceptable to God. A person can form an opinion that Scripture is divine, drawn by some human incentives, without any inward work of the Spirit; the Schools call that human and acquired faith. Many utterly wicked and perverse heretics do not deny Scripture's authority and grant that it is divinely inspired. Unbelieving Jews themselves fiercely defend at least the Old Testament's authority, and Mohammedans are said to hold and revere both Testaments as divine. Still we need not suppose that the Holy Spirit is at work in all those heretics and unbelievers, illuminating their minds within.

source_text: III. Verum ut certam ac legitimam fidem, et quae sit alicujus ad salutem momenti de Scriptura concipiamus, omnino necessarium est ut Spiritus sanctus sese in mentes nostras insinuet, et arcano modo in iis operetur: Unde est quod ejusmodi fidem, Scholae divinam, et infusam vocant. Hoc autem ipsa Scriptura docet multis in locis. Nam apud Johannem Christus Dominus noster affirmat neminem posse ad ipsum venire, id est, in eum credere, et doctrinam ejus amplecti, nisi quem traxerit Pater, et qui Patrem intus docentem non audiverit: Nemo, inquit, potest venire ad me, nisi Pater qui misit me traxerit eum. Scriptum est in Prophetis, Et erunt omnes docti a Deo. Quisquis ergo audivit et didicit a Patre, venit ad me. Joh. cap. 6. Praeterea Paulus, 1 Corinth. 12. disertis verbis affirmat, Neminem posse dicere Jesum Dominum nisi per Spiritum sanctum. Et cap. 2. ejusdem Epistolae, de mysteriis Evangelii loquens, Deus, inquit, nobis ea revelavit per Spiritum suum. Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur, etiam profunda Dei. Nos vero Spiritum mundi non accepimus, sed Spiritum qui est ex Deo, ut sciamus quae a Deo donata sunt nobis. Et paulo post, Animalis autem homo non percipit ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei, stultitia enim ei sunt, et non potest intelligere, quoniam spiritualiter dijudicantur. Atque hinc est quod fides dicitur donum Dei, Eph. 2. Gratia estis salvati per fidem, idque non ex vobis: Dei donum est.
english: Saving, legitimate faith about Scripture — faith that actually matters for salvation — does not arise without the Holy Spirit slipping into our minds and working there in secret. The Schools therefore name that faith divine and infused. Scripture itself says so again and again.

Christ teaches in John that no one can come to him (believe in him and take his teaching) unless the Father draws that person, and unless that person has heard the Father teaching within. His words: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. It is written in the Prophets, And they shall all be taught by God. Therefore everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me" (John 6).

Paul is just as plain: no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12). On the Gospel mysteries he adds (1 Corinthians 2): "God has revealed them to us by his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God. But we have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know the things freely given to us by God." Then: "But the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned." That is why faith itself is called God's gift (Ephesians 2): "By grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God."

source_text:
IV. Porro istam Spiritus Dei in animis nostris operationem necessariam reddit ingenii humani pravitas, et tenebrae quas peccatum accersivit. Etenim Scriptura sacra multa continet, quae pravis et distortis nostris affectibus repugnant. Unde fit ut homo carnalis ab illa abhorreat, et eam aversetur, quod impedit ne ejus veritatem agnoscat, et rectum de ea judicium ferat: quandoquidem prout quisque affectus est, ita judicat. Deinde mens hominis in universum ita per peccatum obscurata est, ut, etiam in naturalibus, non possit non hallucinari, et saepissime falli. Ac proinde multo minus quae supra naturam sunt certo agnoscere et percipere potest. Ad hoc igitur necesse est, ut Spiritus sanctus mentis tenebras nativas dispellat, et fumos illos, quibus affectus pravi intellectum obscurant, et praepediunt ne possit veritatem cernere.

V. Imo hanc Spiritus operationem ad fidem animis nostris ingenerandam necessario exigit, non tantum naturae nostrae depravatio, et tenebrae ex peccato ortae, sed genius ipse doctrinae in Scriptura traditae. Siquidem multa mysteria continet, quae non tantum naturam corruptam, sed naturam humanam in se, etiam citra peccatum, consideratam, omnino superant: ita ut ab ea, non solum non inveniri et excogitari, sed nec intelligi et percipi possint. Ideoque necesse est, ut Spiritus sanctus non tantum mentes nostras peccato caecas sanet, sed etiam ut intellectum nostrum non parum supra statum naturalem extollat, ut ad res tantas possit assurgere.
english: Human crookedness, plus the darkness sin has piled on, forces this need for God's Spirit in the soul. Scripture is full of matter that fights our warped loves. The flesh-bound person therefore recoils and turns away — and that recoil blocks true acknowledgment and right judgment, because we all judge by the grain of our affections.

Sin also darkens the mind so thoroughly that even among ordinary natural things we keep hallucinating and falling into error. How much less, then, can we be sure of what stands above nature? So the Holy Spirit must drive out the mind's native night, and clear the smoke by which wicked desires cloud the intellect and stop it from seeing truth.

Nor is depravity the only reason. The very character of the doctrine Scripture teaches also requires this Spirit work if faith is to be born in us. Scripture holds mysteries that outrun not only fallen nature but human nature taken by itself, even without sin. Nature cannot invent them, think them up, or even understand and take them in. So the Spirit must heal minds sin has blinded, and must also lift the intellect well above its natural level, until it can rise to things that great.

source_text: VI. Quis sit autem istius operationis modus, res valde obscura est et explicatu difficilis: quod forte cuipiam mirum videri posset. Cum enim illa Spiritus sancti operatio in animis nostris fiat, videmur id nosse debere sensu ipso et experientia. Sed tamen in eo nihil est quod mirari debeamus. Etenim multa in nobis experimur, imo multa operamur ipsi, quorum tamen rationem et modum non tenemus, nec valemus intelligere. Sic quotidie experimur nos videre et intelligere, et tamen, quum explicandum est qua ratione visio et intellectio fiat, acutissimi quique et doctissimi viri haerent, nec satis possunt se expedire. Et adhuc lis est inter Physicos et Mathematicos, An visio fiat per radiorum emissionem, An vero per receptionem specierum visibilium. Igitur etsi fidelis quisque experiatur se verbum Dei certa fide amplecti, plenumque et firmum assensum Scripturae sacrae tribuere, admirationem movere non debet, si Theologi haereant in exponendo, quomodo fides illa nobis ingeneretur, et qua ratione Spiritus assensum illum in nobis pariat. Qua de re sententiam nostram breviter exponemus.
english: But what the mode of that operation is remains very obscure and hard to explain — which might seem strange. Since the Holy Spirit's work happens in our souls, we seem as if we ought to know it by sense and experience itself. Yet there is nothing odd here. We experience many things in ourselves, and we ourselves do many things, whose reason and mode we still do not grasp and cannot understand.

Every day we experience that we see and understand; yet when someone must explain how vision and intellection happen, the sharpest and most learned men stick fast and cannot disentangle themselves. Physicists and mathematicians still dispute whether vision happens by the emission of rays or by the reception of visible species.

So although every believer experiences that he embraces God's Word with certain faith and gives full, firm assent to sacred Scripture, it should not surprise us if theologians stick fast when they try to explain how that faith is generated in us, and how the Spirit brings forth that assent. On that we will briefly set out our view.

source_text:
VII. Primo igitur certum et indubitatum nobis est Spiritum sanctum, hominis, quem ad fidem adducit, sic disponere et afficere mentem, quae alioqui in his caligat et caecutit, ut verbi Dei et Scripturae lucem percipiat et agnoscat, hoc est, serio advertat ad ea argumenta, notas, et ἀξιώματα, quibus verbum Dei verum et divinum probatur, et de iis recte judicet, indeque, sicuti par est, de illius divina veritate persuadeatur. Quod dum Spiritus intus agit, inde dicitur nobis novos oculos. De quibus Moses Deut. 29. Vos vidistis, inquit, universa quae fecit Dominus coram vobis in terra Aegypti Pharaoni et omnibus servis ejus, universaeque terrae illius, tentationes magnas quas viderunt oculi tui, signa illa portentaque ingentia: et non dedit vobis Dominus cor intelligens, et oculos videntes, et aures quae possint audire usque in praesentem diem. Et hanc Dei opem implorabat David Psalm. 119. pausa Ghimel, Revela, inquit, oculos meos, et considerabo mirabilia de lege tua. Nam, per legis mirabilia, intelligit divinae sapientiae documenta, quae per legem Dei sparsa sunt: de quibus mens nostra carnalis rite judicare non potest, obstante nativa nostra hebetudine, pravitate et ignorantia, quae sunt veluti quoddam velum mentis nostrae oculis oppansum, quod Spiritus sanctus in fidelibus tollit.

VIII. An autem illa Spiritus sancti operatio, qua sic mentem nostram afficit, ut advertat ad lucem in Scriptura fulgentem, eamque percipiat, praecise et sola per se considerata, sufficiat ad plenam et certam satis fidem de Scriptura sacra nobis ingenerandam, dubitari jure potest. Etenim lux illa Scripturae, de qua jam quaestio est, moralis est tantum quaedam evidentia, quae mentem non ita convincit ut principia per se nota, aut demonstrationes Logicae seu Mathematicae, ac proinde non parem certitudinem gignit, sed inferioris cujusdam generis; ut disputatione praecedenti docuimus. Ideoque, vel dicendum est, fidem, quam sacrae Scripturae adhibemus, per se et ex suo genere, non admittere tantam certitudinem, quanta reperitur in scientiis humanis: quod est contra communem Theologorum sensum: vel Spiritum, ut nobis fidem illam imprimat, aliud quid agere, quam ut simpliciter aperiat oculos, ad Scripturae sacrae lucem videndam et percipiendam. Praesertim, si singulos Scripturae sacrae libros consideremus, multi reperientur, qui, si velimus fateri quod res est, tantum in se lucis non habent, ut eos non solum veram doctrinam continere, sed etiam divinitus esse conscriptos et inspiratos, inde reddatur omnino certum et manifestum. Ut ex. gr. in Vet. Testamento, liber Esther, liber Ruth, et Canticum canticorum: et in Novo quaedam epistolae, ut Judae, et Jacobi. Quapropter, ut aliquis libros illos agnoscat, et recipiat pro divinis certa et firma fide, non satis est cernere eam lucem quae in illis est: quandoquidem lux illa tanta non est, ut possit eum assensum extorquere, quem requirit fides, ad cujus objectum pertinent, cum sint pars regulae fidei, et inter principia fidei connumerentur.
english: Our first settled point: when the Spirit leads someone to faith, he so shapes and moves that person's mind — otherwise groping and blind here — that it can see and own the light of God's Word and of Scripture. The mind seriously watches the arguments, marks, and axioms that prove the Word true and divine; it judges them rightly; and then, as it should, it is persuaded of that divine truth. While he works within, the Spirit is said to give new eyes.

Moses speaks of those eyes (Deuteronomy 29): "You have seen all that the Lord did before you in the land of Egypt to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land, the great trials your eyes saw, those signs and huge wonders: and the Lord has not given you a heart to understand, or eyes to see, or ears that can hear, to this day." David asked for the same help (Psalm 119, pause Ghimel): "Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law." By "wonders of the law" he means the tokens of divine wisdom sown through God's law. Our fleshly mind cannot judge those rightly while dullness, crookedness, and ignorance — a veil over the mind's eyes — stand in the way. The Holy Spirit lifts that veil in the faithful.

May we doubt, though, whether this Spirit work alone — simply making the mind attend to Scripture's shining light and take it in — is enough to birth a full, sufficiently certain faith about sacred Scripture? We may. The light under discussion is only moral evidence. It does not compel the mind the way self-evident principles do, or the way logical and mathematical proofs do. So it yields a lower grade of certainty, as the previous disputation taught.

That leaves a fork. Either the faith we give Scripture, by its own kind, never reaches the certainty human sciences enjoy — against what theologians commonly hold — or the Spirit, when he stamps that faith on us, does more than merely open eyes to Scripture's light. Take the sacred books one by one and, if we speak honestly, many simply do not carry enough light of themselves to make it wholly certain and plain both that they hold true teaching and that God wrote and inspired them. Old Testament examples: Esther, Ruth, and the Song of Songs. New Testament examples: some epistles, such as Jude and James.

So to receive those books as divine with firm, certain faith, spotting the light in them is not enough. That light cannot force the assent faith requires. And that assent belongs to faith's object, because those books stand inside the rule of faith and are counted among faith's principles.

source_text: IX. Ut ergo toti Scripturae ceu divinae, sicuti meretur, firmiter et certo credamus, praeter actionem illam Spiritus sancti aperientis mentis nostrae oculos ad lucem in sacra Scriptura fulgentem, necessarius videtur internus quidam, ut sic dicam, impulsus et instinctus, quo nos ad credendum moveat, vi quadam quae sit omni argumento et ratione major. Et instinctus ille est, quem proprie, per suasionem Spiritus intrinsacam, et internum Spiritus sancti testimonium intelligi debere putamus. Non enim existimandum est, quum Spiritus sanctus dicitur in fidelium cordibus de divina Scripturae veritate testari, fideles intus audire vocem quandam, quae diserte et expresse dicat hoc verum est et Dei verbum. Sed istud accipiendum est de virtuali quodam, ut sic loquar, testimonio: nec per hoc datur aliud intelligi, quam quod arcano modo Spiritus sanctus nos ad credendum instigat, et certam de Scripturae divinitate persuasionem mentibus nostris imprimit. Quo modo intelligendus est Celebris ille Augustini locus qui ex Confessionibus ejus citari solet. Audiam, inquit, et intelligam quomodo in principio fecisti caelum et terram. Scripsit hoc Moses, scripsit et abiit, transivit hinc a te, neque enim nunc ante me est. Nam si esset, tenerem eum, et rogarem eum et per te obsecrarem ut mihi ista panderet, et praeberem aures corporis mei sonis erumpentibus ex ore ejus. Et si Hebraea voce loqueretur, frustra pulsaret sensum, nec meo modo mentem meam quicquam tangeret. Si autem Latine, scirem quid diceret: sed unde scirem an verum diceret? quod si et hoc scirem, num ab illo scirem? intus utique mihi, intus in domicilio cogitationis, nec Hebraea, nec Graeca, nec Latina, nec Barbara veritas, sine oris ac linguae organis, sine strepitu syllabarum diceret, verum dicit; et ego statim certus confidenter illi homini tuo dicerem, verum dicis.
english: So for firm, certain faith in the whole of Scripture as divine — the faith it deserves — opened eyes are not enough. Besides the Spirit’s work of opening our mind’s eyes to the light that shines in sacred Scripture, there seems to need to be a certain inward impulse and instinct (so to speak) that moves us to believe with a force greater than every argument and reason.

That instinct is what we take the Spirit’s inward persuasion and the Holy Spirit’s inward testimony properly to mean. When the Spirit is said to testify in believers’ hearts that Scripture is divine truth, we must not picture them hearing an inward voice that says, clear and express, "This is true and is God’s Word." Take it as a kind of virtual testimony: in a secret way the Spirit urges us to believe and stamps on our minds a settled persuasion of Scripture’s divinity.

That is how to read the famous Augustine passage usually cited from his Confessions. "Let me hear," he says, "and understand how in the beginning you made heaven and earth. Moses wrote this, wrote it and went away, passed from here to you, for he is not now before me. For if he were, I would hold him and ask him and through you beg him to open these things to me, and I would offer the ears of my body to the sounds breaking from his mouth. And if he spoke in Hebrew, he would strike my sense in vain and would not, in my way, touch my mind at all. But if in Latin, I would know what he said — yet how would I know he spoke the truth? And if I knew even that, would I know it from him? Within me, yes within, in the dwelling of thought, truth — neither Hebrew nor Greek nor Latin nor barbarian — without mouth and tongue, without the noise of syllables, would say, ’He speaks the truth’; and I at once, certain, would confidently say to that man of yours, ’You speak the truth.’"

source_text: X. Non est autem metuendum ne, si impulsus ille et instinctus Spiritus sancti in fidelibus admittatur, locus detur enthusiasmis. Etenim ejusmodi vis et actio Spiritus in nobis multum differt ab enthusiasmo. Nam, ut omittam alia quae possent hic afferri, in enthusiasmo Deus ita se in mentes hominum insinuat, ut ea ipsis revelet, quae a nullo homine didicerunt, vel audiverunt. At Spiritus non instigat fideles ad credendum, nisi ea quae extrinsecus credenda proponuntur, in verbo Dei per Apostolos et Prophetas tradito. Nec etiam persuasio, quam impulsus ille Spiritus generat, potest dici caeca, et sui nescia. Non enim Spiritus Dei ad credendum impellit, nisi illa quorum prius ita lucem cernere fecit, ut ea intellectus judicaverit esse credibilia, atque merito, et cum ratione posse credi, licet, quae in illis notat argumenta veritatis, non exaequent certitudinem quam imprimit Spiritus sanctus, nec sint illius regula, et mensura.
english: Do not fear that admitting this Spirit impulse and instinct in the faithful opens the door to enthusiasms. The Spirit’s force and action in us differs greatly from enthusiasm.

In enthusiasm — to leave other differences aside — God slips into men’s minds and reveals things they never learned or heard from any human teacher. The Spirit, by contrast, urges believers only toward what is set before them from outside as to be believed: the Word of God handed down through the Apostles and Prophets.

Nor is the persuasion that impulse births blind or unaware of itself. The Spirit of God does not drive us to believe before he has first made the mind see the light of those things, so the intellect judges them credible and rightly believable with reason. The truth-marks the mind notes in them still do not equal the certainty the Holy Spirit stamps, and they are not that certainty’s rule and measure.

source_text: XI. Porro Spiritus ille sapientiae et revelationis, cujus vi et efficacia homines in verbi Dei notitiam ducuntur, et certam de eo fidem concipiunt, omnibus et singulis in Ecclesia communis est, nec est ullus fidelis et Ecclesiae membrum, qui sit ejus omnino expers. Nam quotquot filii Dei sunt Spiritu Dei aguntur. Quod si quis Spiritum Christi non habet, ille non est ejus, ut testatur Apostolus Roman. 8. Atque etiam, cum ante probatum sit neminem posse verbo Dei credere, et illud tanquam divinum recipere, qui non sit a Spiritu sancto illuminatus; inde manifestum est fidelem quemcunque, qui verbo Dei credit, a Spiritu sancto illuminatum esse.
english: That Spirit of wisdom and revelation — the force by which people are led into knowledge of God’s Word and form certain faith about it — is common to every member of the church. No believer, no church member, is wholly without him.

"As many as are sons of God are led by the Spirit of God. And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his," the Apostle testifies (Romans 8). And since we already proved that no one can believe God’s Word and receive it as divine without the Holy Spirit’s light, it follows that every believer who trusts that Word has been illuminated by the Holy Spirit.

source_text: XII. Verum Spiritus ille inaequaliter datur, nec omnibus eadem mensura. Unde est quod, tametsi omnes et singuli fideles Spiritum Dei habent, aliquo saltem gradu, quidam tamen eorum spirituales vocantur, opposite ad alios, qui dicuntur carnales, ut videre est, 1. Cor. 3. Et Ego fratres, inquit Paulus, non potui loqui vobis quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus: tanquam parvulis in Christo. Nam fratres suos Paulus non vocat, nisi fideles. Et tamen quos ibi compellat, dicit esse carnales, id est, rudes adhuc et mente imbecilla, quique ea mensura Spiritum Christi adhuc non acceperunt, ut ferre et capere possint religionis Christianae mysteria magis abstrusa atque difficilia: ideoque, ut ipse dicit, in Christo quasi infantes. Per spirituales autem intelligit illos quos Spiritus sanctus in statum perfectiorem evexit.
english: Yet that Spirit is given unequally, not to all by the same measure. So although every believer has God’s Spirit at least in some degree, some are still called spiritual over against others called carnal, as in 1 Corinthians 3.

Paul says: "And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal: as to infants in Christ." He does not call them brothers unless they are believers. Yet those he addresses there he calls carnal — still crude and weak in mind, who have not yet received Christ’s Spirit in the measure needed to bear and grasp the more hidden, harder mysteries of the Christian religion. So, as he says, they are as it were infants in Christ. By "the spiritual" he means those the Holy Spirit has raised into a more perfect state.

source_text: XIII. Itaque omnes, qui sunt in Ecclesia, Spiritum Dei non ea mensura accipiunt, ut quilibet eorum possit agnoscere atque discernere quicquid ad Dei verbum et Scripturam sacram pertinet. Etenim, inter fideles et Spiritum Dei habentes, potest esse dubitatio de aliquo Scripturae libro, et de aliquo religionis Christianae dogmate. Sic olim in prisca Ecclesia non omnes viri boni et sancti doctores idem senserunt de libris Canonicis: sed quidam rejecerunt, quos alii admiserunt. Nam ex. gr. Epistolam ad Hebraeos diu rejecit Ecclesia Latina, cujus interim sacram et divinam authoritatem agnoscebat Ecclesia Graeca. Neque qui errat in aliquo Religionis capite, statim est e numero fidelium expungendus. Nam Paulus Phil. 3. vult ut qui perfecti sunt ferant aliter sentientes, et tanquam cum fratribus communionem colant, interim dum Deus ipsis revelet illud, ad quod nondum pervenerunt.
english: So not everyone in the church receives God’s Spirit in a measure that lets each person acknowledge and discern everything that belongs to God’s Word and sacred Scripture. Among believers who have that Spirit, doubt can remain about some book of Scripture, and about some dogma of the Christian religion.

In the early church not all good and holy teachers held the same view of the canonical books: some rejected what others admitted. For example, the Latin church long rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, while the Greek church acknowledged its sacred and divine authority.

Nor should someone who errs in a head of religion be struck at once from the number of the faithful. Paul in Philippians 3 wants those who are perfect to bear with those who think otherwise, and to keep fellowship with them as brothers, in the meantime, as God reveals to them what they have not yet reached.

source_text: XIV. Sed quantumvis inaequali mensura distribuatur Spiritus ille Sapientiae, et revelationis, certum est omnes et singulos, qui Spiritum Dei habent, posse verbum Dei sibi oblatum internoscere, et doctrinam veram a falsa discernere, quantum cuique ad salutem propriam necessarium est. Observandum est enim, non esse ad cujusque salutem necessarium nosse singulos Scripturae sacrae libros, et omnia quae Deus in verbo suo revelavit. Siquidem eorum quaedam necessaria sunt ad salutem singulorum, alia vero tantum commune bonum Ecclesiae spectant. Deinde, si inter singula Ecclesiae membra comparatio fiat, alius plus, alius in verbo Dei minus nosse tenetur. Neque quod ad alicujus privati salutem sufficit, sufficere putandum est iis qui ad docendum in Ecclesia vocati sunt. Atque idcirco Deus cui visum est varie dona sua in Ecclesia dispensat, Spiritum suum non largitur omnibus tanta copia, ut assequi possint omnia, quae verbi ejus ambitu continentur. Sed saltem fideli cuique eum Spiritus modum admetitur, qui necessarius est ut agnoscere et percipere possit quae vocationi ipsius congruunt, et quae illi nosse opus est, secundum statum et conditionem suam: Et juxta hanc limitationem, et accommodam distributionem, intelligenda sunt loca illa Scripturae, quae fidelibus tribuunt facultatem verbum Dei discernendi atque dijudicandi. Quale est illud Christi, Johan. 10. Oves meae vocem meam audiunt: Et Johan. 7. Si quis voluerit voluntatem Patris facere, cognoscet de doctrina, utrum ex Deo sit, an ego a meipso loquar. Item quod dicit Paulus 1. Corinth. 2. Homo spiritualis dijudicat omnia: Et Johan. 1. Epist. 2. Unctionem habetis a Sancto, et nostis omnia. Item, Unctio vos docet de omnibus. His enim, et similibus locis Scriptura non vult docere, omnes et singulos fideles posse statim ope Spiritus dignoscere quicquid ad Dei verbum quovis modo pertinet. Sed hoc tantum, eos Spiritu affectos posse, quantum ad salutem uniuscujusque expedit, veritatem Spiritu instigante et suggerente discernere ab errore contrario.
english: However unequally that Spirit of Wisdom and revelation is shared out, this much is certain: everyone who has God’s Spirit can recognize the Word of God set before him, and tell true teaching from false, as far as his own salvation requires.

It is not necessary for each person’s salvation to know every sacred book, or everything God has revealed in his Word. Some of those things are needed for individuals’ salvation; others look only to the church’s common good. Compare church members one with another and one is bound to know more in God’s Word, another less. What is enough for a private person’s salvation must not be treated as enough for those called to teach in the church.

Therefore God variously dispenses his gifts in the church as he sees fit. He does not give his Spirit to all in such fullness that they can reach everything his Word contains. But to each believer he at least metes out the Spirit-measure needed to acknowledge and take in what fits that person’s calling, and what that person needs to know for his own state and condition.

Read the Scripture places that give the faithful power to discern and judge God’s Word under that limit and fitting distribution. Christ says (John 10): "My sheep hear my voice." And (John 7): "If anyone wills to do the Father’s will, he will know concerning the teaching, whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself." Paul says (1 Corinthians 2): "The spiritual man judges all things." And 1 John 2: "You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things." Likewise: "The anointing teaches you about all things."

By these and like places Scripture does not mean that every believer can at once, by the Spirit’s help, distinguish whatever in any way belongs to God’s Word. It means only this: those the Spirit has touched can, as far as each one’s salvation requires, discern the truth — the Spirit urging and suggesting — from contrary error.

source_text: XV. Atque ita patet, quam necessario, et quomodo, et quousque, Spiritus sanctus in nobis operetur, ad hoc ut Dei verbum et Scripturam sacram possimus agnoscere. Sequitur ut paucis videamus, quid Ecclesiae quoque hac in re tribuendum sit. Quod fuit tertium caput eorum quae in hujusce disputationis initio, examinanda suscepimus.
english: So it is clear how necessarily, in what manner, and how far the Holy Spirit works in us so that we can acknowledge God's Word and sacred Scripture. Next we should briefly see what also belongs to the Church in this matter. That was the third head of the things we undertook to examine at the start of this disputation.

source_text: XVI. Quaeritur ergo, Num ad hanc notitiam adipiscendam opus sit Ecclesiae voce et testimonio. Breviter respondemus, absolute loquendo, ad hoc non esse necessariam ullius hominis operam. Siquidem Deus potest immediate, et absque cujusquam externo ministerio, alicui, Scripturae et verbi sui cognitionem dare, et certam de eo fidem imprimere. Ita Paulus Evangelium ab homine non acceperat, neque edoctus erat, sed per revelationem Jesu Christi, sicut testatur ipse Galat. 1. Sic reliqui Apostoli a Spiritu Paracleto ducti fuerunt in omnem veritatem, homine nullo praeeunte. Sic denique olim Prophetae a solo Spiritu sancto, qui eos inspirabat, didicerunt quae proloquebantur.
english: So the question is whether the Church's voice and testimony is needed to gain this knowledge. Briefly: absolutely speaking, no human labor is required for it. God can immediately, without anyone's outward ministry, give someone knowledge of Scripture and of his Word, and impress sure faith about it.

So Paul had not received the Gospel from a man, nor been taught it; he received it through the revelation of Jesus Christ, as he himself testifies (Galatians 1). So the other Apostles were led by the Spirit Paraclete into all truth with no man going before. So of old the Prophets learned from the Holy Spirit alone, who inspired them, what they spoke.

source_text: XVII. Sed istud fuit extraordinarium. Neque Deo visum est hac via passim uti in hominibus ad fidem adducendis, et in doctrina caelesti instruendis. Sed voluit ut homines ab hominibus docerentur, et fidem acciperent, Spiritu tamen ipso intus docente et cooperante. Ideoque in Ecclesia ministerium sacrum instituit, jussitque ut pastores et doctores publice verbum ejus annunciarent, explicarent et commendarent, et de veritate illius testarentur. Quodque Pastores publice faciunt, et cum authoritate, singuli quoque fideles, ex ordinatione divina, tenentur id privatim pro suo modulo, facere apud eos qui curae illorum commissi sunt.
english: But that was extraordinary. God did not see fit to use that path commonly when bringing people to faith and instructing them in heavenly teaching. He willed that people be taught by people and receive faith, yet with the Spirit himself teaching within and working with them.

So he instituted the sacred ministry in the Church and commanded pastors and teachers to announce, explain, and commend his Word publicly, and to bear witness to its truth. And what pastors do publicly and with authority, individual believers also are bound by divine ordinance to do privately, according to their measure, among those committed to their care.

source_text: XVIII. Itaque, juxta legem ordinariam, ministerium illud necessarium est, ut aliquis doctrinae et Scripturae divinae cognitionem habeat, et fidem concipiat. Nec enim Spiritus sanctus in verbi Dei notitiam immediate nos ducit. Neque quod doctrinam caelestem amplectimur, et veneramur Scripturas, id facimus quopiam immediato Spiritus afflatu. Sed necesse est ut hac in re praeeuntes habeamus Ecclesiae ministros, et eos quibus nostra institutio commissa est, qui nobis doctrinam illam proponant et exponant, et Scripturam indicent, explicent et commendent. Et primum isto Ecclesiae testimonio movemur, ut de doctrina caelesti et Scriptura sacra bene sentiamus, et fidem ei habeamus, alias in perpetua ignoratione illius versaturi. Juxta illud Apostoli, Roman. 10. Quomodo credent ei de quo non audiverunt? Quomodo audient sine praedicante? Item, Fides est ex auditu: auditus per verbum Dei, id est, ex Dei mandato. Quo spectat illud Augustini toties decantatum, Non crederem Evangelio, nisi me Catholicae Ecclesiae commoveret authoritas. Loquitur enim in persona ejus qui ad fidem introducitur, et aliquam de Evangelii divina veritate persuasionem habere incipit. Nam Ecclesiae communis consensus et testimonium ordinarie est primum incitamentum, quo inducimur ad aliquam Scripturae fidem adhibendam. Atque etiam inter ipsos fideles, quum dubitatio oritur de aliquo libro et dogmate divino, fatemur constans atque uniforme Ecclesiae testimonium argumentum esse maximi ponderis et momenti, cui judicium proprium opponere hominis sit insolentis atque temerarii. Praesertim vero, quum agitur de libri alicujus sacri rejectione vel admissione, agnoscimus perpetuum Ecclesiae Judaicae et Christianae consensum argumentum esse ineluctabile, et cui quemvis cedere oporteat.
english: So under the ordinary law that ministry is necessary if someone is to know divine teaching and Scripture and conceive faith. The Holy Spirit does not lead us straight into knowledge of God's Word. Nor do we embrace heavenly teaching and revere the Scriptures by some immediate breath of the Spirit. In this matter we need the Church's ministers going before us, and those entrusted with our instruction, who propose and set out that teaching and who point out, explain, and commend Scripture.

First that Church testimony moves us to think well of heavenly teaching and sacred Scripture and to give it faith; otherwise we would stay forever ignorant of it. As the Apostle says (Romans 10): "How will they believe him of whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher?" Likewise: "Faith comes from hearing; and hearing through the Word of God" — that is, from God's command. Here belongs Augustine's oft-sung line: "I would not believe the Gospel unless the Catholic Church's authority moved me." He speaks in the person of someone being brought into faith, who is beginning to have some persuasion of the Gospel's divine truth.

For the Church's common consensus and testimony is ordinarily the first incentive that leads us to give Scripture some faith. And even among the faithful themselves, when doubt arises about some book or divine dogma, we confess that the Church's constant, uniform testimony is an argument of the greatest weight and moment; for a person to set his own judgment against it is insolent and rash. Especially when the question is rejecting or admitting some sacred book, we acknowledge that the perpetual consensus of the Jewish and Christian Church is an inescapable argument, one to which anyone ought to yield.

source_text: XIX. Neque tamen Ecclesiae consensus et testimonium est propria et praecipua fidei nostrae basis, ad quam certitudo ejus reducenda sit. Nam Ecclesia quidem, ut modo docuimus, ea est quae per ministros suos, et privatos etiam fideles, credenda nobis proponit et explicat, juxta Dei ordinationem, ejusque testimonio et authoritate primum inducimur, ut eis aliquam fidem adhibeamus, verum in eo fides nostra non conquiescit, sed longe solidiori fundamento nititur. Quod si ultra non pergat, non est vera et legitima fides, sed tantum humana quaedam persuasio. Videlicet, Ecclesia idem nobis praestat officium quod olim Samaritana mulier concivibus suis. Nam Ecclesia aditum nobis praebet ad cognoscendum Christum, et doctrinam illius. Et Ecclesiae primum testimonio commonemur ut in Christum credamus. Sed postquam Christum ipsum loquentem audivimus, tam extrinsecus in verbo, quam intus in cordibus nostris, jam fides nostra non amplius nititur Ecclesiae testimonio, eique dicere possumus, quod Samaritani mulieri dicebant, Jam non credimus propter loquelam tuam, ipsi enim audivimus, et scimus quod hic est vere Servator mundi.
english: Yet the Church's consensus and testimony is not the proper and principal basis of our faith, the thing to which its certainty should be reduced. The Church, as we have just said, is what proposes and explains through its ministers — and through private believers too — the things we are to believe, according to God's ordinance. By its testimony and authority we are first led to give them some faith. But our faith does not rest there. It rests on a far more solid foundation. If it goes no further, it is not true and legitimate faith, only a human persuasion.

The Church does for us what the Samaritan woman once did for her townspeople. It opens the way for us to know Christ and his teaching. First the Church's testimony admonishes us to believe in Christ. But after we have heard Christ himself speaking — outwardly in the Word and inwardly in our hearts — our faith no longer rests on the Church's testimony. We can say to it what the Samaritans said to the woman: "Now we do not believe because of your speech, for we ourselves have heard, and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world" (John 4).

source_text: XX. Quod autem res ita se habeat, neque testimonium et authoritas Ecclesiae sit fidei nostrae propria ratio, et praecipuum illud, in quod nostra de verbo Dei certitudo recumbit, probatur multis argumentis. Nam primo, si fides nostra tale fundamentum haberet, humana esset non divina: quia, scilicet, non divina veritate et authoritate, sed testimonio hominum niteretur. Deinde sequeretur fideles Deo credere, non propter ipsum, sed propter homines, et fidelium ipsorum respectu majorem esse hominum quam Dei authoritatem, quod valde absurdum est. Mutanda quoque esset fidei definitio. Nam, ex Doctorum omnium consensu, fides est assensus ille quem Deo loquenti praebemus. At sic per fidem, non tam Deo loquenti, quam hominibus crederemus. Neque fides esset assensus omnino firmus et infallibilis. Nulla enim humana veracitas tanta est, ut possit omnem falsi formidinem tollere.
english: That matters stand this way — that the Church's testimony and authority is not the proper ground of our faith, not the chief thing on which our certainty about God's Word rests — is proved by many arguments. First: if our faith had that foundation, it would be human, not divine, because it would rest on men's testimony, not on divine truth and authority. Next it would follow that believers believe God not for God's sake but for men's, and that for the believers themselves men's authority is greater than God's — which is deeply absurd.

The definition of faith would have to change as well. By the consensus of all the Doctors, faith is the assent we give to God when he speaks. On that view, through faith we would be believing men more than God speaking. Nor would faith be an assent altogether firm and infallible. No human truthfulness is great enough to remove every fear of falsehood.

source_text: XXI. Praeterea nulla unquam in Ecclesia major fuit, aut erit authoritas, illa qua fuerunt praediti Apostoli. Et tamen fides eorum, qui praedicationi Apostolorum crediderunt, non nitebatur ullius Apostoli authoritate. Quod patet ex Pauli verbis, Galat. 1. Licet, inquit, nos, aut Angelus e caelo, evangelizet vobis praeterquam quod vobis evangelizavimus, anathema sit. Nam si Apostolorum authoritas fuisset fundamentum solum vel praecipuum quo nixi fuissent fideles, certe sublato isto fundamento, necesse quoque fuisset fidem illorum tolli, vel labascere. Et tamen si Apostoli, imo Angeli ipsi, contrarium docuissent ejus quod primo praedicatum fuerat, vult Paulus ut nihilo minus Evangelii fides firma sit et inconcussa.
english: Besides, no greater authority ever was in the Church, or ever will be, than the authority the Apostles held. Yet the faith of those who believed the Apostles' preaching did not rest on any Apostle's authority. Paul's words make that plain (Galatians 1): "Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel other than what we preached to you, let him be anathema."

If the Apostles' authority had been the sole or principal foundation on which believers leaned, then once that foundation was removed their faith would necessarily have been removed or would have tottered. Yet even if Apostles — indeed angels themselves — had taught the contrary of what was first preached, Paul wills that the Gospel's faith remain no less firm and unshaken.

source_text: XXII. Deinde Prophetae atque Apostoli, qui primi doctrinam sacram et Scripturam tradiderunt, fidem illam, quam verbo Dei habebant, non poterant in Ecclesiae authoritatem resolvere: quandoquidem doctrinam illam Ecclesiae tradebant, non vero ab Ecclesia commendatam accipiebant. Et fieri potest, saltem extra ordinem, ut quis Evangelio credat a nullo homine doctus, sed forte in aliquem Evangelii codicem incidens. Quo casu fides istius hominis pro fundamento non posset habere authoritatem Ecclesiae, cujus testimonium nunquam audivisset. Et tamen una est omnium fides. Neque specie differt fides nostra a fide Prophetarum et Apostolorum, et eorum qui a Deo immediate docerentur. Fides autem nostra non esset eadem cum eorum fide, si fundamentum aliud haberet, et aliam formalem credendi rationem. Unius enim speciei fidei unicum est proprium et praecipuum fundamentum: nec sunt ejus, ut loquuntur Scholae, diversae formales credendi rationes.
english: Next, the Prophets and Apostles who first handed down sacred teaching and Scripture could not resolve the faith they had in God's Word into the Church's authority. They handed that teaching to the Church; they did not receive it as something the Church had already recommended. And it can happen, at least outside the ordinary course, that someone believes the Gospel though taught by no man — happening, say, on a Gospel codex. In that case his faith could not take as foundation a Church authority whose testimony he had never heard.

Yet there is one faith of all. Our faith does not differ in species from the faith of the Prophets and Apostles, or of those taught by God immediately. But our faith would not be the same as theirs if it had another foundation and another formal ground of believing. One species of faith has one proper and principal foundation. As the Schools put it, it does not have diverse formal grounds of believing.

source_text: XXIII. Adde quod, si qui fingant fidem nostram Ecclesiae authoritate niti, per Ecclesiam intelligunt Ecclesiam universalem. Atqui fideles singuli Ecclesiam illam non audiunt, sed plerique instituuntur ab Ecclesiis particularibus, et earum ministris, qui falli et errare possunt. Ac proinde fides eorum non potest niti Ecclesiae universae testimonio, quod ab ipsis nunquam auditum est.
english: Add this: those who invent that our faith rests on the Church's authority mean by "Church" the universal Church. But individual believers do not hear that Church. Most are instructed by particular churches and their ministers, who can be deceived and can err. So their faith cannot rest on the testimony of a universal Church they have never heard.

source_text: XXIV. Verum explosa illa sententia, quae, fidem verbo Dei et Scripturae sacrae adhibitam, ad authoritatem Ecclesiae reducit, videndum quid ergo sit illud in quo tandem ultimo conquiescit fides nostra, et quod sit ejus proprium et praecipuum fundamentum. Quod ut manifestum fiat, videtur distinguendum esse inter ipsum Dei verbum, sive divinam revelationem: et illa quae Dei verbo traduntur et continentur, et per revelationem divinam patefiunt. Etenim, mysteria quae verbo Dei traduntur fides nostra aliter accipit, et aliter ipsam Dei vocem, seu divinam revelationem.
english: But once that opinion is exploded — the one that reduces faith in God's Word and sacred Scripture to the Church's authority — we must ask what our faith finally rests on, and what its proper and principal foundation is. To make that clear, a distinction seems needed between God's Word itself, or divine revelation, and the things handed down and contained in God's Word, which become open through divine revelation. Our faith receives the mysteries delivered in God's Word in one way, and God's own voice — divine revelation — in another.

source_text: XXV. Nam quod attinet ad res ipsas quae traduntur in Dei verbo, ut sunt quae vocantur fidei dogmata, et alia quae habentur in Scripturis, illis assentimur, eaque ut vera recipimus, quoniam Deus, qui est summe verax, quique nec falli, nec fallere potest, illa per Apostolos et Prophetas nobis revelavit, et in verbo suo docuit. Habent quidem fidei dogmata, praeter divinam revelationem, argumenta multa quibus probentur et suadentur. Neque solet Deus nos ad eorum fidem adducere, nisi mediantibus quibusdam argumentis, indiciis et rationibus, quibus eorum veritas menti nostrae credibilis redditur, et suaviter in animos nostros insinuatur. Unde est quod Petrus 1. Epist. cap. 3. vult ut fideles possint defensione uti, et satisfacere cuivis petenti rationem ejus quae in ipsis est spei. Qui vero absque omni ratione crederet, nec fidei suae rationem ullam haberet, aut reddere posset, ista non esset vera fides, sed levis et temeraria quaedam persuasio. Ideoque non sufficit iis, qui verbum Dei annuntiant, simpliciter doctrinam fidei proponere, sed praeterea opus est, ut suasiones quasdam adhibeant, et vel ex ipsis rebus, vel ex quibusdam adjunctis argumenta eliciant, quibus religionis Christianae mysteria credibilia reddant, et etiam valide comprobent. Attamen fidei nostrae praecipuum fundamentum, et propria ratio, non sunt illae qualescunque rationes et argumenta, sed divina revelatio, in quam praesertim fides nostra recumbit.
english: As for the things themselves handed down in God's Word — the so-called dogmas of faith, and the other things held in the Scriptures — we assent to them and receive them as true because God, who is supremely truthful and can neither be deceived nor deceive, revealed them to us through Apostles and Prophets and taught them in his Word. Besides divine revelation, the dogmas of faith do have many arguments by which they are proved and urged. God does not ordinarily lead us to faith in them except through mediating arguments, indications, and reasons that make their truth credible to our mind and gently work it into our souls.

That is why Peter wills that believers be able to give a defense, and to satisfy anyone who asks a reason for the hope that is in them (1 Peter 3). Whoever would believe with no reason at all, and would have no account of his faith or could not give one, would not have true faith, only a light and rash persuasion. So those who announce God's Word must not merely propose the doctrine of faith. They also need to apply persuasions and draw arguments from the things themselves or from adjuncts, so as to make the mysteries of the Christian religion credible and even strongly prove them. Still, the principal foundation of our faith, and its proper ground, is not those reasons and arguments of whatever kind, but divine revelation, on which our faith especially rests.

source_text: XXVI. Viris doctis quibusdam visum est, si modo mentem eorum percipimus, certitudinem fidei, qua religionis dogmata amplectimur, et rebus a Deo revelatis credimus, fundari in rerum revelatarum luce, et splendore quodam insito veritatis, quo mens nostra convincitur, et ad assensum veluti cogitur. Nimirum, quum aliquis Evangelio credit, et sibi persuadet Filium Dei hominem factum esse, et in mundum venisse, pro nobis passum et mortuum esse, resurrexisse, in caelos ascendisse, et caetera quae ad nostram redemptionem pertinent, in ea sunt sententia, propriam et praecipuam rationem illius assensus, esse ipsam doctrinae majestatem, sanctitatem, sublimitatem, veritatem, et cum ratione recta congruentiam, quae mentem rapit in sui assensum, et manifestum reddit doctrinam illam, non tantum veram esse, sed immediate a Deo prodiisse, quandoquidem ab ingenio humano tanta, tamque miranda, nec inveniri, nec confingi potuerint. Unde sequitur doctrinae caelestis veritatem natura prius a nobis agnosci, quam certi simus illam Deum authorem habere; adeoque ultimam et potissimam illius credendae rationem non esse Dei dicentis veracitatem et authoritatem, et quia Deus ita dixit et revelavit: sed ipsam, ut diximus, rei veritatem et evidentiam. Verum, licet agnoscamus religionis dogmata suam habere lucem et argumenta veritatis, atque etiam originis divinae: Videtur tamen veritati et doctrinae Theologicae magis consentaneum, si dicamus fidei, qua dogmata illa recipimus, rationem propriam et praecipuam esse authoritatem Dei dicentis et revelantis, potius quam ipsam rei veritatem et lucem: quod probatur multis argumentis.
english: Some learned men — if we have their mind right — think the certainty of the faith by which we embrace religion's dogmas and believe what God has revealed rests in the light of the things revealed, and in a certain inborn splendor of truth that convinces our mind and all but compels assent. When someone believes the Gospel, and is persuaded that the Son of God was made man, came into the world, suffered and died for us, rose again, ascended into the heavens, and the rest that belongs to our redemption, they hold that the proper and principal ground of that assent is the doctrine's own majesty, holiness, sublimity, and truth, and its congruence with right reason — which seizes the mind into assent and makes plain that the doctrine is not only true but has come immediately from God, since things so great and wonderful could neither be found nor fabricated by human wit.

On that view the truth of heavenly doctrine would by nature be recognized by us before we were sure God was its author; and so the ultimate and chief ground of believing it would not be the truthfulness and authority of God speaking, and that God so said and revealed, but — as they put it — the very truth and evidence of the thing. We do grant that religion's dogmas have their own light and arguments of truth, and even of divine origin. Still it seems more agreeable to theological truth and teaching to say that the proper and principal ground of the faith by which we receive those dogmas is the authority of God speaking and revealing, rather than the thing's own truth and light. That is proved by many arguments.

source_text: XXVII. Primo enim hactenus in Scholis receptum est fidem, licet non excludat ratiocinationes, potius tamen loquentis authoritate niti. Sed authoritate divina potissimum non nititur fides, si praecipua ratio, cur rebus fidei credimus, sit quaedam, quae ipsis inest, evidentia veritatis, non divina revelatio. Absurda quoque esset fidei definitio, nempe, quod sit assensus quem Deo loquenti praebemus. Tum enim per fidem Deo loquenti non crederemus, nisi materialiter, ut dicitur in Scholis, hoc est, crederemus quidem iis, quae Deus loqueretur, at non, quia Deus illa locutus esset. Sed absurde mentis aliquis habitus ab objecto suo tantum materiali definitur. Si quis enim, verbi causa, Peripateticae doctrinae peritus incidat in aliquem librum Aristotelis, et doctrinam illius exacte considerans, veram esse agnoscat, atque etiam ex acumine styli et differendi modo judicet librum esse Aristotelis, assensus illi doctrinae praebitus nonnisi absurde dici poterit fides Aristoteli dicenti habita. At certe Theologi huc usque communi consensu, non tantum fidem definiunt assensum Deo loquenti exhibitum, et statuunt objectum illius esse Dei verbum, et res a Deo revelatas; sed etiam objecti illius rationem formalem, sub qua fides illud apprehendit, et ob quam illud recipit et agnoscit, docent esse divinam authoritatem et revelationem.
english: First: up to now the Schools have held that faith, though it does not shut out reasoning, rests rather on the authority of the one who speaks. But faith does not rest chiefly on divine authority if the principal reason we believe the things of faith is a certain evidence of truth in the things themselves, not divine revelation. The definition of faith would also become absurd — that it is the assent we give to God speaking. For then through faith we would believe God speaking only materially, as the Schools say: we would believe the things God spoke, but not because God had spoken them. And it is absurd to define any habit of mind from its object only as material.

Suppose someone skilled in Peripatetic doctrine happens on a book of Aristotle, studies its teaching carefully, recognizes it as true, and even judges from the sharpness of style and manner of arguing that the book is Aristotle's. The assent he gives that doctrine could only absurdly be called faith held toward Aristotle speaking. Yet up to now the Theologians by common consensus not only define faith as assent exhibited to God speaking, and take its object to be God's Word and things revealed by God; they also teach that the formal ground of that object — under which faith apprehends it, and on account of which it receives and acknowledges it — is divine authority and revelation.

source_text: XXVIII. Deinde, si propria et potissima fidei ratio esset ipsa lux veritatis, quae in rebus credendis cernitur, quaeque mentem ad assensum necessario determinat, fides esset assensus evidens, et dogmata fidei essent evidentia. Siquidem illud est evidens quod luce sua mentem convincit, et cogit ad assensum. At est veluti quoddam scholarum axioma, in Scripturis fundatum, fidem esse habitum mentis inevidentem; quandoquidem Scriptura fidem opponit aspectui: et docet fidem eorum esse quae non videntur.
english: Next: if the proper and chief ground of faith were the very light of truth discerned in the things to be believed, the light that necessarily determines the mind to assent, then faith would be an evident assent, and the dogmas of faith would be evident. For what is evident is what convinces the mind by its own light and compels assent. But it is almost an axiom of the schools, founded in the Scriptures, that faith is an inevident habit of the mind. Scripture sets faith against sight, and teaches that faith is of things that are not seen.

source_text: XXIX. Praeterea, licet quaedam, quae docet Dei verbum, sint demonstrabilia, et possint ex principiis per se notis colligi: attamen fidei multa credenda proponuntur, quae, nisi quis velit esse contentiosus, fatendum est nec esse per se nota, nec posse probari ullis argumentis necessariis et convincentibus. Sumamus, exempli gratia, praecipuum illum fidei articulum, quo docemur in una simplicissima Dei essentia tres esse distinctas personas. Quis audebit polliceri tanti mysterii demonstrationem, et serio affirmare in eo esse quandam veritatis evidentiam? cum contra ibi mens nostra nihil videat, nisi meras tenebras ad lucem illam inaccessam caligans, ut noctuarum oculi ad solem: vixque acutissimi et subtilissimi quique articulum illum possint a contradictione apparenti vindicare, nedum ut demonstrare queant. Idemque dici potest de satisfactione morte Christi praestita, de futura olim mundi universi conflagratione, et resurrectione omnium mortuorum, de quorum veritate, si quis, praeter Scripturae sacrae authoritatem, probationes quaerat, nihil admodum certi et firmi reperiet, et quod fidei nostrae fulciendae sufficiat. Non improbamus quidem pium eorum conatum qui in eo laborant, ut mysteria ista et similia undecunque quaesitis rationibus probent, et suadeant. Sed, si volumus candide agere, fatendum est argumenta illa, quaecunque tandem sint, esse tantum, ut loquuntur Scholae, congruentias quasdam, quae rem ad summum probabilem et verisimilem reddunt, non vero, quod ita sit, necessario concludunt.
english: Besides: some things God's Word teaches are demonstrable, and can be gathered from principles known through themselves. Still, many things are proposed to faith to be believed which — unless someone wants to be contentious — must be confessed neither known through themselves nor able to be proved by any necessary and convincing arguments. Take that principal article of faith by which we are taught that in one most simple essence of God there are three distinct persons. Who will dare promise a demonstration of so great a mystery, and seriously affirm that there is in it a certain evidence of truth? There our mind sees nothing but mere darkness, dimming toward that inaccessible light as owls' eyes toward the sun. Even the most acute and subtle can scarcely clear that article of apparent contradiction, much less demonstrate it.

The same holds for the satisfaction performed by Christ's death, for the future conflagration of the whole world, and for the resurrection of all the dead. If anyone seeks proofs of their truth besides the authority of sacred Scripture, he will find nothing firm enough, nothing that suffices to support our faith. We do not disapprove the pious labor of those who try to prove and urge these mysteries and the like with reasons sought from every side. But if we deal candidly, we must confess that those arguments, of whatever kind, are only what the Schools call congruences: at most they make the matter probable and likely; they do not necessarily conclude that it is so.

source_text: XXX. Quum vero Israelitae in Aegypto docerentur marem omnem octavo die esse circumcidendum, a sanguine abstinendum esse, quibusdam animalibus vesci licere, aliis non licere, et plura hujusmodi, nemo negare potest quin ista illis fide amplectenda fuerint, ut res Deo gratae et acceptae. Et tamen quis sincere et ex animo affirmare possit ista in se lucem habuisse, qua sufficienter fidem sui facerent, et unde mens fidelium efficaciter compelleretur ut crederet haec a Deo jussa et tradita fuisse. Idemque hodie nostri respectu, dici potest de lavacro illo aquae quod in Baptismo usurpatur, et de sumptione panis et vini in mensa Domini. Cum igitur fide suscipienda sint dogmata, et praecepta multa, quae non eam in se habent lucem et evidentiam, qua se satis certo vera esse comprobent et a Deo tradita, manifestum est fidei, qua res verbo Dei traditas et religionis dogmata suscipimus, rationem et basin praecipuam, non esse ipsam rei veritatem atque evidentiam, sed potius veritatem et authoritatem Dei docentis et revelantis.
english: When the Israelites in Egypt were taught that every male was to be circumcised on the eighth day, that they were to abstain from blood, that some animals might be eaten and others not, and more of that kind, no one can deny those things were to be embraced by them with faith, as things pleasing and acceptable to God. Yet who could sincerely and from the heart say those things had in themselves a light enough to make faith, and enough to compel believers' minds to conclude that God had commanded and handed them down? The same can be said of us today about that washing of water used in Baptism, and about taking bread and wine at the Lord's table.

So when many dogmas and precepts must be taken up by faith, though they do not have in themselves the light and evidence by which they would prove themselves with enough certainty true and handed down by God, it is clear that the principal ground and basis of the faith by which we take up what God's Word delivers and religion's dogmas is not the thing's own truth and evidence, but rather the truth and authority of God teaching and revealing.

source_text: XXXI. At, inquies, quomodo revelationem divinam percipimus? Et unde pendet certitudo fidei qua verbum ipsum Dei amplectimur? Certe Deus loqui non solet quin vox et verbum ejus habeat quasdam notas et indicia, quibus ab humana, vel diabolica impostura et fraude distingui possit atque internosci. Praesertim vero revelatio illa cui fides nostra hodie innititur, et quam habemus in sacris Scripturis consignatam, habet illustria admodum argumenta quibus Deo sese vendicat, sicut thesibus superioribus abunde ostensum est. Neque fides, qua illam suscipimus, est persuasio caeca, et quae sui nullam rationem habeat. Sed qui verbo Dei sicuti par est credit, ad assensum illi praebendum inducitur rationibus et motivis quibusdam, quae viro prudenti suadere possunt revera Deum esse qui loquitur, nec confictam et falsam revelationem pro vera obtendi. Ideoque, praeter argumenta quae ex re ipsa peti possunt, saepe Deus, ut fidem verbo suo crearet, et ad credendum homines compelleret, multa adhibuit signa et miracula, quibus fides eorum qui crediderunt, non raro ascribitur.
