Ita Sergius Paulus vir prudens, quum vidisset caecitatem qua Paulus Apostolus Elymam Magum percusserat, credidit, admirans super doctrina Domini, Actor. 13. Et Centurio qui Christo morienti astabat, videns mirabilia quae in morte Christi contigerunt, glorificavit Deum, dicens, vere hic homo justus erat: Luc. 23. Similiter Joan. 4. Quum Pater quidam agnovisset filium suum moribundum verbo Christi sanatum fuisse, et convaluisse, illa ipsa hora qua dixerat ei Jesus, filius tuus vivit, et credidit ipse, et Domus ejus tota. Unde merito suspecta est eorum ad fidem conversio, qui conversionis suae rationem exposcenti, nihil habent quod dicant, aut trivialia afferunt.
english: You will ask how we perceive divine revelation, and where the certainty comes from in the faith that embraces God's Word itself. God does not ordinarily speak without notes and marks in his voice and word by which it can be told from human or diabolical fraud. The revelation our faith rests on today — consigned in the sacred Scriptures — has very illustrious arguments claiming it for God, as the earlier theses already showed at length. The faith that receives it is not a blind persuasion with no account of itself. A fitting believer is led to assent by reasons and motives strong enough to persuade a prudent man that God is truly the one speaking, and that a fabricated, false revelation is not being passed off as true.

Besides arguments taken from the matter itself, God has often used signs and miracles to create faith for his word and compel men to believe; the faith of those who believed is not rarely ascribed to those signs. Sergius Paulus, a prudent man, saw the blindness with which Paul the Apostle struck Elymas the Magician, and believed while marveling at the Lord's doctrine (Acts 13). The centurion standing by as Christ died saw the wonders at Christ's death and glorified God, saying truly this man was just (Luke 23). Likewise (John 4): a father recognized that Christ's word had healed his dying son, and that the boy had recovered at the very hour Jesus said your son lives — and he believed, and his whole house with him. Conversion is therefore deservedly suspect when someone asked for its reason has nothing to say, or only trivial things to offer.

source_text: XXXII. Attamen non existimamus argumenta illa et credendi motiva, quibus verbum Dei suadetur, et quibus hominum mentes leniter ad ejus obsequium flectuntur, esse illud unde fidei certitudo potissimum pendet, et praecipuum illius fundamentum. His quidem argumentis Deus utitur in fide generanda, et iis quoque fides jam generata alitur et fovetur: non tamen videntur esse fidei potissima basis et certitudinis illius mensura. Et hoc quia, ut jam thesi 8. dictum, consentiunt scholae Christianae certitudinem fidei summam esse, et talem quae vel aequet, vel etiam superet, certitudinem omnem quae reperitur in scientiis humanis, nempe, si fides aestimetur ex suis principiis et consideretur qualis esse potest, et debet: non autem qualis revera sit in multis. Sed fides qua verbum Dei, quod hodie Scriptura continetur, suscipimus, non potest habere illam certitudinem, si nitatur tantum notis et argumentis, quibus Scriptura divina comprobatur. Nec enim sunt demonstrationes quae certitudinem absolutam generent, sed argumenta solum moralia, quae, licet sufficiant ut aliquis ad prudenter credendum inducatur, non tamen per se, et ex sua natura, possunt gignere certitudinem parem illi quam habent, verbi causa, disciplinae Mathematicae: qualem aut etiam majorem supponimus fidem acquirere.
english: Still, we do not think those arguments and motives of belief — the ones that recommend God's Word and gently bend minds toward obedience to it — are what faith's certainty chiefly hangs on, or its principal foundation. God does use them when he generates faith, and by them faith already generated is also nourished and kept warm. They do not seem to be faith's strongest basis, or the measure of its certainty.

The Christian schools already agree on this, as thesis 8 said: faith's certainty is the highest — equal to every certainty in the human sciences, or even above them — when faith is judged from its own principles and taken as it can and ought to be, not as it actually stands in many people. But the faith that receives God's Word as Scripture now holds it cannot have that certainty if it rests only on the notes and arguments that prove Scripture divine. Those are not demonstrations that produce absolute certainty. They are only moral arguments. They can lead a person to believe prudently, yet by themselves and by their nature they cannot generate a certainty equal to what the mathematical disciplines have — the kind of certainty, or even a greater one, that we suppose faith acquires.

source_text: XXXIII. Praesertim vero, si singulos Scripturae sacrae libros consideremus, fatendum est multos esse qui in se non habeant eas divinitatis notas, quibus necessario et evidenter probetur authoritas eorum divina, et quibus tanta possit fundari certitudo, quantam fides requirit. Quales sunt, exempli gratia, liber Judicum, liber Ruth, liber Esther, Canticum Canticorum, quos divinitus inspiratos esse, vix probari potest aliis argumentis, quam generalibus illis, quae petuntur a testimonio et consensu Ecclesiae Judaicae et Christianae. Et tamen libri illi sunt pars verbi divini, et regulae illius fidei certissimae, ad quam omnia, quae religionem spectant, exigenda sunt et examinanda; adeoque pertinent ad fidei objectum in tota sua amplitudine sumptum: et assensus quem illis, sicuti par est, praebemus, non refertur ad aliam virtutem, quam ad fidem. Ac proinde, cum partes quaedam verbi Dei fide suscipiendae non habeant ea divinitatis argumenta, quae per se fundare possint assensum tam certum quam fides exigit, proculdubio argumenta, quibus verbum Dei divinum se probat et a Deo manasse, non sunt praecipuum fidei fundamentum, et ultimum illud in quod fides nostra resolvi debet. Neque ad rem pertinet quod librorum ejusmodi fides ad singulorum salutem necessaria non est. Hic enim non est quaestio, quid ad singulorum salutem necessarium sit, vel non. Sed consideramus in genere naturam, et fundamentum fidei ad cujus objectum pertinent multa, quae non sunt cognitu singulis ad salutem necessaria.
english: Especially when we take the sacred books one by one, we must admit that many do not carry in themselves those notes of divinity that would necessarily and evidently prove their divine authority, or found the certainty faith requires. Judges, Ruth, Esther, and the Song of Songs are examples. That they are divinely inspired can scarcely be proved by anything but the general arguments drawn from the testimony and consent of the Jewish and Christian Church.

Yet those books are part of the divine Word and of that most certain rule of faith by which everything that touches religion must be tried and examined. They belong to the object of faith in its full breadth, and the assent we rightly give them is referred to no other virtue than faith. So when some parts of God's Word that faith must receive lack intrinsic arguments of divinity strong enough by themselves to found the assent faith demands, the arguments by which God's Word proves itself divine and from God are plainly not faith's principal foundation, or the last thing into which our faith should resolve.

It is no answer that faith in such books is not necessary for each person's salvation. The question here is not what each person must know to be saved. We are considering the nature and foundation of faith in general — and many things belong to faith's object that individuals need not know for salvation.

source_text: XXXIV. Quapropter ultimum illud in quod fides nostra tandem resolvitur, et praecipuum illius firmamentum, statuimus esse illum Spiritus sancti impulsum, et instinctum qui a nobis thesi 9. descriptus fuit. Quo nomine designamus Spiritus sancti actionem, et efficientiam, qua nos ad divinam revelationem suscipiendam immediate movet, et certam de ea persuasionem mentibus nostris imprimit. Ad cujus rei illustrationem potest aliquid conferre, si comparatio fiat inter assensum fidei, et assensum scientiarum. Quod ergo sunt in scientiis conclusiones demonstratae, hic sunt fidei dogmata, et alia quae docet et tradit Dei verbum. Quod est medium demonstrationis, conclusionis respectu, istud est Dei dicentis et revelantis authoritas, respectu eorum quae credenda proponuntur. Ut autem medium ipsum, et demonstrationis vim immediate percipimus, naturali et infito rationis lumine: ita divinam revelationem, factam Prophetis atque Apostolis, immediate credimus et percipimus, per internum Spiritus Dei instinctum et testimonium, quod fidei lumen Scholastici vocant. Atque ut rationis lumen non est illud quod ratiocinando percipimus et cognoscimus, sed illud quo cognoscimus et ratiocinamur: Ita istud Spiritus sancti testimonium non est amplius aliquid quod creditur, nec argumentum quod ad credendum moveat, sed illud tantum quo creditur, et actio qua fides menti nostrae imprimitur: quam non necesse est ut omnis fidelis, qui fidei actum elicit, cognoscat et intelligat cognitione reflexa: Non magis quam necesse est rusticum aliquem cogitare de intelligentia et vi ratiocinandi, quum intelligit et ratiocinatur.
english: Therefore we state that the last thing into which our faith finally resolves — its principal support — is that impulse and instinct of the Holy Spirit described in thesis 9. By that name we mean the Spirit's action and efficiency: he immediately moves us to receive divine revelation and impresses a sure persuasion of it on our minds.

A comparison with scientific assent helps. What demonstrated conclusions are in the sciences, the dogmas of faith and the other things God's Word teaches are here. What the middle term of a demonstration is to its conclusion, the authority of God speaking and revealing is to the things proposed for belief. As we immediately grasp the middle term and the force of a demonstration by reason's natural, inborn light, so we immediately believe and perceive the revelation given to the Prophets and Apostles through the Spirit's inward instinct and testimony — what the Scholastics call the light of faith.

And as reason's light is not something we come to know by reasoning, but that by which we know and reason, so this testimony of the Holy Spirit is not a further thing believed, nor an argument that moves us to believe. It is only that by which we believe — the action that impresses faith on the mind. Every believer who elicits an act of faith need not know and understand that action by reflexive cognition, any more than a country laborer must think about intelligence and the power of reasoning while he understands and reasons.

source_text: XXXV. Verum quid Spiritus sancti testimonium conferat, et quid momenti habeant argumenta, quibus authoritas divina Scripturae suadetur, ad hoc ut illi quam par est fidem adhibeamus, non possumus melius explicare quam verbis viri celeberrimi qui sic ea de re loquitur. Maneat ergo hoc fixum, quos Spiritus intus docuit, solide acquiescere in Scriptura, et hanc quidem esse αὐτόπιστον, neque demonstrationi et rationibus subiici eam fas esse: quam tamen meretur apud nos certitudinem, Spiritus testimonio consequi. Etsi enim reverentiam sua sibi ultro majestate conciliat, tunc tamen demum serio nos afficit quum per Spiritum obsignata est cordibus nostris. Illius ergo virtute illuminati, jam non aut nostro, aut aliorum judicio credimus a Deo esse Scripturam: sed supra humanum judicium, certo certius constituimus, non secus ac si ipsius Dei numen illic intueremur, hominum ministerio, ab ipsissimo Dei ore ad nos fluxisse. Non argumenta, non verisimilitudines quaerimus quibus judicium nostrum incumbat: sed ut rei extra aestimandi aleam positae, judicium ingeniumque nostrum subiicimus. Non qualiter superstitionibus solent miseri homines captivam mentem addicere: sed quia non dubiam vim numinis illic sentimus vigere ac spirare, qua ad parendum, scientes quidem ac volentes, vividius tamen et efficacius quam pro humana aut voluntate, aut scientia trahimur et accendimur. Talis ergo est persuasio quae rationes non requirat: talis notitia cui optima ratio constet, nempe in qua securius constantiusque mens quiescit quam in ullis rationibus: talis denique sensus, qui nisi ex caelesti revelatione nasci nequeat. Calv. Instit. lib. 1. c. 7. Sect. 5.
english: But what the Holy Spirit's testimony actually contributes, and what weight the arguments for Scripture's divine authority have when we give Scripture the faith it deserves — we cannot explain better than in the words of a most famous man speaking on the point.

Let this stand fixed: those the Spirit has taught inwardly rest solidly in Scripture; Scripture is self-authenticating; it is not right to subject it to demonstration and reasoning; and the certainty it deserves among us comes by the Spirit's testimony. Its own majesty does win reverence of itself, yet it first seriously moves us when the Spirit has sealed it on our hearts. Illuminated by that power, we no longer believe Scripture is from God by our judgment or by other people's. Above human judgment we settle more certainly than certain — as if we were beholding God's own deity there — that by human ministry it has flowed to us from God's very mouth.

We do not hunt arguments or probabilities for our judgment to lean on. As for a matter already beyond the hazard of weighing and guessing, we subject our judgment and ingenuity to it. Not as wretched people bind a captive mind to superstitions, but because we feel no doubtful power of the deity thriving and breathing there — and by it, knowing and willing, we are still drawn and kindled to obey more vividly and effectively than human will or knowledge can account for. Such is the persuasion that does not ask for reasons; such the knowledge that has the best reason of all, the one in which the mind rests more securely and constantly than in any reasonings; such, finally, the sense that cannot be born except from heavenly revelation (Calvin, Institutes 1.7.5).

source_text: I. Hactenus exposuimus, quam distincte et clare a nobis fieri potuit, nostram de authoritate Scripturae sententiam. Atque, ut rem totam in pauca contrahamus, docuimus 1. Scripturam proprio quodam splendore gerere, et varios divinitatis radios emittere, quibus mentem rite dispositam ferire et afficere possit: et ita ipsi se probare. Lucem tamen illam non esse evidentiam proprie dictam, qualis est eorum, quae sunt per se nota, aut sub demonstrationem cadunt, ut cernitur in rebus Mathematicis et Metaphysicis: sed solummodo quandam moralem evidentiam, quae tota in eo consistit quod Scriptura tam multis et tam probabilibus argumentis suadetur, et habet in se tot et tam insignes divinitatis notas, ut inde vir pius et prudens efficaciter inducatur ut credat illam esse veram et divinam: quamvis divina illius authoritas non sit res per se nota, aut etiam quae demonstrari possit.
english: So far we have set out our judgment on Scripture's authority as distinctly and clearly as we could. To draw the whole into a few words, we have taught first that Scripture bears a splendor of its own and sends out various rays of divinity. Those rays can strike and move a mind rightly disposed, and so Scripture proves itself.

Yet that light is not evidence in the strict sense — not the kind that belongs to things known of themselves, or that fall under demonstration, as in mathematics and metaphysics. It is only a moral evidence. It consists entirely in this: Scripture is recommended by so many probable arguments, and carries in itself so many conspicuous marks of divinity, that a pious and prudent person is effectively led to believe it true and divine — even though its divine authority is not self-evident, and cannot be demonstrated.

source_text: II. Probavimus, ad hoc ut aliquis Scripturae sacrae credat, illamque divinitus inspiratam agnoscat, vera et legitima fide quae sit alicujus ad salutem momenti, opus esse Spiritu sancto intus monente et illuminante. Illam autem Spiritus sancti operationem necessariam nobis esse, non tantum propter tenebras per peccatum inductas, quae sunt veluti quoddam velum, mentis nostrae oculis oppositum, quod occultat nobis Scripturae sacrae lucem, et obstat ne illam possimus aspicere; sed etiam propter genium et naturam ipsius doctrinae in Scriptura contentae: quae, cum mentem nostram in se, etiam citra peccatum consideratam, omnino superet, necesse est ut intellectus noster supra seipsum extollatur, ut ad illam possit assurgere. Adeoque, ut Scripturam et singulos ejus libros pro veris et divinis agnoscamus et recipiamus firmiter et indubitate, et certitudine tanta quantam requirit fides, ad cujus objectum pertinent, opus esse non solum ut Spiritus sanctus, mentis nostrae nativam caecitatem sanet, et dispellat tenebras per peccatum accersitas, quae obstant ne Scripturae lucem possimus percipere; sed etiam ut nos ad credendum compellat arcano quodam instinctu et impulsu, sive interna quadam efficacia, quae sit omni argumento et ratione major.
english: We have proved this: to believe sacred Scripture, and to acknowledge it as divinely inspired, with a true and legitimate faith that matters for salvation, a person needs the Holy Spirit admonishing and illuminating within.

That work of the Spirit is necessary for us not only because of the darkness sin brings — a kind of veil set before the mind's eyes, hiding Scripture's light and keeping us from looking at it — but also because of the character and nature of the doctrine Scripture itself contains. That doctrine altogether surpasses our mind, even considered apart from sin. So our intellect must be lifted above itself if it is to rise to it.

Therefore, to acknowledge and receive Scripture and each of its books as true and divine — firmly, without doubt, and with the certainty faith requires, since they belong to faith's object — we need more than the Spirit healing our native blindness and driving off the darkness sin has fetched in, which blocks perception of Scripture's light. He must also compel us to believe by a secret instinct and impulse, or by an inward efficacy greater than every argument and reason.

source_text: III. Et hoc a nobis ostensum est, licet, absolute loquendo, non sit opus Ecclesiae voce et testimonio, ut Scripturae notitiam et fidem habeamus, attamen juxta legem ordinariam, Deum Ecclesiae ministerio uti in fide de Scriptura nobis ingeneranda; primumque incitamentum, quo movemur ordinarie ad illam suscipiendam pro vera et divina, communem esse Ecclesiae consensum et testimonium. Neque tamen Ecclesiae vocem et authoritatem esse fidei nostrae praecipuum fundamentum, et illud ad quod tandem reducenda est certitudo fidei qua Scripturam sacram amplectimur.
english: We have also shown this: speaking absolutely, we do not need the Church's voice and testimony in order to know and believe Scripture. Still, by the ordinary rule God uses the Church's ministry when he generates in us faith concerning Scripture. The first incentive that ordinarily moves us to receive it as true and divine is the Church's common consent and testimony.
Even so, the Church's voice and authority are not the principal foundation of our faith, nor the last point to which the certainty of the faith that embraces sacred Scripture is to be reduced.

source_text: IV. Docuimus, licet religionis dogmata, et alia quae verbo Dei traduntur, multa argumenta suae veritatis habere possint, tamen argumenta ista non esse propriam et praecipuam rationem cui innititur fides qua res Dei verbo traditas accipimus; sed potius authoritatem et veracitatem Dei docentis et revelantis. Ipsum vero Dei verbum, seu divinam revelationem, habere quidem notas et indicia, quibus internosci possit, et a diabolicis et humanis fraudibus distingui, nihilominus fidem nostram non niti potissimum hujuscemodi notis et indiciis: sed certitudinem illius resolvi in arcanum Spiritus S. testimonium, et internam illam efficientiam, qua fideles certos reddit immediate Deum esse qui loquitur, et firmam hac de re persuasionem mentibus nostris imprimit.
english: We have taught that religion's dogmas, and other things handed down by God's word, can carry many arguments for their truth. Those arguments are still not the proper and principal reason on which the faith rests that receives what God's word hands down. That reason is rather the authority and truthfulness of God as he teaches and reveals.

God's word itself — divine revelation — does have notes and marks by which it can be recognized and told apart from diabolical and human frauds. Even so, our faith does not rest chiefly on notes and marks of that kind. Its certainty is resolved into the Holy Spirit's secret testimony, and into that inward efficiency by which he immediately makes the faithful certain it is God who speaks, and presses a firm persuasion of this on our minds.

source_text: V. Sequitur jam ut videamus quid de istis omnibus Pontificii censeant, ut inde liquido constet, qua in re situs sit status quaestionis de Scripturae authoritate, quae tanta contentione inter nos et illos hodie agitatur. Hic autem ante omnia observandum inter Pontificios duo esse hominum genera. Etenim inter eos multi sunt homines procaces, nullius candoris, vix ullius doctrinae, quibus aliud nihil propositum est, quam nostros importunis disputationibus vexare. Hi saepe pugnant Andabatarum more, non videntes quid teneant, et quo dirigant ictus. Itaque inter disputandum non tantum nostram doctrinam impugnant, sed propria quoque placita convellunt, et sibi ipsis adversantur. Satis enim ipsis est, modo aculeatis quibusdam sophismatis, et captiosa quadam subtilitate molestiam nobis creent; non curantes interim, an ea, quae contra nos proferunt, possint in ipsos retorqueri. Ita, quum de authoritate Scripturae quaestio est, internum Spiritus sancti testimonium exsibilant, et multa in nostros blaterant quae omnem Scripturae sacrae authoritatem detrahunt, et fidem nostram unice suspendunt ex hominum testimonio. Et ita Christianam religionem exponunt opprobrio et ridiculam reddunt, quasi nullo alio fundamento niteretur, quam eorum, qui illam profitentur, authoritate.
english: Next we must see what the Roman doctors judge about all this, so that it may be plain where the real state of the question on Scripture's authority lies — the question fought today with such heat between us and them. First of all, notice that among the Pontificii there are two kinds of men.

Many among them are insolent, without candor, with scarcely any learning. Their only aim is to harass our people with importunate disputes. They often fight like the Andabatae — blindfold fighters — not seeing what they hold or where they aim their blows. In debate they not only attack our doctrine; they also tear up their own opinions and contradict themselves. Pointed sophisms and captious subtlety are enough for them if they can make trouble for us. They do not care whether what they urge against us can be turned back on themselves.

So when Scripture's authority is the question, they hiss at the Holy Spirit's inward testimony and babble against our people words that strip sacred Scripture of all authority and hang our faith solely on human testimony. In that way they expose the Christian religion to reproach and make it look ridiculous, as if it rested on no foundation but the authority of those who profess it.

source_text: VI. Sed praeter istos blaterones, et sophistas nullius inter suos authoritatis, fatendum est, in schola Pontificia multos esse viros doctos, qui magis considerate et exacte loquuntur, majoremque delectum argumentorum habent. Hi certe sententiam Ecclesiae Romanae accuratius tenent, et melius explicant, cautiusque defendunt. Ideoque priores isti vitilitigatores coercendi sunt quidem, et reprimendi, eorumque stultitia, et impietas merito a nostris coarguitur, et publice vapulat. Veruntamen, quum status alicujus controversiae cum Ecclesia Romana quaerendus et constituendus est, non putamus istorum nugis esse inhaerendum: sed inquirendum quid sentiant et doceant posteriores, qui apud suos pollent doctrina et authoritate.
english: Besides those babblers and sophists who carry no weight even among their own, we must admit that the Pontifical school has many learned men. They speak more carefully and exactly, and they choose their arguments better. These hold the Roman Church's mind more accurately, explain it better, and defend it more cautiously.

So those earlier quarrelsome wranglers should indeed be checked and put down; our people rightly refute their folly and impiety and expose it in public. Still, when we seek and fix the real state of a controversy with the Roman Church, we should not cling to those men's trifles. We should ask what the later sort think and teach — the ones who stand strong among their own in learning and authority.

source_text: VII. Rursus tamen illi Pontificiae Scholae duces ac primipili a seipsis distinguendi sunt. Semper enim sibi constare non videntur. Quippe aliter loquuntur quando cum suis agunt, et apud suos animo sedato et composito docent; aliter vero quum nobiscum dimicant, et disputandi atque contradicendi ardor incaluit. Siquidem in suis nobiscum concertationibus, odio nostri et aestu disputationis abrepti, illi ipsi Romanae scholae Antelignani multa temere effutiunt, non tantum nobis, sed sibi ipsis adversa, quorumque eos ipsos pudet. Itaque ea ipsa alibi in eorum scriptis longe mollius et veritati propius exposita reperiuntur.
english: Even those leaders and front-rank men of the Pontifical school must be told apart from themselves. They do not always seem consistent. They speak one way when they deal with their own and teach among them with a calm, composed mind. They speak another way when they fight with us and the heat of disputing and contradicting has caught fire.

In their contests with us, carried off by hatred of us and by the heat of debate, those very Antelignani — front-rank men — of the Roman school rashly blurt out many things that cut against not only us but themselves, and of which they are ashamed. Elsewhere in their writings those same points appear set out far more softly, and closer to the truth.

source_text: VIII. Porro licet ista sic temere effutita, odioque et caeco affectu, potius quam certa animi sententia prolata, justissime a nostris notentur et exagitentur: in constituendo tamen controversiae alicujus statu, respiciendum potius arbitramur ad ea loca ubi sedato animo loquuntur, et rem illam, de qua agitur, ex professo tractant, mentemque suae Ecclesiae clare et distincte explicant. Etenim, non tantum istiusmodi viris, qui malam causam agunt, sed viris quoque bonis, quibus propositum est veritatem tueri, non raro contingit ut, inter disputandum, ab adversa sententia plus nimio recedant, et deferantur in contrarias oras; eaque imprudenter proferant in adversarium, quae ipsis quoque nocent, neque cum veritate, et propriis ipsorum placitis usquequaque congruunt. Quod tam nostri quam Pontificii saepe in priscis Ecclesiae Patribus animadvertunt, dum schismaticos et haereticos confutant et in haereses invehuntur. Sed aequitas et candor exigit, ut quae ita duriter et incommode dicta sunt, explicentur ex aliis locis, ubi autores illi commodius loquuntur, et veritati magis consentanee. Neque diffitemur nostros quoque Doctores aliquando hac venia et indulgentia egere. Ideoque, ut benigne et candide agamus cum adversariis nostris, existimamus etiam hoc ipsis debere concedi, ut sicubi quaedam male et falso prolocuti sint, alibi vero bene et veritati congruenter, priora illa ex posterioribus emolliantur et intelligantur.
english: Those rash blurted words, born of hatred and blind passion rather than a settled judgment, our people may most justly note and press. Yet when we fix the state of any controversy, we think we should look rather to the places where they speak with a calm mind, treat the matter on purpose, and explain their Church's mind clearly and distinctly.

Not only men who plead a bad cause, but also good men set on defending the truth, often pull too far from the opposing view in the heat of dispute and are carried to the opposite shore. They imprudently urge against an adversary things that also hurt themselves, and that do not sit fully with the truth or with their own settled opinions. Our people and the Pontificii alike often notice this in the ancient Fathers of the Church, when those Fathers refute schismatics and heretics and inveigh against heresies.

Equity and candor require that words spoken so harshly and awkwardly be explained from other places where those authors speak more fitly and more in step with the truth. We do not deny that our own doctors sometimes need the same pardon and indulgence. So if we are to deal kindly and candidly with our adversaries, we judge that the same should be granted them: where they have spoken badly and falsely in one place, but well and truly in another, the earlier words should be softened and read from the later.

source_text: IX. Ut autem ista ad rem praesentem applicemus, certum est, non tantum vanos illos homines, et nullius etiam apud suos pretii, sed eos ipsos quoque qui inter Pontificios Doctores familiam ducunt, multa proferre inter disputandum, quae videntur plane contraria his quae hactenus docuimus, de notis Verbi Dei et argumentis quibus Scriptura sacra comprobatur, et de interno illo Spiritus testimonio, ad quod nostra de verbo Dei certitudo referenda est. Saepe enim loquuntur quasi Scriptura sacra nullam fidem mereretur, nec authoritatem haberet, nisi quam ab Ecclesia Romana mutuatur, et quasi in hodiernos Ecclesiae Doctores tota fidei nostrae certitudo recumberet: ita ut, secluso isto testimonio, Scriptura non plus esset apud nos valitura, quam quilibet liber profanus. Cujus generis voces impias et blasphema dicta Doctores nostri notant et congerunt in suis de hoc argumento disputationibus. Attamen, quum doctores illi Pontificii talia Scripturae injuria proferunt, videntur esse sui immemores, et in eo propria placita refigere. Eadem enim fere quae antea docuimus, de Scripturae sacrae et verbi Dei luce, de arcano Spiritus sancti testimonio, de propria fidei ratione et praecipuo illius fundamento, et de ultimo eo in quod resolvitur fidei certitudo, a Pontificiis Theologis traduntur et docentur in scholis. Quod ut clarius ostendamus, breviter percurrenda sunt nobis illa capita, de quibus antea egimus, et quid de uno quoque doceant Pontificii paucis est indicandum.
english: Apply that equity to the matter in hand, and it is plain: not only the empty disputers who count for little even among their own, but the very men who head the Roman school, often urge in debate things that cut clean against what we have taught so far — against the marks of God's Word, against the arguments that prove sacred Scripture, and against that inward Spirit-testimony in which our certainty about the Word must finally rest.

They talk as if Scripture deserved no trust and held no authority except what it borrows from the Roman Church, and as if the whole certainty of our faith lay on today's church doctors — so that, once that witness is set aside, Scripture would be worth no more among us than any pagan book. Our doctors collect those impious and blasphemous lines in their disputations on this subject.

Yet when those same Roman doctors speak so injuriously of Scripture, they forget themselves and pull down their own settled teaching. For nearly everything we have already taught — Scripture's light, the Spirit's secret witness, the proper ground of faith and its chief foundation, and the last point into which faith's certainty resolves — is handed down by Pontifical theologians in the schools. To make that clear, we must run briefly back through the heads already treated and note in a few words what the Pontificii teach on each.

source_text: X. Primum igitur, licet Pontificii nolint ea quae per se et proprie ad fidem pertinent res esse per se notas, aut quae demonstrari possint, quod etiam supra fassi sumus, non negant tamen rebus fidei competere evidentiam quandam externam et moralem; et praeter Ecclesiae suae authoritatem, agnoscunt esse plurima argumenta quibus doctrina Christiana et Scriptura sacra comprobatur, et, ut loquuntur, evidenter credibilis redditur. Id docent communiter commentatores Thomae in secundam secundae quaest. 1. art. 4. Ubi Thomas illud discutit, An objectum fidei possit esse aliquid visum. Nam in eo articulo Thomas, qui statuit objectum fidei non esse aliquid visum sive evidens, sibi objicit locum Apostoli, 1 Corinth. 13. Videmus tanquam per speculum. Ubi Apostolus loquitur de cognitione fidei: Et tamen dicit nos per eam, tanquam per speculum videre. Unde sequitur objectum fidei a credente videri, adeoque fidem esse eorum quae videntur. Ad quod respondet Doctor ille, ea quae sunt fidei considerari posse, uno modo in speciali, et sic non posse esse simul visa et credita: alio modo in generali, scilicet, in communi ratione credibilis, et sic visa esse ab eo qui credit. Non enim, inquit, crederet, nisi videret ea esse credenda, vel propter evidentiam signorum, vel propter aliquid hujusmodi. Ex quibus Thomae verbis Scholastici istud sensum colligunt, ea quae sub fidem cadunt non esse evidenter vera: attamen evidenter esse credibilia et persuaderi multis argumentis maxime gravibus et rationibus admodum validis. Quae argumenta deinde enumerant, quisque, scilicet ea quae sibi maxime valida videntur. Ut videre est apud Dominicum Bannem, Johannem Puteanum, Pesantium, et alios ad locum Thomae supra memoratum.
english: First: the Pontificii will not allow the things that belong to faith of themselves to be self-evident or demonstrable — and we have already granted that. Still they do not deny that matters of faith carry a kind of outward, moral evidence. Beside their Church's authority they admit many arguments by which Christian doctrine and sacred Scripture are proved and, in their phrase, made evidently credible.

Thomas's commentators teach this commonly on the Secunda secundae, question 1, article 4, where he asks whether the object of faith can be something seen. Thomas holds that faith's object is not something seen or evident; then he faces the Apostle's line in 1 Corinthians 13, We see as through a mirror. Paul is speaking of faith's knowledge, yet says that through it we see as through a mirror — so the believer seems to see faith's object, and faith would be of things seen.

Thomas answers that the things of faith may be taken in special, and then cannot be seen and believed at once; or in general, under the common reason of what is credible, and then the believer does see them. He would not believe, Thomas says, unless he saw that they ought to be believed — either by the evidence of signs or by something of that kind. From those words the scholastics draw this: what falls under faith is not evidently true, yet it is evidently credible, and is urged by many weighty arguments and strong reasons. Each writer then lists the proofs that seem strongest to him — Dominic Banñez, John of Poitiers, Pesantius, and others on that same article of Thomas.

source_text: XI. Praecipue vero Gregorius de Valentia, Jesuita doctus et acutus, in eo volumine quod de Analysi fidei inscripsit, primum librum insumit in persequendis argumentis quibus doctrina Christiana et Scriptura, quae ejus liber est, probari et suaderi potest: et argumenta ejusmodi usque ad decem et novem enumerat. In quibus attingit fere omnes illas quas nostri notas verbi Dei vocant, hoc est argumenta, quibus Scriptura sacra a scriptis humanis dignosci et discerni potest. Atque etiam Bellarminus ipse libr. 1. de Verbo Dei cap. 1. Omittens Ecclesiae suae testimonium, quod respuunt illi quibuscum rem habet, multis argumentis et rationibus Scripturae divinam authoritatem probat. Ut, exempli gratia, ex miraculis in Scripturae confirmationem factis, ex admiranda conspiratione et concordia Scriptorum sacrorum, et ex futurorum praedictionibus et Prophetarum vaticiniis in Scriptura contentis, et eventu comprobatis. Quae et alia quaedam profert et vindicat adversus Libertinos Scripturam contemnentes. Itaque non videntur Pontificiorum mentem satis capere illi ex nostris Theologis qui operose probant adversus eos Scripturam sacram quasdam notas habere et quaedam argumenta quibus divina comprobetur; quasi in eo positus esset ardor controversiae de Scripturae authoritate, negarentque simpliciter Pontificii Scripturam ulla divinitatis τεκμήρια et notas habere, sed solo Ecclesiae testimonio posse internosci.
english: Gregory of Valencia, a sharp and learned Jesuit, spends the whole first book of his Analysis of Faith chasing the arguments by which Christian doctrine and Scripture (its book) can be proved and pressed. He counts nineteen such arguments, and in them touches nearly every mark of God's Word that our people name — the proofs by which sacred Scripture can be told apart from human writings.

Bellarmine himself, in On the Word of God book 1, chapter 1, leaves aside his Church's testimony (which his opponents refuse) and still proves Scripture's divine authority by many reasons: miracles done to confirm Scripture, the striking agreement of the sacred writers, prophecies of future things contained in Scripture and proved by the event — and other points he urges against Libertines who despise Scripture.

So those of our theologians miss the Roman mind when they labor to prove against them that Scripture has marks and arguments of divinity — as if the whole heat of the authority debate sat there, and as if the Pontificii simply denied that Scripture has any τεκμήρια or notes of divinity and held that it can be known only by the Church's word.

source_text: XII. Praeterea Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae nobiscum consentiunt, opus esse interna quadam Spiritus sancti operatione, ad hoc ut Dei verbum et Scripturam sacram agnoscamus, et, ea qua par est fide, recipiamus. Quam operationem Spiritus Dei in nobis vocant, ut et nos internam Spiritus illuminationem, revelationem et persuasionem, internumque Spiritus sancti testimonium. Atque de isto Spiritus sancti testimonio tam clare, tam constanter et frequenter loquuntur, ut videri possit superfluum eorum super hac re proferre testimonia. Nequis tamen supersit dubitationi locus, pauca de multis citabimus. Sic ergo Melchior Canus locor. Theolog. lib. 2. cap. 8. Resp. ad 4. arg. Id statuendum est, inquit, authoritatem humanam et incitamenta omnia illa praedicta, sive alia quaecunque adhibita ab eo qui proponit fidem, non esse sufficientes causas ad credendum ut credere tenemur, sed praeterea opus esse interiori causa efficiente, id est, Dei speciali auxilio moventis ad credendum. Et paucis interjectis, Externae igitur omnes et humanae persuasiones non sunt satis ad credendum, quantumcunque ab hominibus competenter ea quae sunt fidei proponantur. Sed necessaria est insuper causa interior, hoc est divinum quoddam lumen incitans ad credendum, et oculi quidam interni Dei beneficio ad videndum dati. Quod ibidem probat authoritate Thomae et Augustini, et multis Scripturae locis, quae in hanc rem citat et urget. Idem docet Stapletonus in relect. princip. controvers. de potestate Ecclesiae in se, quaest. 1. artic. 2. conclus. 4. Et fusius De principiis fidei Controv. 4. libr. 8. cap. 1. cujus lemma est, Impossibile esse sine speciali gratia ac dono fidei divinitus infuso, actum verae fidei producere, aut ex veri nominis fide credere. Atque in suis contra Witakerum disputationibus perpetuo queritur per calumniam doctoribus Ecclesiae Romanae objici, quod negent Spiritus sancti internum testimonium necessarium esse ad fidem ingenerandam. Speciatim triplicat, adversus Witakerum pro Eccles. authorit. cap. 3. Arcanum hoc, inquit, divini Spiritus testimonium prorsus necessarium est, ut quis Ecclesiae testimonio ac judicio circa Scripturarum approbationem credat. Quibus concinit Gregorius de Valentia Analysis fidei lib. 1. cap. 1. Deus, inquit, ipse in primis est qui Christianam doctrinam, atque adeo Scripturam sacram veram esse voce revelationis suae, et interno quodam instinctu atque impulsu humanis mentibus contestatur, atque persuadet ut in ea ipsa Scriptura multis in locis expressum est. Denique Bellarminus hanc doctrinam persequitur integra concione, cui titulum fecit De lumine fidei.
english: The doctors of the Roman Church also agree with us that some inward work of the Holy Spirit is needed if we are to recognize God's Word and sacred Scripture and receive it with due faith. They call that work, as we do, the Spirit's inward illumination, revelation, and persuasion, and the inward testimony of the Holy Spirit. They speak of it so clearly and so often that citing them might seem needless; still, lest doubt linger, a few witnesses from many.

Melchior Canus, Loci Theologici 2.8, reply to the fourth argument: human authority and all those outer inducements used by the one who proposes the faith are not enough for the belief we are bound to give; there must also be an interior efficient cause — God's special help moving us to believe. A little later: no outward human persuasion is enough, however well the things of faith are set out by men; there must also be an interior cause — a divine light that urges belief, and inward eyes given by God's kindness for seeing. He presses Thomas, Augustine, and many Scripture places for the point.

Stapleton teaches the same in his relection on the Church's power, and more fully in On the Principles of Faith (Controversy 4, book 8, chapter 1): without special grace and the infused gift of faith it is impossible to produce a true act of faith, or to believe with faith worthy of the name. Against Whitaker he keeps complaining that Rome is falsely charged with denying the Spirit's inward testimony; and in defense of the Church's authority, chapter 3, he says that secret testimony of the divine Spirit is altogether necessary if anyone is to trust the Church's judgment in approving the Scriptures. Gregory of Valencia concurs: God himself first of all, by the voice of his revelation and by an inward instinct and impulse, witnesses to human minds that Christian doctrine — and so sacred Scripture — is true, and persuades, as Scripture itself says in many places. Bellarmine carries the same teaching through a whole sermon titled On the Light of Faith.

source_text: XIII. Ex his vero manifestum est eos non attigisse hujus controversiae scopum qui quaestionis statum sic explicant. An, scilicet, Scripturae credamus propter Ecclesiae solum testimonium: an vero praecipue, propter testimonium internum Spiritus sancti: quasi Ecclesia Romana internum illud Spiritus sancti testimonium prorsus rejiceret et exsibilaret. Et vice versa nobis injurios esse Pontificios qui nostros exagitant, quasi privatum jactantes Spiritum, et enthusiasmis quibusdam inhiantes. Etenim de Spiritus arcano testimonio non docemus aliud quicquam quam quod ipsi fatentur et docent. Nec per istud testimonium excludimus, ut nobis calumniose objiciunt, necessitatem ministerii Ecclesiastici in proponendis atque exponendis iis quae pertinent ad fidem, ut superiori disputatione abunde docuimus.
english: From all this it is clear that those have missed the mark of this controversy who state the question as: Do we believe Scripture on the Church's testimony alone, or chiefly on the inward testimony of the Holy Spirit? — as if Rome wholly rejected and hissed out that inward Spirit-testimony.

And on the other side the Pontificii wrong us when they harry our people as boasters of a private Spirit, gaping after enthusiasms. On the Spirit's secret testimony we teach nothing beyond what they themselves grant. Nor does that testimony cancel, as they falsely charge, the need of the Church's ministry to propose and explain what belongs to faith — as the previous disputation has already shown at length.

source_text: XIV. Neque minus diserte docent Pontificii Ecclesiae authoritatem non esse fidei nostrae rationem formalem, id est praecipuum illud fundamentum in quod fides nostra recumbit. Istud praesertim docet Melchior Canus locor. Theolog. lib. 2. cap. 8. resp. ad quartum arg. Tertium, inquit, subjiciendum est rationem formalem nostrae fidei non esse Ecclesiae authoritatem, hoc est fidei ultimam resolutionem non fieri in Ecclesiae testimonium. Et infra, Non est Ecclesiae authoritas ratio per se movens ad credendum. Item, Si generaliter quaeratur unde fideli constet ea quae fide tenet esse a Deo revelata, non poterit Ecclesiae authoritatem inducere. Fuerunt quidem nonnulli inter veteres Scholasticos, nempe Durandus et Gabriel Biel, qui fidem Christianam in Ecclesiae authoritatem ultimo resolvebant, quasi ultima credendi ratio fidelibus esset Ecclesiae testimonium. Sed haec sententia pridem explosa est, et communi consensu rejicitur a Scholasticis hodiernis, nominatim vero a Melchiore Cano loco quem jam indicavimus. Eorum, inquit, errorem dissimulare non possum, qui asserunt fidem nostram eo tanquam in ultimam credendi causam reducendam esse, ut credamus Ecclesiam esse veracem. Postea subjungit multa argumenta quibus errorem illum redarguit: ut quod inde sequeretur primam rationem formalem fidei non esse veritatem increatam sed creatam: Et ita fidem nostram non inniti tanquam suo fundamento divinae veritati, sed humanae. Praeterea, cum assensus conclusionis non sit certior principiorum assensu, ostendit inde sequi, quod Deum esse trinum, non nobis esset certius, aut firmius, quam Ecclesiam esse veracem, cui per humanarum causarum incitamenta crederemus. Deinde urget locum Pauli, Licet nos, aut Angelus de caelo, evangelizet vobis, &c. Unde colligit fidei assensionem humanis causis et incitamentis non inniti. Quare, inquit, ne mens nostra vacillet, altius petenda, quam ab hominis vel ratione, vel authoritate Scripturae divinae authoritas est. Quibus addit Apostolos et Prophetas resolvisse ultimo fidem suam in divinam authoritatem et veracitatem: Jam autem fidem nostram eandem esse cum fide Prophetarum et Apostolorum, adeoque in humanam Ecclesiae authoritatem non resolvi, et multa similia.
english: The Pontificii teach no less plainly that the Church's authority is not the formal reason of our faith — not the chief foundation on which faith finally rests. Melchior Canus presses this hardest in Loci Theologici 2.8, reply to the fourth argument. Third, he says, we must hold that faith's formal reason is not the Church's authority: faith's last resolution is not made into the Church's testimony. Below he adds: the Church's authority is not of itself a reason that moves to belief. And again: if the question is asked in general how the believer knows that what he holds by faith was revealed by God, he cannot bring in the Church's authority.

Some of the older scholastics — Durandus and Gabriel Biel — did finally resolve Christian faith into the Church's authority, as if the Church's word were the believer's last ground for believing. That view was exploded long ago and is rejected by today's schools, Canus named among them. Their error, he says, I cannot hide: they claim our faith must be reduced to this last cause of believing — that we take the Church to be truthful.

Then he piles up arguments against it. On that scheme the first formal reason of faith would be created truth, not uncreated; our faith would lean on human truth rather than divine. And since a conclusion is never more certain than its principles, God's being triune would be no firmer for us than the Church's being truthful — a claim we would take on human inducements. He presses Paul's line: "Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach a gospel to you…" (Galatians 1). Faith's assent, he gathers, does not lean on human causes. So, lest the mind waver, Scripture's divine authority must be sought higher than any human reason or authority. The Apostles and Prophets finally resolved their faith into God's authority and truthfulness; our faith is the same as theirs, and so is not resolved into the Church's human authority — with many like points.

source_text: XV. His consentanea docet Stapletonus Controvers. 4. de potest. Eccles. in se quaest. 3. Art. 3. ubi haec est ejus secunda conclusio, Ecclesiae vox non est formale fidei objectum. Id quod probat, Primo, quia absque ea fides esse potest. Et secundo, quia sola Ecclesiae vox et authoritas ad veri nominis fidem non potest inducere. Postea sibi objicit argumenta quorundam veterum Scholasticorum, et inter alia celebrem istum Augustini locum, Non crederem Evangelio, nisi me Catholicae Ecclesiae commoveret authoritas. Ad quod breviter respondet his verbis, Evangelio non creditur, nisi authoritate Ecclesiae commovente, scilicet ordinarie, quia est ordinarius modus quo prima veritas omnia revelat. Ibidemque fatetur fidem nostram non pendere a solo Ecclesiae testimonio, nec principaliter ab illo. Ad illud vero Augustini haec dicit Melchior Canus, loco supra citato, Non, si Ecclesia aditum nobis praebet ad sacros libros cognoscendos, protinus ibi acquiescendum est, sed oportet ultra progredi, et solida Dei veritate niti. Consentit Dominicus Bannes inter suos celebris in secundam secundae quaest. 1. art. 1. dubio 4. ubi haec est ejus secunda conclusio, Assensus fidei nostrae non potest reduci ad fidem acquisitam, qua credimus Ecclesiam esse veracem, tanquam in regulam, vel formalem rationem credendi. Posteaque subjungit, Haec conclusio tam certa est, ut oppositum ejus videatur nobis non solum temerarium, sed erroneum etiam in fide. Unde patet neque hunc inter nos et Pontificios esse quaestionis statum, An, scilicet, fidei quam Scripturae adhibemus, ratio propria et praecipuum fundamentum sit Ecclesiae authoritas.
english: Stapleton teaches the same in Controversy 4, on the Church's power in itself, question 3, article 3. His second conclusion: the Church's voice is not the formal object of faith. He proves it first because faith can exist without that voice, and second because the Church's voice and authority alone cannot produce faith worthy of the name. He then faces older scholastic arguments, including Augustine's famous line: "I would not believe the Gospel unless the Catholic Church's authority moved me."

Stapleton's short answer: the Gospel is not believed except with the Church's authority moving — ordinarily, because that is the ordinary way the first Truth reveals all things. In the same place he grants that our faith does not hang on the Church's testimony alone, nor chiefly on it. Canus on the same Augustine text: if the Church only opens the door to the sacred books, we must not stop there; we must go on and lean on God's solid truth. Dominic Bañez, on the Secunda secundae 1.1, doubt 4, is just as clear: the assent of our faith cannot be reduced to acquired faith that the Church is truthful, as if that were the rule or formal reason of believing. The opposite, he adds, is not only rash but erroneous in the faith itself.
So this too is not the state of the question between us and the Pontificii — whether the proper reason and chief foundation of the faith we give to Scripture is the Church's authority.

source_text: XVI. Quae sit vero propria fidei nostrae ratio sic explicat idem Canus loco saepius memorato, His vero tribus certis stabilibusque sententiis illa etiam conjuncta est, ultimam fidei nostrae resolutionem fieri in causam interiorem efficientem, hoc est, in Deum moventem ad credendum, verbi gratia, huic articulo, Deus est trinus, et huic, Ecclesia non potest errare, et caeteris universis doctrinae Christianae principiis, assentior per infusam fidem, non quod Johannes dixerit, aut quivis alius homo, sed quod Deus revelaverit: huic autem, Deus revelavit, immediate credo, a Deo motus per instinctum specialem. Itaque, ex parte objecti, ratio formalis movens est divina veritas revelata: sed illa tamen non sufficit ad movendum, nisi adsit causa interior, hoc est, Deus etiam movens per gratuitum specialemque concursum. Idem docet Stapletonus quaest. illa prima art. 2. ubi haec est ejus tertia conclusio, Deus revelans est proprie et absolute objectum formale fidei. Idque probat exemplo fidei Prophetarum et Apostolorum, qui non aliud formale fidei suae objectum habuerunt; unde concludit omnium fidem idem objectum habere; quandoquidem una est omnium fides. Ibidem vero resp. ad tertium arg. illius haec verba sunt, Absolute et per se, ultima resolutio credibilium est Deus verax, seu Deus intus in corde revelans, juxta illud Johannis Baptistae, Quem misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur, et qui accipit testimonium ejus signavit quia Deus verax est, Johan. 3. Denique haec est communis Scholasticorum sententia, Assensum fidei nostrae resolvi ultimo in motionem interiorem Spiritus sancti, ut videre est apud Commentatores Thomae in secundam secundae quaest. 1.
english: What then is faith's proper reason? Canus, in the place already cited, joins this to three settled points: faith's last resolution is into an interior efficient cause — God moving us to believe. To the article "God is triune," to "the Church cannot err," and to every other principle of Christian doctrine, I assent by infused faith not because John said it, or any other man, but because God revealed it; and to "God has revealed" I believe at once, moved by God through a special instinct.

So on the object's side the formal moving reason is revealed divine truth; yet that does not move us unless an interior cause is also present — God himself moving by a free and special concurrence. Stapleton's third conclusion (question 1, article 2) says the same: God revealing is properly and absolutely the formal object of faith. He proves it from the Prophets and Apostles, who had no other formal object; therefore every believer's faith has that same object, for there is one faith of all. In reply to the third argument he writes: absolutely and of itself, the last resolution of things to be believed is the truthful God — or God revealing inwardly in the heart — after John the Baptist: "He whom God has sent speaks the words of God, and whoever receives his testimony has set his seal that God is true" (John 3).
Finally the scholastics commonly hold that the assent of our faith is at last resolved into the Holy Spirit's inward motion — as Thomas's commentators show on the Secunda secundae, question 1.

source_text: XVII. Itaque Doctores illi volunt Ecclesiae vocem, et testimonium esse causam sine qua non crederemus, et, ut loquuntur, conditionem quandam objecti fidei nostrae quia Ecclesia medium est per quod Deus revelat, et proponit credenda. Attamen nolunt fidem nostram reduci ad testimonium Ecclesiae, tanquam ad supremam et ultimam credendi rationem, sed ad Deum revelantem, et Spiritum sanctum illuminantem, ut accurate docet Bannes loco quem jam citavimus. Et similiter Stapletonus, cujus haec verba sunt articulo a nobis saepius indicato, Fides quae capit ab Ecclesiae testimonio, quatenus proponit et inducit ad fidem, definit in Deo intus revelante, et intus docente quod foris Ecclesia praedicavit. Praedicatio enim Ecclesiae docet forinsecus, proponit, inducit, adjuvat: sed cathedram habet in caelo qui docet intus, ut docet Augustinus. Quo interno magisterio semel accedente, locum habet illa Samaritanae vox, Jam non propter loquelam tuam credimus: Ipsi enim audivimus, et scimus quia hic est Salvator mundi.
english: Those doctors therefore treat the Church's voice and testimony as a cause without which we would not believe, and, in their terms, a condition of faith's object: the Church is the medium through which God reveals and proposes what is to be believed. Yet they refuse to reduce our faith to the Church's testimony as the supreme and last reason of believing. They reduce it to God revealing and the Holy Spirit illuminating — as Bañez teaches carefully in the place already cited.

Stapleton's words in the article we keep marking are the same: faith that begins from the Church's testimony, so far as that testimony proposes and leads to faith, ends in God revealing within and teaching within what the Church preached without. The Church's preaching teaches from outside; it proposes, leads, and helps. But the One who teaches within has his chair in heaven, as Augustine says. Once that inward teaching has come, the Samaritan line has its place: "Now we do not believe because of your speech; for we ourselves have heard, and we know that this is the Savior of the world" (John 4).

source_text: XVIII. Nec etiam negant Doctores Scholastici fidem, quam revelationi divinae adhibemus, esse prudentem assensum, hoc est, illum qui verbo Dei credit, ad id moveri quibusdam argumentis, quae viro prudenti suadere possunt revera Dei verbum esse quod ut tale ipsi proponitur. Licet non pendeat ab istis argumentis fidei certitudo, aut eis proprie nitatur: ut praesertim videre est apud Gregor. de Valentia, Analyf. fidei, lib. 1. cap. 1. ubi haec sunt illius verba, Sed quia rationi humanae revelatio divina non evidenter patet, aliis quibusdam, praeter revelationem divinam, argumentis, opus est, quibus homines etiam inducti, prudenter sibi persuadeant doctrinam Christianam veram esse. Nec vero ejusmodi argumenta ad eam rem requiruntur, ut propter illa proprie, certe ac firmiter homines credant, (certitudo enim et firmitas fidei, atque adeo ipsius assensio, per se divinae revelationi soli, tanquam fundamento innititur.) Sed ut clariora quaedam habeant motiva, quibus prudenter animum inducant velle certe ac firmiter, propter divinam revelationem, Deo adjuvante, credere. Etenim accurate discernendi sunt animi motus duo in iis qui fidem amplectuntur. Nam et prudentia etiam dictante, judicant dignam esse Christi doctrinam quae certo ac firmiter credatur, et demum credunt assensione fidei, adiuti divinitus, eam veram esse. Quod assensione fidei certa atque firma, adiuti divinitus, credunt doctrinam Christi veram esse, id in solum divinum testimonium, quod revelatione divina continetur, tanquam in causam quidem rationemque credendi, referri debet. Itemque, in Ecclesiae propositionem, tanquam in quandam conditionem, sine qua, Christiana quidem fide minime crederetur. Quod autem in primis prudenter deliberant, atque statuunt merito eam a se doctrinam, tanquam divinam ac veram, certo ac firmiter credi posse, id vero prudentiae judicium quoddam est, quod proprie argumentis aliis praeter divinam revelationem nititur. Quibus conformia tradit Melchior Canus lib. 2. cap. 8. resp. ad quartum arg. Non solum, inquit, necessarium est, ut credituro ea quae sunt fidei simpliciter ab homine proponantur, quasi prima principia discipulo, verum etiam opus est exteriorem aliquam persuasionem, et humanum incitamentum adhiberi. Idque probat exemplis eorum qui miraculis et aliis rationibus commoti crediderunt. Et postea quoque addit, quibus rebus expositis, facile, ut opinor, intelligi potest vera esse quae paulo ante a nobis dicta, hoc est, oportere humana quaedam et exteriora adminicula intervenire ad credendum, nec tamen ea esse idonea per se, nec fidei nostrae resolutionem in ejusmodi fieri, sed in interiorem causam divinam quae excitet et moveat ut credamus. Atque haec est etiam communis sententia scholae Romanae nullo, quod sciam, refragante: ut superfluum sit plura cumulare testimonia.
english: Nor do the scholastic doctors deny that the faith we give to divine revelation is a prudent assent: the one who believes God's Word is moved by arguments that can persuade a prudent mind that what is set before him as God's Word truly is. Faith's certainty does not hang on those arguments, nor properly lean on them. Gregory of Valencia makes the distinction sharpest in Analysis of Faith 1.1: because divine revelation is not evident to human reason, other arguments besides revelation are needed, so that men may prudently persuade themselves that Christian doctrine is true.

Yet those arguments are not required so that people believe properly, surely, and firmly because of them. The certainty and firmness of faith — and the assent itself — lean of themselves on divine revelation alone as their foundation. The arguments only supply clearer motives by which the mind may prudently will to believe surely and firmly because of divine revelation, with God's help. Two soul-motions must be told apart in those who take hold of faith. First, even under prudence's dictate, they judge Christ's doctrine worthy of sure and firm belief. Then, helped by God, they believe by faith's assent that it is true. That sure, firm, God-helped assent must be referred to the divine testimony alone contained in revelation, as the cause and reason of believing; and to the Church's proposing only as a condition without which Christian faith would scarcely be given. The first prudent judgment — that this doctrine may rightly be held as divine and true — is a judgment of prudence, and it properly leans on arguments other than revelation itself.

Canus teaches the same in Loci Theologici 2.8, reply to the fourth argument. It is not enough that the things of faith be simply proposed by a man to the one about to believe, as first principles to a pupil; some exterior persuasion and human inducement must also be used. He proves it from those moved to believe by miracles and other reasons. Once that is set out, he adds, what we said a little earlier is easy to see: certain human, outward supports must intervene for believing, yet they are not fit of themselves, and faith's resolution is not made into them, but into an interior divine cause that stirs and moves us to believe. That is the common teaching of the Roman school, so far as I know with no dissent — so further witnesses would be surplus.

source_text: XIX. At, inquies, quis ergo tandem est status controversiae de Scripturae authoritate? nam in capitibus hucusque recensitis videtur esse consensus inter Orthodoxos et Pontificios. An forte hic est tantum de nomine certamen? minime certe. Hic magnum et maximi momenti dissidium est inter utrosque. Ad cujus intelligentiam notandum est, 1. quasdam esse revelationes quae non nisi per aliam revelationem nobis innotescunt, unde suam quoad nos authoritatem mutuantur. Ita verbi gratia, revelatio facta olim Balaam, per revelationem Mosi factam nobis innotuit. Idemque dico de fragmento illo prophetiae Enochi, cui Epistola Judae authoritatem conciliat. Sed cum hac in re non possit dari progressus in infinitum, nec debeat admitti circulus, quo una revelatio per aliam probetur, et haec vicissim per alteram illam: necesse est, ut detur revelatio quaedam, respectu nostri prima, quae per se, et propter se fidem apud nos obtineat, non autem beneficio revelationis cujusdam notioris.
english: You will ask: what, then, is the real state of the controversy on Scripture's authority? In the heads reviewed so far the Orthodox and the Pontificii seem to agree. Is the fight only about a name? Not at all. The rift between the two sides is large and of the highest moment.

To see it clearly, note first that some revelations become known to us only through another revelation, and they borrow their authority for us from that other. Balaam's old revelation reached us through the revelation given to Moses. The same holds for that scrap of Enoch's prophecy to which Jude's letter lends authority.

Yet there cannot be an infinite regress here, and a circle — one revelation proved by another, and that other by the first — must not be allowed. So some revelation must be first for us: one that wins our faith by itself and for its own sake, not by help from a better-known revelation.

source_text: XX. Praeterea sciendum est, accurate loquendo, distinctionem adhiberi posse inter fidei propriam, et, ut loquuntur Scholae, formalem rationem, si consideretur simpliciter et absolute; et inter externum quoddam fidei principium, sive regulam externam credendorum. Fidei propria et formalis ratio eadem fuit, est, et erit semper apud omnes fideles, nempe Dei revelatio, quocunque tandem modo illa revelatio fiat, sive immediato Dei afflatu, sive per homines, sive per Angelos, sive per Scripturam, sive extra Scripturam. Etenim fidelibus cunctis haec perpetua credendi res fidei et religionis ratio formalis est, nempe, quia Deus talia revelavit. At Deo visum non est satis fidelibus singulis privatim revelare quae ad salutem cujusque necessaria essent, sed ad unitatem et communionem in Ecclesia servandam, et ut obviam iretur Satanae praestigiis, Deus semper voluit in Ecclesia extare communem quandam, externam et publicam revelationem, quae esset fidei regula, ad quam exigenda essent omnia fidei dogmata, et ex qua omnis de rebus fidei contentio decidenda et terminanda esset. Talis fidei regula ante legem datam erant Patriarcharum voces, et viva Dei oracula. Post legem vero a Mose datam et scriptis mandatam, regula fidei in Ecclesia fuit ipsa lex Mosis scripta, et revelationes Prophetis postea factae, et scriptis quoque consignatae. Post Christi vero adventum, haec regula Novi Testamenti accessione auctior et amplior facta est. Itaque jam fidei nostrae in Ecclesia Christiana regula est Scriptura Veteris et Novi Testamenti.
english: Speak carefully and you may also distinguish faith's proper formal reason — taken simply and absolutely, as the Schools put it — from an external principle of faith, an outward rule for what is to be believed.

Faith's proper formal reason was, is, and always will be the same for every believer: God's revelation, however it comes — by God's immediate breath, through men, through angels, through Scripture, or outside Scripture. For every believer the standing formal reason of religious belief is this: because God revealed such things.

Yet God did not judge it enough to reveal privately to each believer whatever that person needed for salvation. To keep unity and communion in the Church, and to meet Satan's tricks, he always willed a common, external, public revelation to stand in the Church as the rule of faith — the measure of every dogma, and the court that ends every dispute about faith.

Before the law was given, that rule was the Patriarchs' voices and God's living oracles. After Moses' law was given and written, the Church's rule was that written law, with the revelations later made to the Prophets and likewise written down. After Christ's coming the New Testament enlarged the rule. So now, in the Christian Church, the rule of our faith is the Scripture of both Testaments.

source_text: XXI. Tertio observandum est, fidei nostrae resolutionem dupliciter fieri posse, respectu objecti, et respectu subjecti, sive respectu nostri, et respectu aliorum. Respectu nostri, et respectu subjecti fides resolvitur, quum quaeritur quid sit internum fidei principium, et illud in quo conscientia cujusque conquiescit, neque licet ultra progredi. Sed respectu objecti, et respectu aliorum fides nostra resolvitur, quum quaeritur ultimum fidei nostrae fundamentum, quod alteri proferre et indicare possumus. Ultimum vero istud fidei nostrae fundamentum quod indicare possumus alteri, necesse est ut sit aliquod externum fidei principium, et externa quaedam fidei regula, in qua sistendum est, et qua non datur alia ulterior.
english: Third: our faith can be resolved in two ways — with respect to the object or the subject; with respect to ourselves or with respect to others.

With respect to ourselves and the subject, faith is resolved when we ask what the inward principle is, and where each conscience rests so that we may not press further. With respect to the object and to others, our faith is resolved when we ask for the last foundation we can show and name to someone else.
That last foundation we can show another must be some external principle of faith — an outward rule of faith — where we stop, with no further rule beyond it.

source_text: XXII. Jam ut ista ad rem praesentem applicemus, constat inter nos et Pontificios, ut patet ex antedictis, fidei nostrae rationem propriam simpliciter et per se, esse divinam revelationem, quocunque tandem modo fiat, neque hac de re ulla est inter nos controversia. Constat quoque ultimum illud in quo fidelis cujusque conscientia conquiescit esse internum Spiritus sancti testimonium. At vero non constat quae sit hodie illa revelatio, nostri respectu, prima et notissima, quae per se et propter se a nobis recipi debeat, non vero propter ullam aliam revelationem, quae nobis sit notior et majoris authoritatis; adeoque quae sit primum et communissimum fidei principium externum, per quod omnia probari debeant, ipsum vero a nullo priore. Hanc revelationem asserimus nos sacra Scriptura contineri: Etenim verbum Dei, libris Veteris et Novi Testamenti comprehensum, tale est ut per se apud nos fidem obtinere debeat; non vero per aliquod aliud Dei verbum, et divinam quandam revelationem, quae publicum et externum testimonium illi perhibeat, quod fidelibus sit ipsa Scriptura notius et certius. Neque est ulla fidei regula, aut ullum fidei principium externum, quod Scriptura sacra sit prius, et quo Scriptura possit tanquam a priori probari. Sed ea est prima et communissima regula omnium quae ad fidem spectant, ipsa ad aliam nullam regulam examinanda. Itaque si quis roget cur hoc vel illud dogma credis, verbi gratia, Deum esse trinum et unum, et fideles esse baptizandos in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus sancti, Respondemus, quia hoc in Scriptura divinitus inspirata habetur, et locum indicamus. Si vero ultra rogemur, cur Scripturam illam divinam esse credamus, jam non proferimus aliud fidei principium, quo Scriptura probetur: sed in eo principio sistendum esse monemus. Adducimus quidem argumenta quibus probare conamur Scripturam divinam esse, et illi merito tanquam divinae credi. Attamen argumenta illa non sunt fidei nostrae principia proprie dicta, et fundamentum illud quo fides nostra praecipue nititur: Sed Scripturae, id est, Deo in Scripturis loquenti, immediate credimus, ad id moti interno Spiritus sancti impulsu.
english: Apply this to the present case. We and the Pontificii agree, as the earlier theses show, that faith's proper reason simply and of itself is divine revelation, however it comes; on that point there is no fight between us. We also agree that the last rest of each believer's conscience is the Holy Spirit's inward testimony.

What is not agreed is which revelation is today first and most known for us — the one we must receive by itself and for its own sake, not because of some other revelation better known to us and of higher authority; and so which is the first and most common external principle of faith, through which everything else is to be proved, while it itself has no prior.

We hold that this revelation is contained in sacred Scripture. God's Word in the books of both Testaments ought to win faith among us by itself — not by some other Word of God, some further divine revelation that would give it a public external witness better known and more certain to believers than Scripture is. No rule of faith, no external principle, stands prior to sacred Scripture so that Scripture could be proved from something earlier. Scripture is the first and most common rule of everything that belongs to faith, and it is not to be measured by another rule.

Ask why we believe this or that dogma — that God is triune and one, or that believers are to be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit — and we answer: because inspired Scripture holds it, and we point to the place. Press further why we take that Scripture as divine, and we do not offer another principle of faith to prove Scripture; we say one must stop there. We do offer arguments that Scripture is divine and deserves to be believed as divine. Those arguments are not, properly speaking, faith's principles, nor the foundation on which faith chiefly leans. We believe Scripture at once — God speaking in the Scriptures — moved by the Spirit's inward impulse.

source_text: XXIII. At vero Pontificii nolunt Scripturam sacram immediate et per se fidem apud nos mereri et obtinere; sed docent esse aliam divinam revelationem per quam Scripturam probari necesse sit, ut publice de ea in Ecclesia constet. Et haec revelatio ipsis est Ecclesiae vox et testimonium, hoc est praepositorum Ecclesiae doctrina. Siquidem Deum ipsum per Ecclesiae pastores hodie loqui volunt, tanquam per organa, quoad fidei doctrinam, infallibilia, quemadmodum olim locutus est per Prophetas atque Apostolos. Itaque admittunt quidem Scripturam esse fidei regulam, sed subalternam atque partialem, quae superiori et ampliori regula probari indigeat. Quapropter ad fidei dogmata comprobanda afferunt quidem Scripturae sacrae authoritatem. Sed si rogentur cur sacrae Scripturae fidem adhibeant, dicunt se id facere propter Ecclesiae suae testimonium, et in hoc testimonio, tanquam inter fidei externa principia supremo, conquiescere ipsos necesse est, si quidem suis placitis stare velint. Nos quidem ad libri alicujus sacri authoritatem comprobandam afferimus quoque constans Ecclesiae testimonium: verum non sicut ipsi, tanquam aliquod fidei principium cui fides nostra subjicienda sit: sed solum tanquam quoddam argumentum a posteriori, validum quidem et bonum, sed non prorsus divinum atque infallibile.
english: The Pontificii will not let sacred Scripture deserve and win our faith immediately and of itself. They teach another divine revelation by which Scripture must be proved, so that the Church may publicly settle its standing. For them that revelation is the Church's voice and testimony — the doctrine of her overseers. They want God to speak today through the Church's pastors as through organs infallible in the doctrine of faith, as he once spoke through Prophets and Apostles.

So they admit Scripture is a rule of faith, yet a subordinate and partial one that needs proving by a superior, fuller rule. When they prove dogmas they do cite sacred Scripture's authority. Asked why they trust sacred Scripture, they say: because of their Church's testimony — and in that testimony, as the supreme external principle of faith, they must rest if they mean to keep their own teachings.

We too bring the Church's constant testimony when we prove a sacred book's authority. But not as they do — not as a principle of faith to which our faith must be subjected. For us it is only an argument from the later effect: sound and strong, yet not wholly divine and infallible.

source_text: XXIV. Atque inde exurgit celebris illa quaestio de Scripturae authoritate. Nobis asserentibus Scripturae authoritatem apud nos esse summam, nec aliunde mutuam sumptam; quoniam Scriptura supra se nullam habet revelationem, aut aliud quoddam fidei principium quo probari possit. Pontificiis vero contendentibus authoritatem Scripturae ab authoritate Ecclesiae pendere: quoniam existimant Ecclesiae testimonium fidei quoddam principium esse Scriptura superius, et quo Scriptura probari indigeat, ut de ea publice in Ecclesia constet.
english: From this rises the famous question on Scripture's authority. We say Scripture's authority among us is supreme, not borrowed from elsewhere: above itself Scripture has no revelation, and no other principle of faith by which it can be proved.

The Pontificii say Scripture's authority hangs on the Church's: they take the Church's testimony for a principle of faith above Scripture, one by which Scripture must be proved so that the Church may publicly settle its standing.

source_text: XXV. Verum ut distinctius appareat discrimen Pontificiae sententiae, et nostrae, et qua in re positus sit controversiae cardo, sciendum est Pontificios ita Scripturam sacram cum Ecclesiae doctrina comparare, ut nos aliquod fidei particulare dogma cum Scriptura sacra comparamus. Sicut ergo aliquem fidei articulum, ut exemp. gr. mortuos olim resurrecturos esse, in se suam veritatem et authoritatem a solo Deo habet, non vero a testimonio Prophetarum et Apostolorum, qui Scripturae libros conscripserunt: ita Pontificii admittunt Scripturam sacram in se suam authoritatem a solo Deo habere, non ab Ecclesiae testimonio. Deinde quemadmodum praecipua ratio fidei, qua dogma illud amplectimur non est proprie Petri, Pauli, Esaiae, etc. authoritas, sed divina revelatio ad nos illorum calamo transmissa, quandoquidem ante Scripturam dogma illud creditum fuit, et adhuc citra Scripturam credi potest. Sic fatentur Pontificii, Ecclesiae testimonium non esse fidei nostrae de Scriptura rationem propriam atque praecipuam, sed simpliciter et absolute divinam revelationem. Rursus tamen, ut dogma illud, et aliud quodvis simile non debet publice in Ecclesia recipi, et credendum proponi, nisi quatenus Scripturae testimoniis probatur ex quibus solis publice constare potest fidelibus aliquid ad fidem pertinere, atque sic dogmatis cujusvis authoritas quoad nos, et certitudo publica et externa a Scripturae sacrae testimonio pendet: Ita volunt Pontificii Scripturae authoritatem quoad nos ab Ecclesiae testimonio pendere, neque de libri alicujus divinitate publice fidelibus constare, nisi ex Ecclesiae approbatione et testificatione. Denique, quemadmodum, non obstante illa dogmatum a Scriptura dependentia, religionis Christianae dogmata multis, praeter Scripturae testimonia, argumentis probari et suaderi possunt, quae tamen argumenta non sunt fidei nostrae ratio et fundamentum, sed tantum motiva quaedam ad fidem inducentia: Ita Pontificii quoque non diffitentur Scripturam sacram, praeter Ecclesiae testimonium, multa divinitatis argumenta et notas habere, quibus probari et suaderi possit, sed quae tamen non possunt publicam de Scripturae divinitate fidem in Ecclesia fundare.
english: To mark the difference between their sentence and ours, and where the hinge of the controversy sits, note how the Pontificii compare sacred Scripture with the Church's doctrine: as we compare a particular dogma of faith with sacred Scripture.

As an article of faith — for example that the dead will one day rise — has its truth and authority in itself from God alone, not from the Prophets' and Apostles' testimony as writers of Scripture, so they admit that sacred Scripture has its authority in itself from God alone, not from the Church's word.

And as the chief reason we embrace that dogma is not properly Peter's, Paul's, or Isaiah's authority, but the divine revelation brought to us by their pen — for the dogma was believed before Scripture, and can still be believed apart from it — so they confess that the Church's testimony is not the proper and chief reason of our faith about Scripture, but simply and absolutely divine revelation.

Yet again: as that dogma, or any like it, must not be publicly received in the Church or set forth for belief unless Scripture's testimonies prove it — since only from those can believers publicly know that something belongs to faith, so that any dogma's authority for us, and its public external certainty, hangs on sacred Scripture's testimony — so they want Scripture's authority for us to hang on the Church's testimony, and a book's divinity not to be publicly settled for believers except by the Church's approval and attestation.

Finally: even with that dependence of dogmas on Scripture, Christian dogmas can be proved and urged by many arguments besides Scripture's testimonies — motives that lead toward faith, not faith's reason and foundation. So the Pontificii also do not deny that sacred Scripture, besides the Church's testimony, has many notes and arguments of divinity by which it can be proved and urged — yet which cannot found public faith in the Church concerning Scripture's divinity.

source_text: XXVI. Ex quibus satis liquere putamus quaenam hic nobis intercedat cum Ecclesiae Romanae Doctoribus controversia.
