Nempe haec, utrum Scriptura sit prima fidei regula, et primum fidei principium externum, quod proinde alio nullo principio probari possit, nec aliunde suam mutuetur authoritatem. An vero Ecclesiae doctrina et testimonium sit principium et regula fidei, Scriptura ipsa quoad nos notior et evidentior, et qua Scripturam probari necesse sit, ut publice de ea apud fideles constet: Prius nos asserimus: Posterius Pontificii, qui per Ecclesiam, ut modo dictum est, intelligunt praesentis Ecclesiae Pastores, et praecipue Pontificem Romanum.
english: From all this the controversy between us and the Roman Church's doctors is plain enough. Is Scripture the first rule of faith and the first external principle of faith — so that no other principle can prove it, and it does not borrow its authority from elsewhere?

Or is the Church's doctrine and testimony the principle and rule of faith, better known and clearer to us than Scripture itself, and the means by which Scripture must be proved so that believers may publicly settle its standing? We assert the former. The Pontificii assert the latter — and by "Church," as already said, they mean the present pastors, above all the Roman Pontiff.

source_text: XXVII. Inde vero error illorum refellitur quod Scriptura est aliquid apud fideles notius quam sit ipsa Ecclesia. Et hoc quia inter omnes Christianos constat quae sint verae Scripturae, saltem quoad partes praecipuas, ut patet per inductionem. Etenim Graeci, Armeni, Aethiopes, Pontificii, Protestantes, et si quae sint adhuc hodie Christianorum sectae, communi consensu agnoscunt libros, quos Ecclesiae nostrae pro Canonicis habent, revera Canonicos esse. Addunt quidem Pontificii quosdam alios libros ad Canonem veteris Testamenti: sed de illis quos Canonicos censemus nobiscum consentiunt. Quod si qui Scripturas in totum negarunt, vel contempserunt, quod patrum nostrorum memoria putantur fecisse Libertini, paucissimi fuerunt, nec ullius nominis, et cito defierunt. At non constat quae sit vera Ecclesia: sed unaquaeque secta pertendit se esse veram Ecclesiam. Nec Ecclesiae Graecae, Armeniacae et Aethiopicae Romanam Ecclesiam pro vera Dei Ecclesia habent, aut illius authoritate ullo modo se obstringi putant.
english: Their error is answered from this: among believers Scripture is better known than the Church herself.

Every Christian body agrees, at least on the chief books, which writings are true Scripture. Greeks, Armenians, Ethiopians, Pontificii, Protestants, and whatever other Christian parties remain today all acknowledge as Canonical the books our churches hold Canonical. Rome adds certain Old Testament books to its Canon; on the books we count Canonical it still agrees with us.

Those who denied or despised Scripture outright — as the Libertines are remembered to have done in our fathers' day — were few, obscure, and soon gone. Which Church is the true one is not settled the same way: each party claims to be it. The Greek, Armenian, and Ethiopian churches neither take Rome for God's true Church nor bind themselves to its authority.

source_text: XXVIII. Adde quod nullus Pontifex, nullum Concilium, nullus Pastorum Coetus tot et tam illustres habet suae authoritatis notas et argumenta, quam Scriptura sacra suae divinitatis. Nam Scripturam sacram commendant quamplurima Thesibus praecedentibus a nobis enumerata: Futurorum praedictiones quae in ea habentur, doctrinae quam tradit sanctitas, sublimitas et efficacia, styli majestas atque simplicitas, consensus veteris et novi Testamenti, miracula in ejus confirmationem facta, genus vitae eorum qui primi eam tradiderunt, perpetua Dei cura in ea conservanda, constantia martyrum in veritate illius tuenda, populorum consensus, et ipsorum etiam hostium testimonium. Quodnam vero Concilium, aut quae Pastorum multitudo, tot et tam insignibus authoritatem suam ingerit argumentis? Atque hic appellanda est conscientia adversariorum, annon, scilicet, notius sit scripta Mosis et Pauli divina et authentica esse, quam Concilium Florentinum, Tridentinum, aut Lateranense legitima esse Concilia, et quae Spiritus sancti infallibilem ductum habuerunt.
english: No pope, council, or gathering of pastors carries so many and so bright marks of its own authority as sacred Scripture carries of its divinity.

Earlier theses already listed what recommends Scripture: prophecies of things to come, the holiness, height, and force of its teaching, the majesty and plainness of its style, the harmony of Old and New Testament, miracles confirming it, the life of those who first handed it down, God's lasting care to keep it, the martyrs' constancy for its truth, the consent of peoples, and even hostile witnesses.

What council, or what crowd of pastors, presses its claim with notes so many and so strong? Ask the adversaries' own conscience: is it not plainer that Moses and Paul wrote divine, authentic books than that Florence, Trent, or the Lateran were legitimate councils led by the Spirit without fail?

source_text: XXIX. Praeterea Scriptura fidelibus est certior testimonio eorum qui Ecclesiae praesunt, ac proinde ab illis authoritatem suam non mutuatur. Nam authoritas Pastorum Ecclesiae non est hodie fidelibus certior, quam fuit primis Christianis authoritas Apostolorum. Sed Apostolis olim viventibus et praedicantibus, testimonium eorum apud fideles minus certum fuit Scripturae testimonio, ut patet ex verbis Petri, Epist. 2. cap. 1. ubi verba faciens apud eos qui jam fidem susceperant, postquam testatus est se vocem audivisse de coelo Christo dicentem, hic est filius meus dilectus in quo mihi complacui, addit fideles habere de Christo testimonium aliud firmius, nempe Prophetarum in Scripturis sanctis. Non enim, inquit, arte compositas fabulas secuti, notam fecimus vobis Domini nostri Jesu Christi potentiam et adventum. Sed ut qui nostris oculis aspeximus illius majestatem. Acceperat enim a Deo Patre honorem et gloriam, voce ad eum delata hujusmodi e magnifica gloria, hic est filius meus dilectus in quo acquiesco. Et hanc vocem audivimus e caelo delatam, cum essemus una cum eo in monte sancto: Et habemus firmiorem propheticum sermonem, cui benefacitis attendentes, quasi lucernae lucenti in caliginoso loco.
english: Scripture is also more certain for believers than the word of those who preside in the Church — so it does not borrow its authority from them.

Pastors today are not more certain for the faithful than the Apostles were for the first Christians. Yet while the Apostles still lived and preached, their testimony weighed less among believers than Scripture's — as Peter shows in his second letter (2 Peter 1). Speaking to people who already believed, after he told how he heard the voice from heaven say of Christ, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," he adds that they have a firmer witness still: the Prophets in the holy Scriptures.

"We did not follow cleverly devised myths," he says, "when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. He received honor and glory from God the Father when that voice came to him from the Majestic Glory: 'This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.' We heard that voice from heaven while we were with him on the holy mountain. And we have the prophetic word made more sure, to which you do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place."

source_text: XXX. Adde quod Scriptura sacra majorem ex omni parte apud fideles authoritatem habet, quam testimonium Pastorum Ecclesiae. Etenim testimonium Pastorum Ecclesiae non est hodie majus quam erat olim Joannis Baptistae testimonium. At Scripturae testimonium testimonio Joannis Baptistae majus erat: ut manifeste docet Christus Dominus noster, Joan. cap. 5. ubi testimonium illud quod ipsi Scripturae sacrae perhibebant, anteponit Joannis Baptistae testimonio. Misistis, inquit, ad Joannem, et testimonium dedit veritati, ego autem habeo testimonium majus Joannis testimonio. Et postea affert triplex testimonium testimonio Joannis majus: et primo quidem opera miraculosa quae patrabat. Opera enim, inquit, quae dedit mihi Pater, ut ea perficerem, testantur de me quod Pater miserit me. Deinde vocem Patris e coelo attestantem, Et qui misit me Pater ipse testatus est de me. Ac denique Scripturae sacrae testimonium. Subjungit enim, Scrutamini Scripturas, quia vos putatis in ipsis vitam aeternam habere, et illae sunt quae testificantur de me.
english: Sacred Scripture also has, on every side, greater authority among believers than the Church's pastors do.

Their testimony today is no greater than John the Baptist's once was. Yet Scripture's testimony was greater than the Baptist's — as Christ our Lord teaches plainly (John 5), where he sets Scripture's witness to himself above John's. "You sent to John," he says, "and he has borne witness to the truth; yet I have a testimony greater than John's."

He then names a threefold witness greater than John's: first the miracles he worked — "the works the Father gave me to accomplish testify that the Father has sent me"; next the Father's voice from heaven — "the Father who sent me has himself borne witness of me"; and last sacred Scripture. He adds: "Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me."

source_text: XXXI. Praeterea Ecclesiae testimonium nullum est illustrius et magis solemne juxta adversarios, quam illud quod perhibetur in Conciliis et Decretis Pontificum. At sensus communis fidelium dictat nullorum Conciliorum tantam esse authoritatem, quam sit Scripturae sacrae. Nec enim ullum Concilium vel Nicenum, vel Chalcedonense, vel Tridentinum, vel aliud quodvis quisquam aequiparare auderet authoritate scriptis Mosis et Prophetarum libris. Neque, vel illi qui sunt Pontificibus maxime addicti, eousque adhuc frontem perfricuerunt, ut aequare audeant Epistolas Papales Paulinis Epistolis, et quatuor Evangeliis. Quod docet ipsa praxis doctorum Romanensium. Etenim, cum digerunt locos unde desumuntur argumenta Theologica, primum locum semper Scripturae assignant, posteriorem vero Conciliis, et PP. Decretis. Et quidem eousque Scripturam, sicuti par est, venerantur, ut agnoscant in ea nullum, vel minimum erratum reperiri posse. At, licet velint Concilia infallibilia esse quoad fidei dogmata, tamen agnoscunt in aliis multis errori esse obnoxia, eorumque conclusiones esse quidem de fide, at Concilia uti posse argumentis non bonis: Et quamvis non errent in quaestione juris, saepe tamen falli in quaestione facti. Adde quod Ecclesiae Pastores et Doctores utuntur Scripturae sacrae testimoniis ad authoritatem suae doctrinae conciliandam; illorumque doctrina potest et debet ad Scripturae sacrae examen revocari. Unde est quod laudantur fideles Beroenses qui, audita Pauli praedicatione, consulabant Scripturas, an quae dixerat ita se haberent. Ad. 17. Cum ergo Scriptura sacra apud fideles sit majoris authoritatis, quam sint Ecclesiae Pastores, proculdubio suam authoritatem a testimonio illorum non accipit, quandoquidem quod majorem authoritatem habet, authoritatem sumere non potest ab eo quod habet minorem. Nihil enim potest conferre authoritatem majorem illa ipsa quam habet.
english: On their own showing, no Church testimony is brighter or more solemn than what Councils and papal Decrees give. Yet common Christian sense says no council matches sacred Scripture's authority. No one dares set Nicea, Chalcedon, Trent, or any other beside Moses and the Prophets. Even Rome's warmest friends have not yet hardened their faces enough to level papal letters with Paul's epistles and the four Gospels.

Roman practice itself proves it. When they rank the sources of theological argument, Scripture always comes first; Councils and papal Decrees come later. They so honor Scripture, as they should, that they grant no error can be found in it, even the least. Councils they want infallible on dogmas of faith — yet they admit many other slips: conclusions may be of faith while the arguments are poor; they may hold the question of right and still err on the question of fact.

Pastors and doctors also use Scripture's witnesses to recommend their own teaching — and that teaching can and must be tried by Scripture. So the Bereans are praised: after hearing Paul preach, they searched the Scriptures to see whether those things were so (Acts 17). If Scripture carries more weight with believers than the Church's pastors, it plainly does not take its authority from their word. What is greater cannot draw its authority from what is less. Nothing can give an authority greater than its own.

source_text: XXXII. Quomodo vero posset Scripturae authoritas quoad nos ab authoritate Ecclesiae pendere, cum contra, authoritas Ecclesiae quoad nos ab authoritate Scripturae pendeat. Etenim ex Scriptura discimus quae sit vera Ecclesia, et quae et quanta sit illius authoritas. Nec authoritas illa potest aliunde certo probari. Ideoque patres olim ad Scripturas revocarunt haereticos qui veram Christi Ecclesiam non agnoscebant, et ex iis veram Ecclesiam demonstrandam esse censuerunt. Sic enim Augustinus cum Donatistis agit: Utrum ipsi, inquit, Ecclesiam teneant nonnisi divinarum Scripturarum canonicis libris ostendant. Et ipsi Pontificii hodie Ecclesiam suam, et authoritatem ejus infallibilem, contra nos ex Scriptura sacra probare conantur, et eo se officio egregie defungi putant dum nobis afferunt illa Scripturae loca, Ero vobiscum usque ad consummationem saeculi, Rogavi pro te, Petre, ne fides tua deficiat, Spiritus vos deducet in omnem veritatem, Dic Ecclesiae, et similia quaedam quae proferunt tanquam fundamenta authoritatis illius quam Ecclesiae tribuunt. Cum igitur, ipsis fatentibus, ex Scriptura authoritas Ecclesiae nobis innotescat, nec certior possit ejus afferri probatio, planum est vice versa certitudinem nostrae fidei de Scriptura, Ecclesiae testimonio, tanquam praecipuo suo fundamento, non niti. Alioquin hic admittetur circulus. Nam Scripturae authoritas per Ecclesiam probabitur, et vicissim authoritas Ecclesiae per Scripturam; Et rursus a Scriptura ad Ecclesiam redibitur, et sic in infinitum.
english: How then could Scripture's authority for us hang on the Church's, when the Church's authority for us hangs on Scripture?

From Scripture we learn which Church is true, and what force it has. That authority cannot be proved with certainty from anywhere else. So the fathers once sent heretics who denied Christ's true Church back to the Scriptures, and held that the true Church must be shown from them. Augustine tells the Donatists: if they hold the Church, let them show it only from the canonical books of divine Scripture.

Rome itself today tries to prove its Church and its infallible authority against us from sacred Scripture, and thinks the work well done when it cites places such as "I am with you to the end of the age," "I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail," "the Spirit will lead you into all truth," "Tell it to the Church," and the like, as foundations of the authority it gives the Church. Since, by their own confession, the Church's authority is known to us from Scripture, and no surer proof can be offered, it is clear the other way that our certainty about Scripture does not rest on the Church's testimony as its chief ground. Otherwise the circle is open: Scripture is proved by the Church, the Church by Scripture, and back again without end.

source_text: XXXIII. Huc accedit quod Pontificii docent Scripturam in manibus Ecclesiae esse instar literarum quas vocant credentiae, hoc est, quibus fides sit alicui qui mittitur ab aliquo superiori, et quibus ad illum remittimur, ut plenius de mittentis mente et voluntate informemur: Sic enim volunt Ecclesiam nobis exhibere Scripturam, tanquam diploma quo ejus divina vocatio et authoritas confirmatur, ac nobis obsignatur. Et quo ad illam remittimur, ut plenius de voluntate Dei edoceamur. At literarum illarum, quas credentiae vocant, authoritas non pendet ab eo qui illas exhibet: sed contra authoritas ejus qui literas exhibet per literas illas nobis innotescit et confirmatur. Et qui affert literas non est causa cur literis credamus: sed illi credimus propter istas literas quibus fides ei sit.
english: Rome adds that Scripture in the Church's hands is like letters of credit: papers that accredit an envoy from a superior, and that send us back to that superior for a fuller account of his mind and will. So they want the Church to present Scripture as a diploma sealing its divine calling and authority, and remitting us to the Church to learn God's will more fully.

But letters of credit do not draw their force from the one who shows them. The opposite is true: the bearer's authority is known and confirmed by the letters. The one who brings the letters is not why we trust the letters; we trust him because of the letters that accredit him.

source_text: XXXIV. Ad hoc Argumentum mirum est quomodo respondeant Pontificii. Etenim Stapletonus, qui omnium accuratissime hanc controversiam tractasse videtur, concedit authoritatem Ecclesiae quoad nos ab authoritate Scripturae pendere. At negat inde sequi authoritatem Scripturae non pendere vicissim ab Ecclesiae authoritate. Idque probare conatur quibusdam instantiis in negationis suae rationem adductis. Nam, inquit, authoritas Christi quoad nos ab authoritate Johannis Baptistae pendebat. Johannes enim missus erat ut Christo testimonium perhiberet, et ut omnes per illum in Christum crederent. Et tamen vicissim Baptistae authoritas quoad nos a Christi testimonio pendebat. Christus enim Baptistae testimonium perhibuit, et vocationem illius confirmavit. Verum haec Instantia, et similes quas affert, nihil faciunt ad rem. Nam per hoc tantum ostenditur, duo quaedam sibi posse testimonium mutuo perhibere, et sese invicem probare. At non duo ita esse comparata, ut authoritas primi ab authoritate secundi pendeat, et vicissim authoritas secundi ab authoritate primi, saltem eorundem respectu. Etenim verum est quidem Baptistam testimonium perhibuisse Christo, et Christum indicasse, atque homines ad Christum adduxisse. At tamen Christi authoritas ab authoritate Baptistae non pendebat, neque qui ad Christum adducti fuerant et Christum agnoverant Baptista indicante, in Christum credebant propter Baptistae testimonium, tanquam praecipuum fidei suae fundamentum. Neque major et certior quoad illos erat Johannis Baptistae, quam Christi authoritas. Itaque damus quidem authoritatem Johannis Baptistae ab authoritate Christi pependisse, at pernegamus Christi authoritatem vicissim pependisse ab authoritate Johannis Baptistae. Et certe impossibile est duo ita esse comparata, ut unius authoritas ab alterius authoritate pendeat, et vicissim, saltem quoad eosdem, et eodem tempore. Nam id cujus authoritas ab alio pendet, quoad nos minus certum et notum est eo unde dependet. Ita si Ecclesiae authoritas quoad nos ab authoritate Scripturae dependet, tum certior et notior est quoad nos Scripturae authoritas. Si vero vicissim Scripturae authoritas ab authoritate Ecclesiae pendet, tum Scriptura quoad nos minus certa erit et nota. Et sic Scripturae authoritas simul erit quoad nos certior et minus certa, notior et minus nota quam Ecclesiae authoritas, quod implicat contradictionem. Jam vero hic non quaeritur simpliciter, an Scriptura possit per Ecclesiam probari, et Ecclesia vicissim per Scripturam. Sed an Scripturae authoritas proprie loquendo pendeat ab Ecclesiae authoritate, tanquam ab aliquo fidei principio quod sit certius et notius quoad nos.
english: Their reply to this argument is strange. Stapleton, who seems to have handled the controversy with the most care, grants that the Church's authority for us hangs on Scripture's. He denies that Scripture's authority therefore fails to hang in turn on the Church's — and he tries to prove it by instances.

Christ's authority for us, he says, hung on John the Baptist's, for John was sent to witness to Christ so that all might believe through him; yet the Baptist's authority in turn hung on Christ's witness, for Christ attested John and confirmed his calling. The instance — and others like it — does not reach the point. Mutual testimony can prove two things to each other. It does not show that the first's authority hangs on the second's, and the second's on the first's, for the same people at once.

The Baptist did point men to Christ. Those who came to Christ that way did not believe in Christ chiefly on the Baptist's word, nor was John greater or surer for them than Christ. We grant that John's authority hung on Christ's; we deny outright that Christ's hung on John's. Two authorities cannot each hang on the other for the same persons at the same time. Whatever hangs on another is less certain and less known to us than that on which it hangs. If the Church's authority depends on Scripture's, Scripture is more certain and better known for us. If Scripture's hangs on the Church's, Scripture is less certain and less known. Then Scripture would be at once more and less certain, better and less known, than the Church — a contradiction.

The question here is not merely whether Scripture can be proved by the Church and the Church by Scripture. It is whether Scripture's authority, properly speaking, hangs on the Church's as on a principle of faith more certain and better known for us.

source_text: XXXV. Secundo respondet Stapletonus, authoritatem quidem Ecclesiae quoad nos ab authoritate Scripturae pendere, non tamen ita ut Ecclesia non possit aliunde quam per sacram Scripturam innotescere. Nam, inquit, citra Scripturam ex Symbolo discunt fideles Ecclesiam esse et ipsi esse credendum. At certe Symbolum per se authoritatem non habet, sed authoritatem suam sumit ex Scriptura sacra, ex qua totum desumptum est. Nec Symbolum aliud est, quam declaratio eorum quae fideles, juxta Scripturam sacram, se credere profitentur. Praeterea inde sequitur authoritatem Symboli quoad nos, notiorem esse ipsa Ecclesiae authoritate, quod valde facit contra adversarios, qui authoritatem Symboli, ut caeterorum omnium credendorum, ab authoritate Ecclesiae pendere contendunt, tanquam a fidei quodam notiori principio et argumento. Nam Ecclesia juxta adversarios ipsa est quae Symbola condit, et conciliat illam authoritatem. Adde quod in Symbolo profitemur nos credere unam sanctam Catholicam Ecclesiam. At Symbolum non docet quae sit illa sancta et Catholica Ecclesia, an scilicet Romana, potius quam Graeca aut Aethiopica. Nec ullis ex Symbolo probationibus istud elici potest. Sed ut authoritas Scripturae per authoritatem Ecclesiae nobis confirmetur, qua ratione volunt Pontificii, non sufficit ut in genere sciamus in terris esse Ecclesiam, sed necesse est ut determinate sciamus quae sit vera Ecclesia, praedita, scilicet, authoritate divina atque infallibili.
english: Stapleton's second reply grants that the Church's authority for us hangs on Scripture's, yet denies that the Church can be known only through Scripture. Apart from Scripture, he says, the faithful learn from the Creed that the Church exists and must be believed.

The Creed has no authority of its own. It draws its whole force from sacred Scripture, from which it is taken. It is simply the faithful's confession of what they believe according to Scripture. That already makes the Creed's authority better known to us than the Church's — which cuts hard against those who say the Creed's authority, like every other article of belief, hangs on the Church as on a better-known principle of faith.

On their own showing the Church is the body that frames Creeds and confers that authority. Yet in the Creed we confess one holy Catholic Church, and the Creed never tells us which Church that is — Roman rather than Greek or Ethiopian. No proof from the Creed settles it. If Scripture's authority is to be confirmed to us through the Church's, as Rome wants, bare knowledge that some Church exists on earth is not enough. We must know determinately which Church is the true one, clothed with divine and infallible authority.

source_text: XXXVI. Praeterea quod certitudo fidei, qua Scripturam sacram fideles amplectuntur ut fidei regulam, non pendeat a publico et solemni aliquo Ecclesiae judicio, quo tanquam oraculo divina authoritas Scripturae confirmatur, inde patet quod, citra ullum ejusmodi judicium, Scriptura multis seculis publice innotuit et recepta est, tanquam fidei Canon. Etenim per aliquot annorum centurias a tempore Apostolorum, nullum Concilium, nec ullus Pontifex certum Scripturae Canonem consignavit, et librorum sacrorum catalogum contexuit. Nam primum Concilium in quo librorum Canonicorum numerus recensitus est Laodicenum fuit, quod non habitum est ante trecentesimum a Christo nato annum, et adhuc particulare fuit, non generale. At ante Concilium istud certus fuit Scripturae Canon, et certa fidelibus Scripturae authoritas. Neque Laodicenae Synodi, ut nec subsequentium Conciliorum quae librorum sacrorum numerum recensuerunt, scopus fuit novam quandam authoritatem libris illis acquirere, sed tantum indicare et declarare qui jam Canonici fuissent.
english: The certainty with which believers receive sacred Scripture as the rule of faith does not hang on some public, solemn Church decree that confirms Scripture's divinity like an oracle. For ages Scripture was publicly known and received as the Canon of faith with no such decree at all.

For several centuries after the Apostles, no council and no pope sealed a fixed Canon or drew up a catalogue of the sacred books. The first council to review the number of Canonical books was Laodicea — not before the three-hundredth year from Christ's birth, and still a particular council, not a general one. Yet before Laodicea the Canon was already certain, and Scripture's authority was certain to the faithful.
Neither Laodicea nor the later councils that listed the sacred books aimed to give those books some new authority. They only marked and declared which books were already Canonical.

source_text: XXXVII. Neque hic recurri potest ad traditionem aliquam Ecclesiae, quasi ante Concilia quae librorum sacrorum numerum definierunt, Ecclesiae traditio fuerit fidei de Scriptura fundamentum. Nam Pontificii volunt traditionem esse quidem medium quo Ecclesia utitur in dijudicandis eis quae fidei sunt, attamen traditionem dubiam esse volunt, non minus quam libros Scripturae, nec esse certum fidei fundamentum, antequam publico Ecclesiae judicio probata fuerit.
english: Nor may one fall back on some Church tradition, as if before the councils that fixed the number of sacred books tradition itself had been the foundation of faith concerning Scripture.

Rome grants that tradition is a means the Church uses in judging matters of faith. Yet on Rome's own terms tradition is as doubtful as the books of Scripture, and is no certain foundation of faith until a public Church judgment has proved it.

source_text: XXXVIII. Nec etiam est magis ad rem commentum Stapletoni qui duplex Ecclesiae testimonium distinguit. Unum solemne et expressum, quod Ecclesia scilicet perhibet in Conciliis universalibus et PP. Decretis. Alterum tacitum et interpretativum, quo Ecclesia censetur probare illa quae a suis ministris patitur doceri, et a populo fideli teneri; quasi Ecclesia ante Conciliorum determinationem, jam de Canonicis libris judicium pronuntiasset, et testimonium perhibuisset, non illud quidem solemne et expressum; sed alterum istud tacitum et interpretativum: quatenus nimirum sinebat Pastores libros Scripturae tanquam Canonicos fidelibus tradere, nec fidelium illos acceptantium fidem improbabat. Nam judicium, sive testimonium illud, quod vocat interpretativum, non poterat fidem fidelium fundare, nec ab eo fides Christianorum pendebat, quandoquidem judicium illud fidem fidelium sequitur, non praecedit. Quod enim sinit Ecclesia fieri, intelligitur esse et fieri, prius quam Ecclesia illud fieri sinat et patiatur. Itaque rogo Pontificios quodnam fundamentum habebat illa priscorum Christianorum fides, quam Ecclesia toleravit, et quam probasse censetur sua tolerantia. Nam certe non potuit niti Ecclesiae tolerantia, et tacito consensu, fides illa quae concipitur tanquam aliquid ista tolerantia prius.
english: Stapleton's further device helps no more. He distinguishes two kinds of Church testimony: one solemn and express, given in general councils and papal decrees; the other tacit and interpretative, by which the Church is said to approve whatever she lets her ministers teach and her people hold.

As if, before any council decided the Canon, the Church had already judged the Canonical books — not by a solemn sentence, but by this tacit reading: she let pastors hand the books to the faithful as Canonical, and did not reject the faith of those who received them.

That so-called interpretative judgment cannot found the faithful's belief, nor did Christian faith hang on it. It follows their faith; it does not precede it. What the Church allows to happen is already happening before she allows it. So I ask Rome: what grounded that early Christian faith which the Church merely tolerated and is said to have approved by her silence? A faith conceived as prior to that tolerance cannot rest on the tolerance and the tacit consent.

source_text: XXXIX. Deinde, quicquid sit de illo tacito Ecclesiae testimonio, saltem quod ad aliquos Canonicos libros attinet, docent Pontificii per aliquod tempus Ecclesiam super illis non pronuntiasse suam sententiam: dicunt enim de quibusdam Novi Testamenti libris olim dubitatum fuisse, eo quod Ecclesia de illis mentem suam non satis testata fuerat. At licet quidam de illis dubitarent, tamen apud plerasque Ecclesias libri illi etiam tum publice recepti fuerunt, et pro divinis atque authenticis habiti. Unde liquet publicum Ecclesiae testimonium necessarium non esse ut de cujuspiam libri divinitate publice constare possit, et de eo certi sint fideles. Quandoquidem ante Ecclesiae determinationem librorum illorum, de quibus quidam addubitabant, certa fuit et publice agnita authoritas in Christiani orbis maxima parte. Quamvis enim Epistolae Judae et Jacobi quibusdam viderentur ἀντιλεγόμεναι, ut ait Eusebius: tamen, eodem teste, apud alios erant ὁμολογούμεναι et publice receptae. Et similiter, cum Joannis Apocalypsin quidam rejicerent, tamen Johannis alumnae Ecclesiae, ut loquitur Tertullianus, illius authoritatem tuebantur. Et de Epistola ad Hebraeos eodem modo res se habuit. Quanquam enim de illa aliquandiu dubitatum fuerit in Ecclesia Latina, Hieronymus tamen docet Epistola ad Dardanum, Ecclesias Orientis illam fuisse veneratas tanquam divinam et Apostolicam.
english: Whatever one makes of that tacit testimony, Rome herself teaches that for a time the Church gave no sentence on certain Canonical books. Some New Testament books were once doubted, they say, because the Church had not yet made her mind clear enough about them.

Even so, while some doubted, most churches already received those books publicly and held them divine and authentic. Public Church testimony is therefore not required before a book's divinity can stand publicly and believers be sure of it. Before any Church determination of the disputed books, their authority was already certain and publicly owned across the greater part of the Christian world.

Jude and James seemed disputed (ἀντιλεγόμεναι) to some, as Eusebius says; yet on his own witness others acknowledged them (ὁμολογούμεναι) and received them publicly. Some rejected John's Apocalypse, yet the churches John had nursed, as Tertullian puts it, defended its authority. Hebrews stood the same way: though long doubted in the Latin Church, Jerome tells Dardanus that the Eastern churches had venerated it as divine and Apostolic.

source_text: XL. Quod si libet ad Veteris Testamenti tempora regredi, quando Prophetae libros suos edebant, libri illi authoritatem et de jure habebant, et de facto apud fideles Israelitici populi obtinebant, antequam sacerdotes Ecclesiae tum praepositi, libros illos probassent, et divinos esse declarassent. Imo cum plerique eorum in eum finem praecipue a Deo missi essent, ut Sacerdotum vitia et socordiam arguerent, illos ut plurimum habuerunt adversos; et tamen, non obstante illa Sacerdotum repugnantia, Prophetarum libri pro divinis et authenticis habiti et agniti fuerunt. Quod patet praesertim Jeremiae exemplo. Etenim cap. 8. libri sui sic eos increpat qui tum Judaico populo praeerant. Quomodo dicitis nos sapientes sumus et lex Domini nobiscum est: vere mendacium operatus est stylus mendax Scribarum, confusi sunt sapientes, perterriti et capti sunt; verbum enim Domini abjecerunt, et sapientia nulla est in eis, a Propheta usque ad Sacerdotem omnes faciunt mendacium. Ideoque cap. 18. videmus in Jeremiam insurrexisse istos Ecclesiae praepositos, dicentes, Venite et cogitemus contra Jeremiam cogitationes. Non peribit enim lex a Sacerdote, et consilium a sapiente, nec sermo a Propheta. Venite et percutiamus eum lingua, et non attendamus ad universos sermones ejus. Et tamen quamvis ita Jeremiae repugnarent Ecclesiae Judaicae praepositi, nedum ut illius prophetias probarent, tamen, inquam, gravissime increpatur Jehojakim, quod prophetiarum illius a Barucho exscriptarum authoritatem respuisset, ipsasque scalpello Scribae laceratas combussisset, ut habetur Jeremiae cap. 36. Sed juxta placita Pontificiorum quodnam tantum crimen admittebat rex ille, pro divino non habens scriptum, quod nondum Ecclesiae judicio probatum erat, imo tunc ab Ecclesiae praepositis impugnabatur.
english: Go back to Old Testament times. When the Prophets published their books, those books already had authority by right, and in fact held it among Israel's faithful, before the priests then ruling the Church had approved them or declared them divine.

Most of the Prophets were sent chiefly to rebuke the priests' vices and sloth, so the priests were usually their enemies. Even so, against that resistance the Prophets' books were held and acknowledged as divine and authentic. Jeremiah makes it plain. In chapter 8 he rebukes Judah's rulers: How can you say, We are wise, and the Lord's law is with us? The lying pen of the scribes has wrought a lie; the wise are shamed and taken; they have cast away the Lord's word, and there is no wisdom in them — from prophet to priest they all work a lie.

In chapter 18 those same rulers plot against him: Come, let us devise devices against Jeremiah. The law will not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, let us strike him with the tongue, and ignore all his words. Far from approving his prophecies, they fought him. Yet Jehoiakim is charged most heavily for rejecting the authority of those prophecies that Baruch had written out, and for cutting them with a scribe's knife and burning them (Jeremiah 36). On Rome's principles, what great crime was the king committing in refusing as divine a writing the Church's judgment had not yet approved — a writing her rulers were then attacking?

source_text: XLI. Denique, quandoquidem per Ecclesiam unde pendet quoad nos Scripturae authoritas, Pontificii intelligunt Pastores et Episcopos qui Ecclesiam regunt, rogamus eos unde pendeat Scripturae authoritas quoad Pastores ipsos, et unde constet eis hos libros divinos esse et a Deo inspiratos. Certe hic recurrere non possunt ad Ecclesiae judicium, quo Pastorum fides de Scriptura fundetur. Nam Pastores et Episcopi sunt ipsa Ecclesia de cujus testimonio et judicio agitur: adeoque Pastores illi ex seipsis discerent, quae sint verae Scripturae, et fides eorum in proprio suo testimonio fundaretur: nam, nequis sit ullus exceptioni locus, sumemus in exemplum eos qui primi tale quoddam judicium pronuntiarunt, neque pastorum aliorum judicio niti poterant. Et tamen adversarii nolunt Pastores Ecclesiae enthusiasmis agi, et Scripturae notitiam ex immediata Dei revelatione habere. Siquidem enthusiasmi et immediatae revelationes non amplius habent locum in Ecclesia Dei. Sed statuunt Episcopos et Doctores Ecclesiae ad cognitionem illam pervenire, Spiritu quidem sancto docente et ducente, sed tamen etiam mediante ipsorum studio, et diligentia, et consideratione accurata librorum ipsorum, ac sedulo examine multorum argumentorum, quibus Spiritus S. utitur ad fidem de Scriptura ipsis ingenerandam. Quid autem absurdi est, si dicamus fideles eo modo, Spiritu sancto in Scripturae sacrae cognitionem duci? saltem ex eo manifeste sequitur de Scriptura sacra nobis constare posse citra enthusiasmum, et immediatam revelationem, et tamen etiam citra Ecclesiae quoddam judicium authenticum et infallibile.
english: Finally, since by the Church on which Scripture's authority for us is said to hang Rome means the pastors and bishops who rule the Church, we ask: whence does Scripture's authority hang for the pastors themselves, and how do they know these books are divine and God-inspired?

They cannot appeal here to a Church judgment that founds the pastors' own faith in Scripture. The pastors and bishops are that Church whose testimony is in question. They would then learn from themselves which writings are true Scripture, and their faith would rest on their own word. To leave no escape, take those who first gave such a judgment: they could not lean on other pastors' rulings.

Yet Rome will not have the Church's pastors driven by enthusiasms or taught Scripture by immediate revelation — for such enthusiasms and immediate revelations, they say, no longer have place in God's Church. Bishops and doctors reach that knowledge with the Holy Spirit teaching and leading, but also through their own study, diligence, careful reading of the books, and close weighing of the many arguments the Spirit uses to beget faith in Scripture in them. What absurdity is it, then, to say the faithful are led the same way by the Spirit into knowledge of sacred Scripture? At least this much follows plainly: Scripture can be established for us without enthusiasm or immediate revelation — and also without some authentic, infallible Church judgment.

source_text: I. DISPUTATIONE proxime praecedenti quaestionis hujus statum explicuimus, veramque sententiam confirmavimus iis argumentis quae nobis maxime idonea visa sunt. Restat ut excutiamus argumenta adversariorum, et eorum vanitatem, quam breviter et dilucide a nobis fieri poterit, ostendamus.
english: In the immediately preceding disputation we set out the state of this question and confirmed the true view with the arguments that seemed to us most fit. What remains is to sift the adversaries' arguments and show, as briefly and clearly as we can, how empty they are.

source_text: II. Primum ergo sic authoritatem Scripturae ab authoritate Ecclesiae pendere, probare conantur. Scriptura, inquiunt, per Scripturam probari non potest. Ergo, ut de Scriptura apud fideles constet, necesse est ut sit testimonium aliquod divinum et infallibile, quo Scriptura probetur. Sed hoc testimonium aliud esse non potest quam Ecclesiae testimonium, quo in terris nullum est certius et augustius. Quod si dicas Scripturam multis in locis se divinam asserere, regerunt illi, ut Scripturae credamus se divinam asserenti, necesse esse ut de illius divinitate jam aliunde persuasi simus. Nec enim, ut scriptum aliquod pro divino habeatur, sufficit ut se divinum afferat: quod fecere libri plerique Apocryphi, qui merito tamen rejecti sunt. Et certe Scripturam per Scripturam ipsam probari non posse inde manifestum videtur, quod probatio omnis est a notioribus. At idem non est seipso notius et ignotius. Neque authoritatem Scripturae nescienti, aut de Scriptura dubitanti ex Scriptura quicquam probatur.
english: Their first attempt is to prove that Scripture's authority hangs on the Church's. Scripture, they say, cannot be proved by Scripture. So for the faithful to be sure of Scripture, some divine and infallible testimony must prove it. That testimony, they claim, can only be the Church's — none more certain or august on earth.

If you answer that Scripture in many places asserts its own divinity, they retort that we would already have to be persuaded of that divinity from elsewhere before we could believe the assertion. Mere self-claim is not enough: most of the Apocrypha claimed to be divine and were rightly rejected.

And it seems plain that Scripture cannot prove Scripture, because every proof moves from what is better known — and the same thing cannot be both better and less known than itself. Nothing from Scripture proves anything to someone who does not yet grant Scripture's authority, or who still doubts it.

source_text: III. Respondeo hoc argumentum meram esse fallaciam qua Pontificii possunt aeque ac nos urgeri. Sic enim in ipsos retorqueri potest. Ecclesiae vox et testimonium non est suprema fidei regula, sed ejus authoritas ab alio quodam fidei principio quoad nos notiori et certiori pendet. Nam necesse est ut sit testimonium aliud divinum, Ecclesiae testimonio notius et certius, per quod de Ecclesiae testimonio constet. Et hoc quia Ecclesiae authoritas et testimonium per ipsius Ecclesiae testimonium probari non potest. Cum idem seipso non sit notius et ignotius, neque authoritatem Ecclesiae ignoranti, aut de authoritate Ecclesiae dubitanti, quicquam possit ex testimonio Ecclesiae probari. Itaque, si quicquam valet hoc argumentum, omnem prorsus fidem subvertit: quandoquidem non potest ulla proferri fidei regula, tanquam prima et suprema, contra quam non liceat simili argumento uti.
english: I answer that this is a mere fallacy with which Rome can be pressed as hard as we can. Turn it back on them: the Church's voice and testimony is not the supreme rule of faith; its authority for us hangs on some other principle of faith better known and more certain.

There must be another divine testimony, clearer and surer than the Church's, by which the Church's testimony itself is established — because the Church's authority cannot be proved by the Church's own word. The same thing is not better known and less known than itself; nothing from the Church's testimony proves anything to someone ignorant of that authority, or still doubting it.
If the argument is worth anything, it overturns faith altogether. No rule of faith can be offered as first and supreme without leaving room for the same objection.

source_text: IV. Ut autem hujus argumenti fraus et vitium detegatur, ad formam revocandum est. Sic igitur necesse est ut illi argumententur. Quod ex se non est evidens, nec seipsum probare potest, illud non est primum fidei principium, et suprema fidei regula, cujus authoritas aliunde non pendet, sed ipsum per aliud probari necesse est. At Scriptura non est aliquid evidens, nec seipsam probare potest. Ergo, &c. Jam vero major hujus argumenti est falsi manifesta. Nam plane contra necesse est, ut quod est primum fidei principium, neque seipsum probet, nec per aliud probetur; nec tamen sit aliquid evidens. Etenim quemadmodum in disciplinis humanis quaedam sunt prima principia, unde reliqua pendent, et per quae caetera probantur, ipsa tamen neque a se, neque ab aliis in hoc genere pendent, alioqui prima non essent, sed per se fidem et assensum obtinent: ita quoque res se habet in fidei doctrina. Vel enim debet hic admitti circulus, aut dari progressus in infinitum, quorum utrumque est absurdum; aut necessario sistendum est in principio aliquo, unde pendeant, et per quod probentur caetera quae ad fidem pertinent, ipsum tamen a nullo priori, scilicet, probetur, neque etiam a seipso: quandoquidem idem non potest a seipso probari: sed per se fidem et assensum obtineat, et cui immediate credamus et assentiamur.
english: To expose the cheat, reduce the argument to form. They must argue: whatever is not evident of itself and cannot prove itself is not a first principle of faith or supreme rule whose authority does not hang elsewhere — it must be proved through something else. But Scripture is not evident, nor can it prove itself. Therefore, and so on.

The major is plainly false. On the contrary: what is a first principle of faith must neither prove itself nor be proved through another — and yet need not be something evident. In the human sciences some principles are first: the rest hang on them and are proved through them, while they hang on nothing else in that order, or they would not be first, and win assent of themselves. Faith is the same.

Either admit a circle, or an infinite regress — both absurd — or stop at some principle on which the rest of faith hangs, proved by no prior principle and not by itself either, since the same thing cannot prove itself, yet winning immediate belief and assent of itself.

source_text: V. In hoc quidem differunt principia fidei, et principia scientiarum, quod principia scientiarum per se nota sunt et evidentia, et sua luce cogunt intellectum ad assensum: principia vero fidei, quamvis moralem aliquam evidentiam habeant, tamen, logice et proprie loquendo, sunt inevidentia, neque sua luce assensum, qualem fides requirit, impetrant. Attamen in hoc conveniunt quod sicut principiis naturalibus assentimur immediate, per naturale lumen intellectus: ita quoque fidei principiis immediate credimus, per illuminationem et impulsum Spiritus sancti. Verum ut nihil obstat quominus aliquando principia naturalia probentur a posteriori: sic etiam fidei principia probari quidem possunt, sed a posteriori, et ad hominem tantum.
english: Faith's principles and the sciences' differ here: the sciences' principles are self-known and evident, and by their own light compel the intellect to assent. Faith's principles, though they have some moral evidence, are — strictly and properly — inevident, and do not by their own light win the assent faith requires.

Yet they agree in this: as we assent to natural principles immediately by the natural light of the intellect, so we believe faith's principles immediately by the Spirit's illumination and impulse. And as nothing stops natural principles from sometimes being proved a posteriori, so faith's principles can be proved — but only a posteriori, and only ad hominem.

source_text: VI. Inde ergo planum est in fidei negotio deveniendum esse ad principium aliquod, quod neque ex se sit evidens, neque etiam possit per seipsum probari, et tamen a nullo priori principio pendeat, sed per se authoritatem et fidem mereatur. Quamvis igitur Scriptura neque ex se sit evidens, nec seipsam probare possit, inde tamen concludi non potest illam non esse primum istud fidei principium quod authoritatem suam aliunde non mutuatur.
english: So in the matter of faith we must come down to some principle that is neither evident of itself nor able to prove itself, yet hangs on no prior principle and of itself deserves authority and belief. Though Scripture is neither evident of itself nor able to prove itself, it does not follow that Scripture is not that first principle of faith which borrows its authority from nowhere else.

source_text: VII. Et certe quocunque se vertant Pontificii, omnino fateri cogentur Ecclesiae testimonium, quod tanquam primum et supremum fidei principium obtendunt, non esse rem per se evidentem, nec per ipsam Ecclesiae vocem et testimonium idonee posse probari. Cum ergo nihilominus Ecclesiae testimonium ab alia nulla priori authoritate pendere, sed per se suam authoritatem apud fideles obtinere velint, aperte contra seipsos pugnant, quum ex eo quod Scriptura per Scripturam probari non possit, concludunt authoritatem illius non esse primam, et illam superiori indigere testimonio, quo nobis comprobetur. Huc ergo redit summa responsionis nostrae, Scripturam quidem per Scripturam ipsam probari non posse; non tamen inde sequi authoritatem ejus aliunde pendere, et nobis per authoritatem Ecclesiae debere probari, tanquam per quoddam fidei principium Scriptura ipsa prius et superius: quoniam Scriptura, tanquam primum fidei principium, fidem et assensum apud fideles obtinet, non probationis talis interventu, sed immediate per internam Spiritus efficaciam certam de illa persuasionem mentibus nostris imprimentis.
english: Whichever way Rome turns, it must confess that the Church's testimony — which it offers as faith's first and supreme principle — is not evident of itself, and cannot well be proved by the Church's own voice. Yet they still want that testimony to hang on no prior authority and to hold among the faithful of itself. They fight themselves when, from Scripture's inability to prove Scripture, they conclude that Scripture's authority is not first and needs a superior testimony to establish it for us.

The sum of our reply comes to this: Scripture cannot indeed be proved by Scripture itself; yet it does not follow that its authority hangs elsewhere and must be proved to us by the Church as a principle prior and superior to Scripture. As faith's first principle, Scripture wins the faithful's belief and assent not by such a proof intervening, but immediately, by the Spirit's inward efficacy impressing a sure persuasion of it on our minds.

source_text: VIII. Quae tamen dextre accipienda sunt. Primo enim, cum concedimus Scripturam sacram non posse per Scripturam ipsam probari, hoc tantum volumus illa testimonia quibus Scriptura se esse divinitus inspiratam praedicat, non esse argumenta idonea quibus convincatur, et persuadeatur ille qui Scripturae sacrae authoritatem negat. At hoc non obstat quominus alio sensu Scriptura dici possit seipsam probare, quatenus, ut thesibus praecedentibus ostensum est, Scripturae sacrae insunt multa divinitatis signa et argumenta, quibus seipsam veram et divinam asserit. Non secus ac coelum et terra praedicant et ostendunt suum authorem Deum esse, non simplici aliqua voce et testimonio, sed ex ipsa suae naturae praestantia, et potentiae ac sapientiae divinae vestigiis, quae in illis notari possunt. Aut, ut liber aliquis Aristoteli, et Euclidi se vendicat, non ex solo titulo, sed ex ipsius doctrinae genio, acumine styli, et disserendi modo, qui ejusmodi est, ut non possit, nisi praestantibus illis ingeniis tribui.
english: These points, though, must be taken carefully. When we grant that sacred Scripture cannot be proved by Scripture itself, we mean only that the places where Scripture proclaims itself divinely inspired are not fit arguments to convince and persuade someone who already denies sacred Scripture's authority.

That does not stop us saying, in another sense, that Scripture proves itself: as the preceding theses showed, sacred Scripture bears many marks and arguments of divinity by which it asserts itself true and divine — just as heaven and earth proclaim and show God as their author, not by a bare spoken claim, but by the excellence of their nature and the traces of divine power and wisdom visible in them.

Or as a book claims Aristotle or Euclid as its author not from the title alone, but from the genius of the teaching, the sharpness of style, and the manner of argument — the sort that can belong only to those rare minds.
